speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
The report of this committee was placed before the House only a day or two ago. It contains a number of recommendations and is somewhat lengthy, and I doubt if hon. members of the House other than those who were members of the committee have had an opportunity to study it carefully. Among the recommendations there is, for example, an important one suggesting the introduction of a superannuation scheme. The report says:
Your committee is of the opinion that the adoption of a superannuation scheme substantially on the lines of that above described would remove one of the greatest deterrents to efficiency and curtailment of stalls in many of the departments of the public service and it therefore recommends that such a scheme be adopted by parliament at the earliest possible date.
In reference to that recommendation I may say that were it contemplated that the House should continue in session for any considerable time the government would be prepared to bring down forthwith a superannuation bill along the lines suggested by the committee. But as there will hardly be time to consider as important legislation as that at the present session, I may say that at the beginning of next session the government will be prepared to present to parliament a bill along the lines of the recommendations made. As to the other recommendations, some of them are of a minor character; some of them require a little more careful consideration, and I think it is only right that the government as well as hon. members should have an oportunity to go into them very thoroughly during the recess. T would not like to say at the moment that they will all be adopted or that any of them will be adopted; the disposition of the government would be to meet the wishes of the committee as far as appears to be in the public interest. With this assurance, Mr. Speaker, I hope my hon. friend will not press his motion for the adoption of the report, but will allow the report to remain on the Table.
Motion withdrawn.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. COPP (Secretary of State):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to return to the order of motions for the purpose of laying a return on the table?
Louder.
Order. The acoustic properties of the House are far better this year than they were last, and I do not see why the members should have to strain their voices to be heard by the House

We cannnot hear at all down here.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Supplementary Estimates, I923-t-Harbours and rivers-Ontario, $2,800,090.06.

I find some astonishing items in this vote, but no worse than practically all the rest of these estimates. I was not here when these estimates were first submitted, but I want to say now that the conduct of the government in submitting estimates of $14,700,000 accompanied by other commitments that aggregate at least $70,000,000 or more, probably $170,000,000 in the last week of the session is an affront to parliament, an affront to the country. To say that it is a blazing violation of their own professions when they were seeking office is, of course, only to repeat what everybody now knows. So bad indeed is it that I understand their own followers not far from here have expressed disgust and resisted their conduct; indeed, cast it out the door. The fact of bringing in estimates of this character and pretending that they can get consideration at the hands of the House when we are a few hours from prorogation, a few days at the most before they ever come down-and those days crowded with legislation the most important of any submitted the whole session, more important than all that the government has submitted to parliament in all the five months of the session-is a reflection of the character of the administration and the way it is serving this country.
I would ask particularly for some statement as to what is to be spent on the second item. The first I do not know just where it is,

but what is to be done in the way of harbour improvements at Belle River?

As the town of Belle River is in the constituency I come from I may take it upon myself to answer the right hon. leader of the Opposition. This is the enly port on that shore of lake St. Clair. It is used at the present time for the distribution of gravel which goes to build the provincial highways and the county roads in this district. Every government for the past twenty years has wasted money on this harbour by attempting to keep it open without putting in any permanent protection. This vote provides for a permanent protection on one side of the harbour. It may be necessary that both sides of the'harbour be permanently protected. If so I am going to advocate doing that work. This locality has been the centre of a fishing industry. And there is a great demand for gravel and sand there. The people of that district are entitled to have this harbour protected, the expenditure is justified in every way, and the total capital invested will pay for itself in two years by the amount of gravel and sand used. Every municipal and provincial purpose in the district will be served by this improvement.

Will the minister tell us just what is intended to be done under this vote? The hon. member for the riding tells us there is to be some protection on one side of the harbour, and that he hopes it will go on to the other side, and that this expenditure will pay. I should like to know just the basis of it. I think we are all the more entitled to know because there has been a recent by-election there, and it is just possible that this vote has some relation to that election. One might almost imagine that, at least. I never had representations made to me as to the business value of this investment, in fact I think I had representations that were quite the contrary-that this is a purely political placing of money in order to take care of political obligations.

I would be very pleased to answer the leader of the Opposition, in fact I am glad he has brought up the subject of the election at this time. We of the locality were delighted to have a visit from the leader of the Opposition. I am sorry, but I think his attitude in regard to this vote represents, perhaps, the disappointment he felt over the result of the election. I am also sorry that the applause my right hon. friend received in this very town of Belle River did not represent the real feeling of the people. When

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
distinguished gentlemen such as the leader of the Opposition visit our locality we attempt to show them every respect; and the party to which my right hon. friend belongs went so far as to hire, or have donated, about twenty-five automobiles. They filled these with political friends and made a tour through the county. If I were to use an expression common in theatrical circles I might say that those who followed the right hon. gentleman on that occasion were professional claqueurs. At any rate I can inform him that the applause he received on his visit to Belle River came from the gentlemen who followed him from the city of Windsor, and other places, and did not emanate from the people of Belle River. Consequently, when the election resulted as it did the right hon. gentleman was disappointed, because he had been received with applause and the vote did not bear out that applause. I also wish to thank the leader of the Opposition for the many speeches he made in this district during the election. He orated, I think, from milkstands and in town halls and in school houses-I do not think he spoke from any bams, but he did speak' from nearly every other description of building in the riding. When I advocated this very vote which was then proposed, for an improvement so urgently needed, he said, I believe, that it was log rolling. I do not like to make that statement, for this reason. During the by-election the leader of the Opposition sought to have the press correct so many statements published about what he said that I am afraid he will call upon me to make a retraction. However, I will leave it to the right hon. gentleman if he did not use that term on the occasion referred to.
What was the term?
" Log rolling."
Very probably I did.

Well, I am awfully glad to get that acknowledgement from you at least. As far as this vote is concerned, the people of this locality are entitled to it. My information is that it makes a breakwater on one side of this harbour and gives eleven or twelve feet of water thus permitting coal to be brought in through the channel, also the sand and gravel needed in the locality which comes in under a contract made with the Dominion government/. I may say that the provincial government insists on sand and gravel being furnished to the people of the locality at a cost of forty or fifty cents a yard less than they can buy it from private individuals. The engineer has
reported on this work, the late representative for the riding was in favour of it, and this expenditure is justified in every way. I will take the responsibility for this vote because I, not the leader of the Opposition, represent the riding. I repeat that it is justified in every way and I am going to insist on it going through.

I am sure the House must have been impressed with the exceedingly argumentative and able presentation of the business value of this investment made by the member for North Essex. He says that I am very much disappointed that this vote is in the estimates. No, I am not disappointed in the least, I fully expected this vote; I had every reason to expect it. Nor was I very much disappointed in the result. I wonder if the hon. member feels that a great tribute was paid the government of the day by the vote in North Essex. I am not usually in the habit of arguing that election results are a reason against any public action. I leave that to those who can find no real reasons; but when the hon. member for North Essex-
I understood you to say that this was a political appropriation.

Yes, and I will show a little reason for that in a moment. I leave the mere boasting of votes to those who are not competent to advance any other argument. But when a majority is reduced from 7,195 to about 1,000 it takes a pretty selfsatisfied representative to initiate the subject himself in the Commons as a matter of selfcongratulation. No, I am not disappointed in this vote being introduced. When I used the word "political" I used the most euphemistic adjective I could think of. During the campaign the promise of a vote of this kind wa,s the chief argument on behalf of the hon. member. Indeed, I can recall no other. As for correcting press misrepresentations, the correction I made was against the Minister of Finance and I made it out of a Liberal paper. The report of the Liberal newspaper of Windsor was right but the Minister of Finance was all wrong. He based his statement on some contortion appearing in the Globe from the Canadian Press, and I have in my office an apology from the Canadian Press for making a wrong report. So much for that. What has that to do with the proposition?
Hear, hear.

I hope the hon. member takes the castigation that these "hear, hears" imply.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
You started the political discussion.

Yes, and I intend to end it. I hold in my hand a poster containing the announcement of this harbour improvement. This is the first of the literary efforts of the hon. gentleman's friends in regard to this marked achievement at the expense of the taxpayer. I will read it:
Vote for Healey and get
$86,000 Gov. Docks and Breakwater $25,000 Waterworks
Free gift from James Cooper.
$75,000 Brick and Tile Yard
to employ 30 hands the year round.
Vote for Robinson and get nothing but hot air.
King needs Tim; so do you.
Tim and King-that is the thing.
This is worth repeating. Of course it is illegal and it is a violation of the law which this government is sworn to obey; published without a statement as to who publishes it, but it is published on behalf of the member, by the man whose name appears here, and who is chief henchman in the riding. Everyone knows who he is. Everyone knows what he did to elect the hon. member and all about it.
Vote for Heals- and get $S6,000 government docks.
The note is maturing now and the country is paying for it.
And the breakwater; and the 825,000 waterworks-when that is to come is a matter, of [DOT] course, in the hands of the gods-and, I suppose, of Tim. The information I have- and it comes from the people of Belle River- is that this is utterly worthless, that it is chiefly for the personal benefit of the man who got out the dodger and for the political benefit of the representative of the riding. This vote is brought down the last few days of the session. I have a letter, which I will have here shortly, which deals with this matter. It is dated the 24th March, just a few days after the election, and states that the Liberals are now boasting that a vote of-I forget how many thousand dollars-will be in the estimates, but not in the main estimates. It will be held for the supplementaries, in order to carry out this pledge to the people, held till the last few days of the session so as to be jammed through in the dying moments, because "King needs Tim; Tim and King, that is the thing."
It would be interesting to have that letter read.

I had it here a day or two ago, thinking this matter would come

up then. I will get the letter; the hon. member need not worry. And I have two or three others. This is no worse than the rest of the administration of this government. It is just of a piece with all the rest. This is how they purpose to carry these estimates, with appropriations of the money of the people of Canada, looking to the by-elections that will probably be held this summer. I have often wondered what it is going to cost the Dominion to provide a Liberal successor for the prospective judge of the Exchequer Court? This is part of the cost of having this House adorned by the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Healy). The information I have-and I believe it is correct-is from citizens of the town, that this is chiefly for the benefit of the man who got out the dodger and for his business and in pursuance of his pledge, contained in an illegal dodger, to elect illegally the hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
The records
of the Department of Public Works show that my right hon. friend is very unjust to the member for North Essex. The record here shows that this matter was first brought to the attention of the Department of Public Works during the lifetime of the late lamented Hon. Mr. Kennedy by a resolution dated 7th April, 1922, of the municipal council of the township of Rochester, concurring with the village of Belle River and other municipalities re the urgency of the Belle River improvements. Later there was a letter from the Reeve of Belle River stating:
That- this is the only place on North shore of Essex county which could be made fit for a port and is the logical place for distribution of coal, gravel, etc., resulting in a saving of $5 a ton on coal.
Could the hon. member give the House any information of the chief article that is included in the word " etc."?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I am reading from the representations which were made by the reeve of Belle River-and I take it that that gentleman is a man of responsibility, and that the municipal council of the township of Rochester, who verify what the reeve of Belle River says, are also responsible. I think this House, recalling the late Minister of Railways who promoted this matter long before there was any election to fill the vacancy occasioned by his lamented death, will hardly credit my right hon. friend with all he says as to the reason of the vote being due to the by-election. The reeve of Belle River stated:
A tile and brick yard is building which will use 2,000 tons of coal a year, in addition to other in-

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
dustries. It would re-establish the local fleet of sand boats which used to operate from here and have had to lie idle on account of the mouth of the river filling up.
The record shows that this little discussion about the North Essex by-election had no relation whatever to the consideration of this question by the Department of Public Works. The local municipality of Belle River, and the municipal council of which it formed a part, and the late Hon. Mr. Kennedy, had been pressing this matter, on the Department of Public Works, on behalf of the locality and the constituency, long before the death of the late minister.
Is it a dock or a piece of a dock? Or what is it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I should
have thought my right hon. friend ought to have known a little more about it before he denounced everybody indiscriminately.
I just know what is here. I am asking what the vote is for.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I will give the hon. member the information, if he will wait and forget there was a hand-bill and a North Essex election.
I will not forget it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
One of the troubles of my right hon. friend is that he belongs to that school of people known as the Bourbons. The work here is:
To construct 1,500 lineal feet double sheet pile wall, consisting of double three-inch sheeting for the length of 1,000 feet, and double 4-inch sheeting for the length of 500 feet, sheeting to be from eight to twenty feet in length, securely walled to round piles on each side of sheeting placed at 5-foot centres; also seven round pile stone filled cribs, 18 feet by 18 feet in area.
The memo I have reads:
The original estimated cost of this work was $72,500, the sheet pile wall being estimated at $60,000 sufficient to provide for an ultimate depth in the channel of 18 feet; but after further consideration it was decided that a wall to provide for the maintenance of a 10-foot channel would meet the requirements for some time to come at the above greatly reduced cost.
Perhaps the minister could tell us whether the merchandise which comes in under the heading " etc." comes in by motor boat.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I am not versed as to the Ontario Temperance Act operation or matters of that kind. Perhaps my hon. friend would know more about that.
I do not live there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I am giving to the House the information from the Department of Public Works coming from sources I have indicated, and this is to justify the expenditure which has been made there. Everyone is aware of the movement of the sand and the important business that has grown up in gravel alone lake St, Clair.
I am free to say that the record I have, showing the representations made by responsible people in the constituency and the efforts of the late Hon. Mr. Kennedy to have this matter dealt with before he departed, is so clear that it cannot be doubted.
I understand from what my hon. friend says, that the basis of this appropriation is representations made by the former member, the Hon. Mr. Kennedy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
And the
reeve of Belle River and the municipal council.

Who joined with him in those representations, as I understand the matter. What possible excuse is there for this delay? We were told before that the reason why these supplementaries were bought down now was that there was no time to include them in the Main Estimates. Now we have something which, on the confession of the minister, is old, hoary, with nothing at all done recently to draw it to the attention of the government. The only excuse and reason for the late date of these supplementaries is that the matter could not be considered before. The government, on their own showing and their own admission, show that they have deliberately delayed the submission of this appropriation for the purpose of these supplementaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Might I add a word of comment on the first part of the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen)? He said that it is an affront to parliament and the Canadian people to bring down estimates of this character at this late stage. I wonder if the word "effrontery" is a matter of parliamentary privilege. I am afraid it is not, and therefore I shall have to substitute a more moderate word. If I were not so familiar with the methods of my right hon. friend in dealing with public questions in this House, I would be amazed at the audacity of the statement he made to-day. The right hon. gentleman waxed indignant in the words he uttered to-day, and he repeated what he said a few days before in the evening when these estimates came down. 'He said "I

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
would like the minister to tell where in the history of Canada"-a pretty large story- "estimates of that magnitude were ever brought down in the last week of the session." If my right hon. friend had been here last night, he would have had the information which he apparently had neglected to obtain. He is indignant because we in these last days of the session have brought down estimates of $15,000,000. In the last session of the government of my right hon. friend, the session of 1921, and in the last week of that session, to use the very words he used, they brought down estimates of $23,000,000. At that time the Main Estimates were not all through the House, but that point is not important. According to the records, the message was brought down on a Monday, but, as a matter of fact, it was brought down in the email hours of Tuesday morning, according to my information, and the House prorogued on Saturday. They used all the machinery to Growd those estimates through the House. What can the country think of the right hon. gentleman who, in parliament, is virtuously indignant because we bring down estimates amounting to $15,000,000, and who challenges anybody to show anything of the kind in the history of Canada, when the record shows that he brought down in the last week of the session of 1921 estimates amounting to $23,000,000. It is things like this which prevent the public from having confidence in the statements of the right hon. gentleman. It is his utterly reckless manner of discussing public affairs which has tended to discredit him and to put him in the position which he now occupies.
Let me again repeat what the Prime Minister (Mr. Makenzie King) said the other day. There is no desire to rush these estimates through. If this House desires time to consider them, time shall be given, so far as the government is concerned. There will be no closure to crowd these estimates through, there will 'be no coercion-nothing that is not consistent with the principles of sound parliamentary government and free discussion. But when the right hon. gentleman indignantly challenges anyone to show when, in the history of all Canada, a government had brought down estimates of this magnitude in the last week of a session, and I point out the fact that, in the last week of the session of 1921, he brought down estimates amounting to $23,000,000, I think the right hon. gentleman will come to the conclusion that, perhaps, he had better think before he speaks.

Oh, oh.
[Mr. Fielding.)

I would like to wait until hon. gentlemen have a good chance to get this off their chests, because they will get a rude disappointment in a moment. When I spoke the other day as I spoke to-day, I referred to all the government was committing the country to this last week.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. His challenge was: " When did a government bring down Supplementary Estimates like this in the last week?"

I do not think we ever did. Those estimates were nothing like the length of these, nor were the commitments of the last week of that session a fraction of what this government has brought down this last week. The minister himself is responsible for coming to this House and keeping out of the estimates, an amount which, I believe, will run to over $100,000,000. He brings this down in the last week of the session, and merely because it is in separate bills, he says that it is not estimates. The conduct of the minister, instead of being more to be commended on that account, is on that very account the most discreditable to a government in the history of our country. This government this week is down, in the dying hours of the session, with commitments that will run to $150,000,000 to this Dominion-commitments so preposterous that his own followers, not far from him, some of them the most loyal he ever had, have cast them ignominiously out of the door. That is where the government stands. What does the minister think of this kind of conduct? The minister says: " Oh, you have plenty of time; we are in no hurry." In the last week of 1921, I stood as Prime Minister and told the House that all the time the House wanted would be given to consider the estimates we had, and that was all we had. There was no closure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There was.
I do not think there was.
There were sittings all night.
Yes, there were sittings all night, but I am satisfied they were not on the, estimates. That does not matter anyway; there was plenty of time given for consideration of the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The vote for the Merchant Marine was put through under closure.
That was not an estimate.

Oh, oh.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
It was not a supplementary estimate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It represented an expenditure of $70,000,000.

It was in the Main
Estimates. The question was considered for days, and there was no hurry whatever. Hon. members stood up and asked us to put on the closure. That was what they were asking for. That was what they were keeping us all night for. It was the greatest bluff that was ever put up. During the last week of that session I said that all the time wanted would be given for the consideration of what was brought down, and there was not a fraction or, at least, only a small fraction, of the commitments that1 this governlment has brought down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Did not the right hon. gentleman each evening resist strenuously the request of the opposition to adjourn at twelve o'clock, so that time might be given for proper discussion of the estimates? Did he not keep the House in session until the early hours of the morning, refusing any opportunity to consider them?
Has this government not kept us sitting until the early hours of the morning?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, it has not.
This House has sat in the m6rning time and time again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The House
this session, and last, has not sat past eleven o'clock a single night without the consent of every member; and during the discussion of estimates, the minute there has been a request that the House should adjourn, and if there has been any indication that that was the wish of hon. members, the House has adjourned.

I am prepared to admit that the opposition has been much more reasonable than was the opposition of that day. The opposition of that day kept the talk going merely in order that they might force closure if they possibly could, and even in certain cases they got up and asked for it. That was the character of the opposition then, and I do not see that there has been much improvement now that those of that opposition have come into power.
On this estimate, in reply to the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), who did not think I had the letter, I will read now from a letter I have from a private citizen of Belle River. This is dated the 24th March, the date I gave the House.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Who signed it?
I stated that it was a private letter.
Oh, oh.

Some hon. members
think it would be of great value to know the name. Do they think I have not the letter?
Surely under the rules of the House an hon. member may not read part of a letter, which he makes public by the reading, and then say that the rest is private.
He can.
He might by following the example of some of my right hon. friend's followers in Toronto. But it is a rule of the House that any document from which a quotation is made must be laid on the Table.

There is a rule, which I think my hon. friend has been in the House long enough to know, that if a member of the government quotes from a government document that document must be laid upon the Table. There is no rule that every member must divulge the name of a private citizen 'because he wishes to read from any letter written by such a person. Even if he quotes from the letter he is at liberty to divulge the name or not, as he sees fit, and that principle has been acted on time and time again.
The hon. member knows better than that.

I know that what I have stated is absolutely correct. However, I have no particular objection to disclosing the name if I can obtain the consent of the writer to do so. But I will not give the name until I do obtain that consent.

I am not objecting to the fact that my hon. friend does not give the name. I do object, however, as I think I have a right to object, to his making public *a part of a letter which he says is private and 'asking us to fake it for granted that the letter is from some citizen.

Would the hon. member be good enough to recall the incident? I did not say I was going to read from the letter until the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) inquired whether I had it, suggesting, I think, that I read from it. Now I am only answering his challenge.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Apart from the point of order, which I do not raise, does my right



Supply-Harbours and Rivers
hon. friend not admit that the force of a letter must be drawn from the signature? And if the right hon. gentleman reads a private letter-his right to do which I am not questioning

surely he must realize that no one will pay respectful attention to it if its source is concealed.

It is not very material to me whether I read the letter or not, but when I am challenged by an hon. member to read it and I am ready to do so it does seem strange, to say the least, that the same hon. gentlemen should raise an objection. However, I think the country will draw the same inference from the objection as it would draw from the letter, if I read it.
The most important part of the letter would be the signature of the person who wrote it. It might have been dictated to an office boy, or an office boy might have written to the hon. gentleman.

The signature appears on the letter; there is no doubt about that; and I have so much respect for it that I am ready to disclose the name to my hon. friend. These are some of the words it contains:
The Liberals here seem confident that a government dock will be built at Belle River this year, and state that the cost of same is to be included in the Supplemental Estimates.
The date of the letter is March 24, 1923. I have further communications to the effect that while some dredging, so as to allow a certain depth, could be justified, the work the government contemplates cannot be justified on any business ground whatever.
Are they signed?

They are signed, just as all letters are signed. I thought -the hon. gentleman had attained a business eminence that would have acquainted him with that fact. Now, -this is merely the payment of a political debt.
Anyone could write letters of that kind.

I will move that the vote be reduced by $30,000. The fact that the debt is a fulfilment of a bribe is sufficient to nullify it in the judgment of the House. The hon. minister (Mr. Macdonald) says that someone wrote about the matter before the election. I do not doubt that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Pardon me; I did not say that someone wrote about it before the election. I stated that this municipality had passed a resolution concerning the matter and that there was a communication

from the reeve of the municipality on the same subject. I further pointed out that the late Hon. Mr. Kennedy, for over a year before he departed this life, had been dealing with the question with the Public Works department. The committee will see how my hon. friend argues. He said that I made the statement that someone had written about the matter before the election. What I said was precisely what I have just stated.

Some one had written; the reeve, I think, wrote about the matter. The minister states that a resolution was passed by the municipal council, and that is the justification for going on with the work. Well, you can get resolutions of council for anything; and anyone who publishes a poster such as the one I have read, and has the ingenuity of the man that did it. can engineer such a resolution, even if it is to his own advantage to have the money spent in the municipality that passes the resolution. What I note is that the only commitment made was made when the by-election was on. There was no commitment made by the Hon. Mr. Kennedy; it was made as a bribe at the time of the by-election.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Not at all.
And the bribe is now being paid. I shall move that the item be reduced by $30,000.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
On this
question my right hon. friend is speaking recklessly. The evidence points conclusively to the fact that the matter was initiated the same as any other public work of importance in any locality originates. It was first dealt with by the local authorities over a year ago, and I can inform the committee that there had been improvements at Belle River, but owing to a movement of the sand
12 noon the proposed wall extension became imperative. The municipality considered the matter and it was placed before the late Mr. Kennedy long before there was any probability of his death or the possibility of any by-election. There is some question that this matter should have been brought down in the Main Estimates. The Main Estimates were laid on the Table immediately after the opening of the session, on the 1st of February, and the death of Mr. Kennedy did not occur until after that date, so that the by-election did not take place until March. Let me read what the engineer reports:
Wall extension proposed is of a public nature. Local municipality wishes to have entrance channel

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
redredged and proposed protection work constructed to permit bringing in coal, lumber and building materials, the carrying on and development of fishing industry and the taking out of sugar beets by water to Wallaceburg and Chatham. They have also asked for proposed extension to wrest pier to prevent the prevailing westerly winds from filling up bar across entrance to channel. New brick and tile works under construction and to be placed in operation at this point.
This shows why, beyond all question, the Department of Public Works took the matter into consideration. Having gone through the various reports touching these items, I am struck forcibly by this fact, that in these estimates there is no item behind which there is such an accumulation of evidence to establish an independent interest in behalf of the municipal and local authorities as in the case of this particular item. My hon. friend cannot forget that there was an election in North Essex or that bills were posted in that campaign, and for that reason we have had this exhibition this morning.
What was the date of the engineer's report?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I have not the exact date; it is not in the record. The deputy tells me it would be about two months ago.

Really the merits of this
vote have been lost sight of in the political discussion that has arisen upon it. The first knowledge I had of any vote, or of any work proposed at Belle River, came to me one night when I was attending a meeting there. I was confronted with the engineer's report and a letter written by the late Minister of Railways in which statements were made that the people of the district were desirous that the work should be gone on with; and the vote mentioned in the poster was $86,000. I made the statement that any promise made by the late Minister of Railways would be carried out so far as my influence could bring about this end. I made that statement then and I stand by it now. And this is the only opportunity I had of getting anything placed in the estimates, because I was not elected until the first of March. The letters with reference to this matter are contained in the files of the Public Works department and if my right hon. friend wishes to secure the information he can consult them. He can see the letters written by the late Minister of Railways as well as the report of the engineer and that of the municipality. The vote is entirely justifiable. It may be true that the handbill was circulated in the district, but I
want to tell the leader of the Opposition that it was the first circular I had ever seen.
I have some others.

I heard that such a circular was published, and the wording of it follows the wording of a circular that was used extensively by the leader of the Opposition. There is no doubt in my mind that the gentleman who wrote the circular considered that, while the effect would be different in this case, the phraseology was quite appropriate.
Now, I am not responsible for that circular. As a matter of fact the whole proposition comes from a squabble between two gentlemen who lived in Belle River, two gentlemen, I believe, who got into trouble between themselves over a shipment of goods that came into Belle River. One gentleman happens to be a strong Liberal; the other happens to be a strong Conservative. That is the secret of the whole thing. That accounts for the letters being produced. That accounts for this poor little vote for the poor little town of Belle River, which happens to be in the north riding of Essex, being attacked by the right hon. leader of the Opposition. A local political squabble, and it is brought up here at this time. The vote is justified; the people are entitled to it. They have been recognized by every government of this country for twenty years, but it is the first time that an intelligent effort has been made to put money where it belongs, where it will make a permanent improvement at a small cost, thus avoiding the expenditure of large amounts each year on dredging. This expenditure has been reduced from $86,000 to $30,000 at my own insistence. I conferred with the engineer and with the people of the district, and decided that a breakwater costing this amount would do the work as well as a larger expenditure. Any member of the House who knows the locality, or who would agree to visit the locality, would come to the same conclusion.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
Let me recall the facts. The large items were loans to the railways, $75,000,000 and so forth. It will be remembered that those were the cases in which my hon. friends opposite used to make their great speeches against public ownership. When these items were up during the session they took occasion to harangue against the disastrous character of public ownership, and for days and nights they kept this hall ringing with denunciations and the scandal of putting $75,000,000 in the estimates for this public ownership that was going to ruin Canada and bring it to the brink of bankruptcy-yea, push it over the precipice. By such speeches they held up the estimates all the session, and then at the last-with their own consent the same as in any other case-[DOT] those estimates had to go through; there was no closure applied. What relation on earth, all this has to the subject we are discussing to-day-I am entirely at a loss to understand.

I will not discuss the remarks of the leader of the Opposition in regard to public ownership at the present time. An occasion will come probably, before the House closes, to point out who really are the enemies of public ownership in endeavouring at every step to wreck the Canadian National Railways.
Oh, oh.

The right hon. gentleman referred to "another place." I wiil not make any reference to it I will only say that I am surprised that the right hon. gentleman has such intimate knowledge of what is going to go on over there.

I did not, at any stage,
make a reference to what was going to go on, I referred only to what had gone on.

I think it had. I was
so informed; perhaps I was wrongly informed.
I was informed it had been done on the motion of a Liberal Senator. ,

There was a motion made in another chamber last night by the leader of my right hon. friend's party in the Senate for the six months' hoist for a certain bill, but unless' the vote was taken a few moments after the House met this morning the matter was still undecided. However the facts as to that will develop in time. I wish to suggest to the committee that we get back to this item. I want to say this with respect to any

circulars that were issued: I suppose there is not a party represented in this House but has at some time or other issued such circulars. I remember some beautiful illustrations on the bill boards in the last general election containing my right hon. friend's physiog., and an inscription stating that the country would be wrecked if he did not stay at the helm.
-"Arthur will lead us through."

Yes. "Let Arthur do it". This is not a new work at Belle River. Up to this date $28,000 has been expended in keeping the harbour at Belle River open. Those who understand the situation will know that that vicinity is a flat country, almost on a level with lake St. Clair. Belle river runs in from the lake. Consequently in that entrance to the harbour up into the river there is constant silting, which has to be dredged practically every year. The proposition made now will be an economic one, to my mind, to put up a protection wall along the side of the channel and dredge it out, in the hope that this protection wall will do away with the necessity of an annual grant, which both sides of the House have been giving for years, to keep the channel open. As to coal and other commodities which are used and handled there, the desire is to make the channel deep enough to take a boat of a fifteen-foot draft. That is the whole story, and it is absolutely defensible. It will be an annual saving instead of being an annual grant to keep this channel clear.
I am not going to discuss the question of the election. I suppose even in Grenville there may have been some discussions. I have no doubt that it was said that when the Welland canal was finished they would have the elevators at Prescott. But I want to point out that one of the things impressed on me-* and I urged strongly to have it go into the estimates-by my predecessor in office was this very item, and before he went South he handed me a memorandum of this item to have it put in the estimates, stating that it was absolutely necessary for Belle River. If there had been no election and our late lamented friend had not been called away-and nobody ever dreamed of the sad occurrence that necessitated the by-election-the item would have been in the estimates just the same. This item can be defended on the ground of utility and economy.

My hon. friend's party
adopts the "Holier than thou" attitude.

We can deal with my hon.
friend some other time. We are not at all afraid. It may seem presumptuous for some members who have not been in parliament very long to make a few remarks and compel some of those of superior wisdom to keen quiet during the time we have the floor. We are very much enlightened by the remarks which come from these quarters. I
do not know if I understand just exactly whether this is a proper item or not. It has been said that dredging has been carried on year after year. Now, if the government has been incurring this expense for years, and if this vote will obviate that expenditure in the future, I think it should pass. I am anxious-and I know the members behind me are anxious-to do what is right in this matter. I will confess that the quotations made by the Prime Minister a few moments ago were something of an eye-opener to me, in regard to passing these large sums of money in the closing days of the session. But that does not make it right. I think it is bad practice and should be discontinued as far as possible. At the same time I think I will have to vote for the appropriation in this particular case.

I think, perhaps, the item
sinks into relative insignificance compared with the principle, or the lack of it, which has just been enunciated by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). On many occasions in this House we have been treated to declarations by the hon. member, and by some of the members of his party that the two old parties, not venerable at all because of their age, were absolutely worn out, and that we must look to these members to give us a lead and direction, and-shall I say-an uplift, in matters of public life. Yet we are read another lecture this morning, and we are told that matters which have been discussed are matters of utter indifference to this would-be great party. If there is anything in the matter bqing discussed this morning it is the question of whether the expenditures made by this parliament should be dictated by necessity and by principle, or whether the moneys of this Dominion should be flagrantly and openly used for the debauching of a particular constituency. And the hon. member for Brandon is utterly indifferent to such a thing as that. He refers to the two old parties and says that he will take no part in what he terms the squabble between those parties. If that be his attitude and the attitude of his party, he need not be at all surprised that the public is treating that party just in the way that that party deserved to be treated, in proportion to its hypocrisy with regard to the needs of .public life. If debauchment is a matter of indifference to this party, if they care not whether expenditures are right or wrong, if they see no principle or lack of principle, if they will not rise and condemn a violation of principle in public life, what shrift can they expect from the electors who sent them here

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
to represent the higher principle of driving these errors of the two old parties out of public life?
What my hon. friend wants to know is only this, not whether this wharf is to be used for bootlegging or for some suspicious boat or boats to be tied up to, but where it will be located and how much it will cost. It is a matter of utter indifference to him whether it is applied to a constituency or not. As he speaks in the name of his party, so may he expect his party to be judged by the electorate of Canada-and the handwriting is pretty plain upon the wall at the present day. You have been "weighed in the balances and found wanting." You have lickspittled to the government through the whole of one session and part of another, and you have traded upon the rights of the rest of Canada. You have got what you could; you have got your small pittance, and in the hour of your disappointment you say to the people of Canada: "These matters in connection with the two old parties are of no interest to me." It is not a new road in the West; it is not a question of grain rates; it is only a violation of public principles, only a lowering 01 the standard of national honour

and these things are all matters of indifference to the men of the great, boundless sweep of the prairies.

I said that I
wanted to ask a question with regard to this item. We were told that there was a recommendation for some large sum of money. This item is for only $30,000. I should like to have it clearly stated what the estimate was on the recommendation made by the engineers.

Admitted

Might I be permitted to
ask a question? I am afraid the hon. gentleman misunderstood me. I have known for some time that the leader ot fhe Opposition (Mr. Meighen) had in his possession a circular which he proposed to use at an opportune moment. I have never seen the circular. I had heard that circulars were issued, but this is the first time I have ever seen it or heard it read. Whether it was issued by a friend of mine or by an enemy, I do not know. But I do know that the leading Conservative of Belle River and the gentleman who is mentioned in the circular got into a personal row over a shipment of a cargo of beer into that locality. Probably the gentleman whose letter has been produced here to-day, but whose name has not been given to us, is the man. I am not prepared to say. There is a circular, the only one I have ever seen. Whether it was issued by a friend or an enemy, 1 do not know. It is in print and there is no signature to it.

I do not know what the hon. gentleman interrupted me for. His interruption was certainly not to ask a question. What I said was that he said he had not seen this circular, and I did not know how he could dodge seeing it. He says that he does not know whether it was printed by a friend or an enemy. Let me tell him that it is printed by his friend, Mr. James Cooper.
And paid for.

How does the
right hon. gentleman know that?

It is printed. I do not propose to be drawn away from what is a real matter of public moment, and that is this: Does this government that wants to enforce the law, propose to be a party to this kind of illegal treatment and illegal practice? It is admittedly illegal. Or does the government intend to argue that this poster is legal? The government cannot do that; it knows that this is illegal. I will assume for the minute that it would be quite impossible to expect this government to enforce the law against its friends-let us assume that that will be too high a standard altogether to expect from this government, and that the law as against one of its friends will never be enforced. Let us go a step further. Is

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
this government of the view that public moneys ought to be voted by it for the purpose of implementing a corrupt election practice? That is the grave question to which we want an answer. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that he had never seen a greater scandal than what went on in former years when votes were being put through. I think the scandal consists rather in what is being done than in the amount of business that is being performed. I would ask my hon. friend if he could find in any of those votes consideration for value received, for goods delivered, for votes purchased? "King needs Tim'-So do you. Tim' and King, that's the thing." "Tim" is the first in this wonderful organization.
Quite a good organization.

They are delivering the goods, I admit. "Tim" starts the thing, but "King" is the man who is now supplying the money which enables this thing to be done. Hon. gentlemen say something about other circulars. They know that has absolutely nothing to do with the question. They know there can be honest circulars; they know there can be dishonest circulars which affront every single principle of our election law. It is cheap, easy, to refer to circulars, placards, of my right hon. friend adorning fences and that sort of thing. There was absolutely nothing wrong in that. No bribe was offered in any of those. We were not trying to bribe the electorate, nor did we.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen laugh. They think it is a matter for laughter that their party and their name can be associated with direct illegal promises, with direct bribes; and when anyone tries to say anything in connection with the matter, he is to be met with laughter, which is the only argument that can be advanced against a criminal proceeding.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question? Does he honestly say that that is what we are laughing at?

I do not know what my hon. friend could not or would not laugh at. He laughs when he thinks that will serve any party advantage. I do not know how many of them are real laughs and how many are forced laughs or laughs of another character.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: What kind is my hon. friend's laugh?
This, of course, is the only sort of argument.
The laugh that "speaks the vacant mind."

Then there must be an awful lot of rooms to let over there. The government is responsible for the proper conduct of public business; it is responsible for the enforcement of Dominion legislation. Have hon. gentlemen no sense of decency loft at all? When the result of this purely, absolutely, admittedly, illegal thing is brought to their attention it is met by bursts of laughter displaying the "vacant minds" which the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) alludes to. Is that their idea of public decency? The Prime Minister talks about "scandal." Well, he is exhibiting the biggest kind of scandal; he is showing that the government are prepared to implement corrupt promises by votes.
