Supply-Public Works
When we have asked for public buildings in various districts in Canada, we have been met with the objection that the country was poor and could not afford it. The people wanted some buildings in my riding, and I think other districts were in the same position, but they were put aside owing to the war. Large sums have been voted, but the construction was delayed owing to the war. If the policy of the government is to start a new programme now, and commence to erect public buildings in very unimportant places, I think the House should know it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Unless the necessities of the district require the building, it is not the policy of the government, except in exceptional cases, to indulge in the erection of any new buildings. But hon. members will recall the terrible fire that took place at Terrebonne last winter; they will remember that the town and all the facilities for carrying on the public affairs, post office and customs, were destroyed, and at present they have no building. In such a case the government feel it is only right the building should be replaced in order to enable the community to do business.
The whole town was swept out of existence-

Resolution agreed to.
Public buildings-Ontario, $316,400.
One item here is "Hailey-bury-Armoury and post office 335,000." Surely this government is not building a new armoury?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The town of Haileybury suffered from a disastrous fire. The building was insured, and we are simply taking insurance money to replace the buildings. There are no other new buildings.
It was insured by the municipality.
Does the committee decide by the majority vote to take the estimates item by item, or otherwise?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.
Then I move that these estimates be taken item by item.

That point was decided yesterday. The hon. member was not in the House yesterday, but that was not the fault of the committee. I do not see that we should reverse our decision simply because the hon. member did not see fit to attend the sessions of the committee yesterday.
However, I am willing to stay here till September.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not know that the decision yesterday would bind the committee during all its sessions. It was simply decided to adopt that course yesterday.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I have no objection to the motion.
The hon. member stayed away yesterday, but returns to-day and objects to these items being taken in the manner we decided yesterday.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The Chairman will read each item, and if the hon. member wants any information in regard to an item as we go along, I will be delighted to give it to him. If any new expenditures are being inaugurated, it is only right and proper that they should be discussed. In the case of simple repairs, which have all been reported upon by the permanent engineers of the department, it seems to me that no good purpose will be served by going over them all. I hope the hon. member will adopt my suggestion.

With
regard to the armouries and post office at Haileybury, I may inform the committee that practically about all that is asked for in this $35,000 vote is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1,000. If you consider interest on $33,000 since the 10th of last October up to the present time, it will bring the amount close to $34,000, or about that sum. The armouries in Haileybury have been rented. It seems that the Public Works department or the Militia department do not rent their buildings, but they give them on the understanding that they shall be insured. The people of Haileybury were insuring these buildings any time they got the use of them for tombolas, dances or other entertainments, and they found it was expensive to insure them by the day-or night-or by the week. The board of trade and city council got together and decided to take out a yearly insurance. They placed $33,000 on the armouries, and about two months after the insurance had been effected the armouries were burned. Immediately afterwards, about the 10th October, the money was turned into the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and all they are asking here is practically $1,000, in conjunction with their own money and interest to build a post office and put a roof on the armouries; so that they will be available for use.
Supply-Public Works

I do not think that is quite a fair statement of the situation. I do not pretend to know the conditions at Haileybury, or whether the armouries are needed or not. I never had very much sympathy with this talk about nothing being needed in military expenditure because of the League of Nations and because the last war was fought. That never appealed to me. It appealed more to hon. members of the government.

Would
the hon. member be in favour of voting $1,000 to the people who have been burned out and lost everything they owned there, so as to provide them with a post office, leaving out the question of the armouries?
I am not saying whether the vote is right or wrong. I do not think the statement of the hon. member was an exact statement of the facts.
Why?

The fact that the armoury has been burned does not make the insurance money the property of the people of the district. It is the property of the people of Canada. It may be the insurance premium was paid as and by way of rental for the building, for the privilege of using it, because the danger of fire is greater in that case. That is the usual practice. That does not establish any claim on the insurance money. What we are deciding is whether we should erect the building. I am not objecting to that, but I do not want the hon. member's statement that it is the money of the district to go unchallenged.

If it had not been insured the government would not have got anything, and we should have been asked to vote this money just the same; but in the Militia department they endeavour to exact the protection of the public building by asking those who use it to insure. In this case the armoury was being used continually by the people of Haileybury. They carried the insurance and it did not cost the government anything. In the vote of this amount of money, we just place our building, with the insurance money, where it was before, and put up an armoury more suitable to Haileybury. It must be remembered that Haileybury was wiped out. I received a cheque for the insurance myself and handed it in to the Receiver General.

I do not think any one is disputing the receipt of the cheque. My hon. friend is buying some new building

in Ottawa. Where is it? We start with $26,000. The item is:
Ottawa-towards purchase of building for government work shops, $26,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: While the hon. minister is looking up that information, does the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) desire to have his motion put to the committee, that we should deal with these estimates item by item while they are being passed?

I was interrupted. I was going to speak again on that matter. I am sorry I was not present yesterday, but I do not understand that the vote was that all the contents of these pages should be voted in a lump sum. I thought it referred only to certain specified blocks of items. If I was misinformed, and if this committee and all the component parts of it agreed to a general principle of putting through the items, I shall have to abide by that decision. But it seems to me a very foolish kind of decision, if I may say so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I call the hon. member's attention to the fact that each numbered item is a vote made up of certain parts, any one of which, or the whole item, can be debated, and amendments introduced.

If we had had time to go
through these lists carefully and to mark those items that we wished to take up, the situation would be different. As .it is, we are considering this very largely for the first time; and at the rate at which you read, it is pretty hard to form any adequate understanding of what is in one of these blocks of, maybe, twenty-five items. Very little longer time will be consumed if we take each item by itself, and if there is no objection, let it go through. If, however, the committee has come to a decision, I shall have to abide by the consequences.
While we are considering this as a bulk vote, that does not prevent any hon. gentleman from discussing any item in the vote to his entire satisfaction.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Good) claims that he has not had time to read the item. I would suggest that in order to make progress, we might suspend proceedings for about ten minutes, in order to give him an opportunity to read it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
The workshops in connection with the Public Works department in Ottawa have been reported on by the foreman of heating and plumbing, the assistant mechanical engineer and the

Supply-Pubhc TTorfcs
junior mechanical engineer, as being absolutely unsanitary, and having conditions which have resulted in illness to the employees who work therein. Recommendations have been made to the department that they should obtain a building known as the Wine Vault building on George street, for government workshops in place of the Harris and Campbell building at the corner of Queen and O'Connor streets.

What is meant by
"government workshops?" What kind of work is carried on?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Carpenters,
plumbers, masons-all men of that character who are employed, I understand, permanently in connection with carrying on all the repairs of this building and every other public building in Ottawa belonging to the government.

Who is the
owner of the building?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Labelle & Brule.

What is the
assessed value of the property?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I do not
think we have that here. Negotiations have not been closed.
Has the government not a large number of buildings on Wellington street which are at present unoccupied?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I am going to take that matter up in a moment. *

Why are we
voting this money to purchase another building when we already have buildings unoccupied?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will remember that a plan of a most comprehensive character was prepared a number of years ago. If he looks at item No. 490, he will see that it reads:
Ottawa-new departmental buildings-compensation to architects for designs submitted, $30,001).
Hon. gentlemen are, perhaps, aware that a large tract of property running from the Supreme Court in a northwesterly direction along Wellington street was expropriated a number of years ago by the government. It was planned that there should be erected, in place of those old buildings which are very dilapidated, a series of permanent buildings where all the departments might be housed, instead of having them as they are to-day, in rented buildings scattered throughout Ottawa.
294J
In 1912, the then government asked for competition among architects for the submission of plans and designs for buildings that would cover that particular part of the city, so as to carry out the idea of the then government. Owing to the war and the financial conditions that followed, all proceedings in connection with those plans were abandoned. Until the country is in a position to carry on a comprehensive plan for dealing with the situation, it is the policy of the government not to spend any money in connection with it. I am instructed by the departmental officers that reports are on file in the department, having regard to the health of the men employed in the present workshops, as to the impossibility of their carrying on under present conditions. This building is situated in the immediate vicinity of and convenient to the Hunter building where the present offices are. The whole matter has been reported upon and recommended by the officials.

The minister
himself shows that nothing is being done with the large plan. There are some very good buildings on the site. I do not think that the Minister of Finance is of opinion that we ought to embark on that large and expensive plan for many years. Why .could we not use some of our own property and stop buying property that we do not require?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The deputy minister advises me that all buildings there suitable for present governmental purposes are occupied and used by other departments.

Will this amount be
sufficient to buy the building?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: No.

Is this only a starter?
I really think the government should consider the withdrawal of this item for the purpose of buying a new building at this time, especially in view of the fact that the other Chamber is likely to give our bill in connection with railway extensions the six months' hoist on the ground that we have not the money to build branch lines to feed our present system of railways. It looks as if we were casting about in the archives of the old departments for plans or suggestions that we might spend more money. At this ti.me we should consider very seriously any new expenditures. There should be a great objection to bringing down Supplementary Estimates of this size at this late date of the session, but I am not going to discuss that feature of the question now. I have no objection even at this late date to Supplementary Estimates being
Supply-Public Works

brought down for necessary repairs for carrying on the necessary work of the country, but an item for the purchase of a new building should not be put in the Supplementary Estimates, and I would urge strongly on the minister that he consider the advisability of withdrawing this appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: It is proposed to sell the present building which, according to the sanitary authorities, the medical authorities and the engineers, is not suitable, owing to the conditions under which the men have to work. It is proposed to negotiate for the purpose of the other building, using this particular vote for the purpose. That, I am instructed by the department, is the only reason why this should be done.

Where is the building
that is probably to be sold, and what price could the government get for it? Have we any idea what the new building will cost?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The building at present used is situated at the corner of Queen and O'Connor streets. It is the policy of the department that they should utilize the sale of this other building as a site for building purposes in connection with stores for the purpose of obtaining the new building. Under the exchange which, it is expected, will be made, this appropriation will cover the whole of the cost of making the change, with the result that the men who work in Ottawa permanently will work under better conditions.

Could the present building not be remodelled and made so that it would answer the purpose just as well? I do not wish to delay the discussion on this item, but I feel very strongly that this should be cut out. In order to facilitate business, I move that this item be reduced by the sum of $26,000, so as to cut out the item in connection with purchasing a building for government workshops.
That is a queer way of not delaying the proceedings.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
On this
matter the government has no policy except the desire to do what is absolutely necessary. I think that the committee will pretty generally agree that the government cannot allow to continue a state of affairs in which carpenters, plumbers, masons and other workmen who are permanently employed by the department must carry on their work in unsanitary conditions that inevitably lead to bad health and sickness.
[Mr. Caldwell.!

How much of the plumbing, or of the masonry, on this house is done in buildings in some other part of the city? It seems to me that men who are engaged on a particular building should not have to spend very much of their time in some other part of the city.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I am neither a carpenter nor a mason, nor do I believe my hon. friend is. I know enough about these occupations, however, to be convinced that these men must have some shops or some place where they can prepare their material before working on the particular building on which they are engaged. I am instructed by the officials that the conditions under which these men work are not satisfactory. As a matter of fact they are unsanitary, and it :s imperative that they be improved. My hon. friend must realize that a carpenter uses a variety of tools and a great quantity of accessories whi-h it is impossible for him to carry around with him. He simply must have a shop; at least, every carpenter and every plumber that I have ever known have found it necessary to have some place in which to store their tools, and all the appurtenances of their trades. Of course, if the workman is an itinerant gentleman and is content to walk around with his hat on his head then the conditions to which my hon. friend refers might exist.

I quite realize that a plumber needs a shop; but the minister's idea of a carpenter's work seems to me to be somewhat like a story I once heard of a tramp. He asked a farmer for dinner and was told to go and hoe some beans. The tramp wanted the dinner first and he got it, and when the farmer asked him, "What about the beans?" he replied, "Bring along your beans if you want them hoed." Evidently there are a lot of carpenters engaged on this work who want the work taken to them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio

speechtext: Are these shops underground?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Apparently
they are.
I do not think anybody wants an unsatisfactory condition of affairs to continue. That is not the point. But here is a government that owns any amount of property in the city, a great deal of it idle.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: That is not correct.

Yes, a great
deal of it, as anyone can see for himself.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I am instructed by the deputy that that is not correct.
Let anyone look for himself and see the vacant land owned by the government which is not being put to use.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: My hon. friend's government tried architects from all over the world and arranged for people to supervise the plans of this building. Does he mean to say that all that was done must be rendered futile?

My hon. friend told us before that the government had to stop on account of financial conditions, and he knows perfectly well it will be many years before the plans can ever be gone on with. He knows also that we have any amount of property which we are renting at nominal rates because we cannot get any use for it: and this is the case both east and west. We have large tracts which are bringing in nominal rents of a dollar a year and the like. And yet the government at a time like this, undertakes new investments. The thing is ridiculous.

I think my hon. friend would be the first to oppose any suggestion on the part of the Department of Public Works that we should vote 310,000,000 to put up new buildings. It should be done, but he would oppose it because this government is in power.

I appeal simply to the sense of fairness of the committee. I happen to be one of the members representing the city of Ottawa and as such I think I might offer an explanation. If any hon. member
who has spoken against the purchase of this property will go and examine for half an hour the building that now stands at the corner of Queen and O'Connor streets, and after that declare that the men working there are working under conditions that would be put up with in any civilized country, then he is not fit to be a member of this House. In that building at present there are about two or three hundred employees. It has been stated that some carpentering goes on there, and that is true. All the furniture that is repaired for the various departments is sent there, and the upholstering is done there. The masons and the plumbers have their quarters in the building, but thetir work constitutes only a small portion of the activi-4 p.m. ties that are carried on in the place. The men employed in the forge and those who are welding pipes are working underground in the areas under the sidewalks along Queen and O'Connor streets. These men are using drills and machinery weighing two or three tons, some very much .heavier than that; besides presses of all kinds. Molten metal is also taken out of some of the machines and formed into the equipment that is required in connection with the various departments. These men have to work in artificial light, and the only ventilation they have comes through the small windows situated immediately between the sidewalk and the ceiling. This condition has not been condemned by the provincial authorities because ihey have no power in the matter. In over ninety per cent of the offices there is no light because they are hemmed in by the adjoining buildings. There is a system of ventilation, it is true, but in all the offices the employees work in artificial light from morning till night the year round. It is true that the government owns large tracts of land along Victoria street and along Sussex street, and hon. gentlemen ask, why not establish the workshops in some of these buildings? Have they considered the practicability of installing the forges in these buildings in Victora street that are in a ramshackle, tumble-down state? Why two or three turns of the flywheel and the buildings would fall. Right along Sussex street, where this proposed purchase is to be made, there is the old Geological Museum now used for some purposes similar to those of the workshops in question. Next to that there is the large tract of land now used by the Department of Public Works for the storage of their cranes, trucks, sand, stone, piping and the like. This building is the only one that the architects have found suitable for the pur-
Supply-Public Works

pose, because of its reinforced concrete walls, ceilings and foundations, which will permit of the installation of the plant and will provide workable conditions for the employees. It was proposed in 1920 that this item should form part of the estimates. In 1921, it was recommended that the item go in, but for reasons of economy, probably, it was not included. I have always stood for economy, but I refuse to stand for economy when it is to the detriment of the working people. The government has had this building for eight years at a rental of 88,000 a year, eo that the building will in due time pay for itself. There is no doubt that, if not within the next few years, at least some time in the future, the proposed development in the matter of departmental buildings for Ottawa will take place, and in that event this building is just where it will serve the best purpose. I appeal to the spirit of fair play of the committee on behalf of the workingmen now engaged in the public service of Canada.

Does the
government own the building on the corner of Queen and O'Connor streets?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Yes.

What is
to be done with that building?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I have explained that it is the intention to sell it.

I am sure
that hon. members have no desire to keep our masons, plumbers and other workingmen in unsanitary surroundings, and the proposal of the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) that this item be reduced should not be coupled with any suggestion of that kind. Why, there are offices in the Parliament buildings where the members cannot carry on their work without the continuous use of artificial light, and where there is no ventilation except what is afforded through a window or door. So that the conditions are similar in some parts of this building to what has been described by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevier). The government owns a considerable quantity of land in the city upon which they intend ultimately to erect departmental offices, and I rather think the present is a poor time to embark upon the purchase of more property. If this building is unsanitary, why not fix it up; why not make it sanitary? That would be much better than starting out on the purchase of new property. This item is for 826,000, but the minister tells us that will not complete the purchase.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I said it would, when the proceeds for the sale of the present building are added.
Will that complete the entire plan which is proposed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: That is what I am instructed.
How many buildings in Ottawa are used by the government?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
My hon
friend has asked me a big question. I thin! he had better wait till the Minister of Public Works himself is here.
When we are voting this item, it is important to know what buildings are used by the government.

This is not an item that should be in the Supplementary Estimates. The condition is not one that arose within the last month or two months; it seems it has been a permanent condition. I still think we should cut this item out and if necessary put it in the Main Estimates next year. We will have a chance then of considering it.

My hon. friend and colleague (Mr. Chevrier) has stated the present condition of the shops: it is simply disgraceful. The present building was purchased sixteen or seventeen years ago at a price of, I think, 842,000; to-day it is worth two or two-and-a-half times that amount. The point is that it is not now suitable for the purposes for which it is used.
How long has it been used for its present purpose?
Ever since it was purchased-I think about seventeen years if my memory is correct.
How long is it since the government found it was not sanitary?

It has been complained of for the last four or five years. The question has been raised whether any of these other buildings which were purchased in 1912 could be used for this purpose. The answer to that is that they are practically all old buildings which were taken over in connection with the plan for the erection of the new departmental offices. It seems to me that this is a very good exchange. The old building is in the central part of the city, and is very valuable. It could either be changed in some respects so that the upper parts could be used as offices, or it could be sold, and if it is sold I am convinced that the government can make a very good deal in connection with

Supply-Public Works
it. We do hope in time to have proper departmental buildings in Ottawa so that the payment of heavy rentals may be avoided. That may not be a very popular thing for me to say, but it is the sane, businesslike way to deal with the matter. I speak subject to correction on the advice of the Deputy Minister of Public Works, but I am sure that the government has no building suitable for this purpose. I think, therefore, that we should carry the item, not only because to do so will be in the interests of the workingmen, but because it is a sound business proposition.
Has the government an option on this property?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio

speechtext: What will be the cost of repairs, installation of machinery and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The estimate is 825,000.
Has the government any assurance as to what it will get for the old building?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Valuations have been made upon it.
But no offer?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
The whole thing is to go through subject to that.
Amendment (Mr. Caldwell) negatived; Yeas, 38; Nays, 74.
I should like a little information on two of these items, the Toronto casualty clearing station and the Toronto building for the Seed branch.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
In regard to the casualty clearing station item, which is in full and final settlement of all claims of the Canadian National Railways for property expropriated, this is really nothing more than a book-keeping entry; it is required to pay the Canadian National Railways in full and final settlement of all claims whether for compensation or otherwise in respect to the expropriation and possession of land lying west of McLennan Avenue. These lands originally belonged to the railway and they were taken over by this department during the war for the purpose of building a casualty clearing station. There is no further use for it, and this is simply a book-keeping entry to clear up the matter.
In regard to the building for the Seed branch this is simply a preliminary vote which has been placed in the estimates at the request of the Department of Agriculture, who desires to obtain a building in Toronto in connection with their seed work.

We have had
difficulty for a good many years now in securing proper accommodation for our seed laboratories. It is very essential to have a northern light for seed inspection and examination, and this vote is for the purpose of securing a site for such a building so that we shall not be dependent forever on rented quarters that invariably are not suited for the purpose.
Why is this money being spent in Toronto?

That has been the headquarters of the seed laboratory work for many years. It serves all of western Ontario and is the centre of a large portion of the clover and grass seed work which are two of the most important items in connection with our laboratory work.
I notice that 8113,000 is being spent in Toronto. Is the minister sure that none of this is to debauch the Tory electors of Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: My hon. friend lives closer to Toronto than I do, but it seems to me it is pretty difficult to lead those Toronto Tories back to the true faith.

What about a custom
house for Toronto?
We have a number of experimental farms and is there any reason why this laboratory could not be located on one of them?

There is only one
experimental farm on which it-could be located, and that is the Central farm at Ottawa. That is not the centre of the work. You would have to bring the whole of the work of western Ontario to Ottawa. Besides, the headquarters have been in Toronto since the inception of this laboratory work, right in the centre of the field where the work is required. The work has grown into great importance especially for export purposes.
What is the great urgency for going on with this work this year? Cannot we wait a year or two longer? We have been doing very well, you know.

The urgency is that we have been constantly changing our quarters in the past on account of having to rent, and we have had great difficulty in getting
Supply-Public Works

quarters with the proper light. We think the time has come in the importance of this industry when we should have quarters of our own. Why not wait?-the hon. member says. Because we have frequently to change our quarters, and we have great difficulty in securing the proper light, and good light is the first essential in this work.
If the minister can give no better reason for going on with the work this year-
I think the hon. gentleman does not know enough about the work to know if it is a good reason or not.

That may be the honourable and parliamentary retort of the minister. He usually retorts that way when he gets into difficulties. But may I suggest that he has not, in my opinion given a sufficient reason? And if there is no better reason I do not think the vote is justified this year. It may be that the time will come when it will be justified, but not under existing financial conditions. In two short years of parliamentary experience I have come to the conclusion that this government, which came into power on an economy platform, has been spending money like a drunken sailor. I think this item may well stand over.

Mr. Clark, the Seed Commissioner, tells me that in some of our laboratories we are not getting over sixty per cent efficiency, due to the bad light. If you can scarcely see to do your work you have to take just so much longer time. Mr. Clark has made a close analysis of the work performed by the staff under different lighting conditions and has found that between good and bad lighting conditions there is just the difference of between one hundred per cent and sixty per cent, and in addition you do not get proper results with a poor light. Why should we give excuses for this work? These are absolute reasons I am giving. Why should we object to spending money in Toronto on work that is required? This accommodation has been required for some years, and the need is becoming more urgent all the time because of the increased importance of the work.

I did not ask for any excuse when I asked my question. I asked for a reason and I have not yet obtained it. Why could not the laboratory be located at the Experimental farm? There is good light there, and the only reply I got was that the laboratory has always been in Toronto. That is no reason. If Ottawa is sufficiently central to carry on experimental work of all 
kinds I cannot see why it would not be suitable for this work rather than spending money here, there and everywhere all over the country for buildings. I asked if there was any underlying reason why this work could not be done in connection with an experimental farm, and the minister has not yet given me an answer.

My hon. friend
speaks of this as experimental work.

I did not use the
expression that this was experimental work. I asked why it could not be carried on in connection with an experimental farm.

Yes, implying that it was experimental work. My hon. friend is familiar with the quarters in Winnipeg where the grain inspection is performed, and knows that the very first essential in this work is light. It is the same with this seed inspection work, only even more essential because the grass seeds are much smaller than the cereal seeds. Ottawa is not sufficiently central. Toronto is a more central city. Therefore if we are to give the proper service such as we want to do the building must be suitably located for the work necessary to be performed.
Will the minister tell us what this vote is for? Is it to buy land and construct a building suitable for the purpose?

I do not know the details of the vote; that information can be given by the Public Works department. I presume it is for the purpose of making a start. The first investment usually is to secure a site.
I should like to have information on this point. I know something in regard to the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
As far as
the department of Public Works is concerned the position of affairs is this. The amount is required towards the purchase of a site on which to erect a building for the Seed branch of the Department of Agriculture. No plans or specifications have yet been decided upon. The matter was initiated for the first time by the Department of Agriculture a few weeks ago. Dr. Grisdale the Deputy Minister of Agriculture, writes as follows:
The department has been looking into the possibility of acquiring certain land and erecting a new building for our Seed branch in the city of Toronto. A site has been located for this purpose at 84 Collier Street, about two blocks north of Blcor street and about 200 yards east of Yonge street. This property contains a frontage of 84 feet and a depth on the level

Supply-Public Works
of the street of about 120 feet where the lot drops into a ravine 60 or 70 feet below the level of Collier street. The total depth of the lot is said to be 164 feet.
Nothing has yet been done beyond this request to the Department of Public Works to provide a vote for enabling a commencement to be made.
What is the proposed cost of this site? Surely we can have some general estimate of that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: As a department we have no information on the subject.
Is not the site for this building very far up? What is the reason for the selection of such a site?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Dr. Grisdale, Deputy Minister of Agriculture simply suggests the site on Collier street as a possible one. Nothing has been done by this department in the matter of making a purchase. The whole matter will be reviewed by the officials of the Public Works department before anything is done in regard to it.
Is this building intended to serve for the province of Ontario, and therefore Toronto chosen, or is it intended to serve the whole Dominion?

The Dominion is
divided into, I think, six areas for seed purposes. This is the one for the province of Ontario. There is one at Calgary, another at Winnipeg, and still another in the Maritime provinces-five or six in all. There is a centre selected for each area and Toronto happens to be the centre for this particular one. If any better centre could be secured I suppose there would be no objection to taking it. Toronto is the centre for Ontario just -'S Winnipeg is the centre for Manitoba, and Calgary the centre for the western part of the prairies.
I do not think the minister can be accused of partisanship in this matter. If he desired to germinate political seeds in favour of the government he would hardly go to Toronto.

I think hon.
members may be well assured of one thing: Any single advantage that this government gives to Toronto is given because it cannot be helped.

It seems to me, from the letter which was read from Dr. Grisdale and from the other information which we have had, that this is a new idea, in fact the statement
was made that it originated only a few weeks ago. It occurs to me that the vote should stand over for further investigation.
I happen to know something about the University buildings at Toronto and the buildings of the Agricultural co'lege at Guelph, and I should like to see whether some arrangement could not be made to utilize the buildings of these two institutions, which are empty for a great part of the year and where the most excellent facilities may be enjoyed.
I am not in a position to say that it would be convenient to do so, but it seems to me we should go rather cautiously in a proposition of this kind. I would strongly recommend that the matter be held over for further investigation. I do not think we have sufficient evidence at the present time to justify this expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I desire to say on behalf of the Department of Public Works that the department will not regard itself bound to any particular site. It will go into the whole question with the greatest possible care in order to have the site for this building located in the proper place with the least expense and with a view to promoting the best interests of the country. Nothing whatever has been done to commit the department in any way, and the whole matter will be carefully considered before any expenditure is made.
Is this vote for the site only?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: It is only for the site.
What further expenditure is anticipated? Where is it going to end?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Nothing
further can be done without parliament voting the money. But you cannot start to build without securing a site. My hon. friend will see I am sure, that fault would be found if we proposed to parliament a large expenditure without making all necessary inquiries and having complete information. We are proceeding cautiously. Nothing has been settled about a site; we have simply had a rcommendation from the Deputy Minister of Agriculture. Nothing further can be done without coming to parliament for authority and I say, on behalf of the department that nothing will be done without the greatest possible care and thorough examination of the location.
Supply-Public Works
Who are the present owners of this property on Collier street?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I have no information on that point. The only information the department has is contained in the letter from Dr. Grisdale.
He selected the site apparently?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: No, he suggests a site on Collier street. He does not say anything in his letter as to whom it belongs to.

I see an item here for Postal Station "A", Toronto. The receipts for the past fiscal year from the post office at Toronto amount to nearly 86,000,000 and the accommodation is not what it should be. It is deplorable to have a building of that character in the city of Toronto. The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) asked the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) the other day what the government intended to do in the way of improvements, and was told that he would find that out from the Minister of Public Works, (Mr. King, Kootenay) when the Supplementnary Estimates came down. The receipts from the post office, customs, and other sources bring the total revenue which Toronto yields to the government up to 890,000,000. Cannot the minister give us better facilities than we now have there in the customs building? The building is a very dilapidated one and the business men are complaining very much. I should like to find out what is going to be done to improve matters in the next twelve months. The custom house is a public utility, but business men cannot satisfactorily transact business there with the existing facilities. Surely when Toronto is giving the treasury a revenue of 890,000,000 the government should do something better than they are doing in the matter of providing improvements. Business men say that the existing facilities at the custom house are a positive detriment to trade. I should like the minister to look into this matter during the recess, and see whether something cannot be done to meet the wishes of the industrial community, to say nothing of the general public. I warn the government that if better facilities are not provided the treasury will suffer a great loss of revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I am instructed by the deputy in regard to this vote of $30,000 to complete postal station "A" in Toronto, that it is the end of an expenditure of over $1,000,000 for that particular pur-

pose. I am also instructed that the postal station in Toronto, when completed will be one of the finest stations of the kind in the Dominion. The other matter to which my hon. friend refers has been engaging the attention of the minister and of the officials of the department.

I must say, Mr. Chairman, tha,t the vote for Ontario is most inadequate. You cannot take care of the post office and the custom house for the next fiscal year with this vote. You have no custom house in Toronto; you have simply a vacant lot. Surely you will not leave matters for another twelve months in the position in which they are at present, when the customs house does a business of $50,000,000 a year. Money is being spent in other parts of the country to provide facilities for doing business, but in the case of Toronto you are not 'giving anything back to the business men, from whom you are getting the money. I hope the minister will take this matter up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I have not a local knowledge of the wonderful city which is so ably represented by the distinguished member who has just spoken; but I may say that he has some ground of complaint in reference to the inadequate facilities in the customs house. I am sure the permanent minister of the department will read what the hon. member has said, and I will personally direct his attention to the necessity and wisdom of providing better facilities.
In connection with the casualty clearing station, will the minister tell us what is the reason of that vote?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: That is for the purpose of settling up with the Canadian National Railways for the site.
I do not see what possible harm can come from leaving this matter over until we have further information. It is evident that nothing can be done this year-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Oh, yes.
*-other than to purchase the site, and we have not had sufficient information to enable us to decide as to whether or not that is justifiable.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
What information does the hon. member desire? I have told him that this vote does not commit us to any particular site. Its purpose-and this is the uniform practice, and the only way in which it can be done-is to enable the de-

Supply-Public Works
partment to find a suitable piece of ground on which a building can be erected. If we came to the House next session and said "We have bought a site and erected a building for seed purposes," my hon. friend would tell us we had no right to do it, because no vote had been passed. There is only one way by which these things can be done properly, and that is by taking the course we have adopted.
What is the cost of the building?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: We will have to come to the House next year and get the House to authorize the vote. We cannot spend a five-cent piece without the authority of parliament.

I will tell the minister what we want, and why I think we should object to this item at the present time. We should not embark upon an enterprise of this kind without seeing our way clear and realizing the need. We do not know the need at the present time, and I would want some further information from the Seed Commisisoner himself in regard to the need for this particular building, and also in connection with the impossibility if such there be, of using some of the buildings already in existence for that purpose. I know that at the agricultural college at Guelph, which is not far from Toronto, They have a fine building largely devoted to the same purpose; and in the University of Toronto there are many places which might be used, so far as I know, for a large part of the year for this purpose. At both these places there are fine buildings which are not being used for six months of the year. I would like to have some information which would enable us to justify such an expenditure. What is the use of voting the money for the land, unless we are satisfied the whole project is justifiable? What is the objection to letting this matter stand over? We have been getting on well to-day; let us have full information in the Main Estimates next year. I am not taking an out-and-out stand against this proposition, but we have not sufficient information to justify the appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I am afraid it is most difficult to satisfy the hon. member. Here is something primarily and solely in the interests of agriculture, and my hon. friend objects to it. I am afraid I will have to ask my colleague the Minister of Agriculture to explain.

I do not want to
press this matter unduly. If the hon. member has any information he can give the department in regard to some other site where we
can get better accommodation, we want it; but I can assure him the work demands accommodation such as we have not had in the past. The work has been neglected for some time for lack of accommodation, We have been in rented quarters not suitable for the purpose. We have not been located permanently, and have had to move from time to time, thus disorganizing the work. What would the hon. member do, if he were in my place? This proposition has grown to great proportions. A large proportion of it is an export trade for which we must keep up the quality of the seed; and to do good work we must have good accommodation. Does the hon. member propose we should defer taking steps for another year? If he, in turn, has some reasons to give me, I will be agreeable to the suggestion to let this stand over until I get such information as will assist me in providing better accommodation in a better city or in a better location. I do not want to be exacting in regard to the matter; but, on the other hand, these are the requirements of my department, as I understand them. We have had difficulties in other cities in getting accommodation. In the city of Quebec, after spending a long time, we have got similar accommodation by renting premises. If my hon. friend has anything that he can furnish me as justification for dropping the matter and neglecting the work for another year, and seeking new temporary accommodation, it may be to our advantage in the end to drop it. I would like to hear from him along that line.

I am not objecting to the
carrying on of the work. I know it is important work; but I do object to going into this expenditure, the extent of which we do not know at the present time, without any definite idea as to the needs of this particular matter of looking after our seeds. I have already made suggestions to the Minister of Agriculture regarding the possible utilization of buildings in Toronto and Guelph, which I think are very well suited for the purpose. I think the minister should have something definite from the seed commissioner himself in regard to the expenditure. If he has this information and will submit it to the House and give us the details, we may be in a position to approve, and I for one do not wish to withold my endorsation of the scheme, except that at the present time I do not know and have no information to enable me to form a judgment.

It may be thought a bit extraordinary that a man from Quebec should rise in defence of a proposition in Toronto-
Supply-Public Works
It is not a Toronto proposition, and that is the reason the minister is up.

I wish to point out that, if a
better building is required for the inspection of seed grain and particularly clover and grass seed, for a central location in Ontario, I submit Toronto is the right place to have that building; and I think I can convince the committee why it is more economical. For instance, we have a department of inspection under the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the headquarters for inspection are in Toronto. This grain for export must be inspected and when it goes to the markets of the world must carry the inspector's certificate. There is another reason; the largest exporters of clovers and grass' seeds have headquarters in Toronto, where there are two very large firms, and the centre of the clover trade gravitates into Toronto; and I submit, without arguing whether the building is necessary or not, we must accept the statement of the men who are at the head of it, that it is necessary and that Toronto is the proper location; and I am convinced by what has been submitted to us that a better building is required. You cannot put up your machinery for inspecting grain and be under the necessity of moving about every year or two. We should have a permanent building for this work because the clover and grass seed export trade is becoming of enormous benefit to the agricultural districts of this country.
Have we any idea of the total expense which will be involved before this project is completed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: My hon. friend apparently does not appreciate that all that is being done here is to enable a site to be bought somewhere, not necessarily in Toronto Nothing can be done, no money can be spent m connection with a building, without everything in connection with the matter being submitted first to parliament. All that is involved in this appropriation is a sum of money to purchase a site. If the government comes to parliament later on for an appropriation to erect a building, my hon. friend will be able to go into the question.

The minister would not recommend spending $25,000 to purchase a site if there was some possibility of having the whole thing negatived next year owing to some outrageous expenditure for a building. The first thing we should do is to decide what kind of building is necessary.	t

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
There could be no outrageous expenditure for a building

or a dollar spent upon a building without the leave of parliament next year.
I know that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Then why is my hon. friend talking about the country being committed to an expenditure of an outrageous character?
What is the use of buying the land -without having an idea as to what sore of building is to be put on it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: My hon. T-iend is putting the cart before the horse. If it is desirable-and the Department of Agriculture says it is-to have a building in connection with their Seed branch, before you can get a building, you must have a property somewhere to put it on. That is all we are proposing to do. Nobody has been committed to an expensive building, and we are not suggesting that anybody should be. Next year the government may ask for an appropriation for a building. If my hon. friend thinks the amount is too large, or the building is in the wrong place, he can argue that out then. The only question at present involved is: Can a site be purchased for the building, not necessarily in Toronto, but anywhere the government may deeide that it should be purchased?
Has the Minister of Agriculture a definite recommendation from the Seed Commissioner in this connection?

Yes. The primaiy object of this laboratory is to give service to the farmers who grow the seed and to maintain the quality, especially for export. I shipped carloads of seed before the western laboratories were opened. I am surprised my hon. friend, who is familiar with the grass seed and clover seed industry, would seem to stand in the way of this enterprise, because it is urgently required. Mr. George Clark is one of the most careful and efficient officers in the service of the Department of Agriculture, and he certainly entered into this matter very carefully before making his recommendation.

Would it not be better
for the minister to bring in an estimate next year covering the cost of the land and the building, and then we could consider the whole thing on its merits.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
We are proposing to ask the committee to vote this money. If my hon. friend wants to move against it, he can, but I think we have given

Supply-Public Works
him all the information that can possibly be given.

I wish to support the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) in his stand. If you are going to buy an expensive lot. surely you have an idea of what sort of building you want to put on it. We should know what expenditure is involved in this. This reminds me of an incident where a lot was bought in a western town some ten years ago for some $10,000, to put a building on. The government never erected a building on that lot, and that lot is worth less than $200 to-day. We should have more details. The hon. member for Brant is on very good ground in the stand he is taking.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is again putting the cart before the horse. Pie is suggesting, if you are getting a place to install the Seed branch in, you should decide to buy your building before you buy your lot. The first question to be decided is where you want to put your building in Toronto or anywhere else; then you come to parliament and submit your proposal for the building you intend to erect.

I do not suppose there is
any use in discussing this particular matter any further. There is another matter, not a very popular subject, to which I wish to call attention, because I think it is my duty to say something about it. Last year I made some comment upon the expense of Government House. There is an item in this	appropriation for alterations	andimprovements to Rideau Hall, $17,100. I have the highest regard personally for the Governor General; but last year I figured	up	the expense	that	this
country was put to in connection with this institution, and I think the total last year amounted to about $225,000. If I remember aright, there was in the estimates of last year an item of somewhat the same amount for improvements and alterations to Rideau Hall. It seems to me that at this time, when so many people in this country are in dire distress and want, these expenditures are totally unjustifiable. In that particular direction we ought to cut down.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
My hon.
friend's policy is one that should be considered, but it is never a wise thing for people to allow their buildings to fall down or into disrepair. It is true economy to spend money in order to keep buildings in the necessary repair. Otherwise, when the catastrophe comes in the end, one will find that one was
penny wise and pound foolish. This amount of $17,100 is required for alterations to the palm house of the conservatory at Rideau Hall, which is in a very dangerous condition and must be renewed. The work includes alterations to the iron superstructure and steel framing, including the necessary glass, and also repairs to the substructure and foundations and the heating and water services, The reports are that this work is entirely necessary, or otherwise the building will not only fall into disrepair, but be in danger of falling down altogether.
If this is simply a matter of repairs to prevent decay and dilapidation, then I withdraw my objection.

On that matter I
notice in the Main Estimates an item has already been passed for Rideau Hall including grounds improvements, and so on, amounting to $60,000. I am glad this matter has been brought up by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good). I know some may hes [DOT] tate to speak of a matter which concerns an official who may be regarded more or leas as a guest of this country. However, when we put together the various items concerning the upkeep of Government House, they amount to a very large figure. I am inclined to think the Governor General has been verv poorly advised with regard to conditions in Canada and the temper of Canadian people if this style which he has undertaken to keep up, is maintained. I should like to call attention to certain items which I have noticed in various departments and which have their bearing on this particular item: Governor General's salary, $48,666; Governor General's Secretary, $2,400; Governor General's Secretary, office, salaries, $31,915; printing and stationery, $3,000; sundries, one item, for which we have not the detail, $63,000. Under Public Works there is an item in connection with Rideau Hall of $60,000, and now in the Supplementary Estimates the sum of $17,100. Further allowance for fuel and light $19,000. In connection with another department, that of Railways and Canals, we find that for repairs to the Governor General's cars there has already been voted $10,000, and I notice that there is still an item in the Supplementary Estimates of not less than $40,000 additional fpr repairs. I cannot conceive at all what items can be involved in these large sums. There is nothing whatever down in the list for travelling expenses and I do not know how far the railways supply the equipment for that. I presume, however, that it amounts to a considerable sum. I have not seen in
Supply-Public Works

what department that comes or how it is arranged for, but these items alone that we know of total $295,081.66. When you have an expenditure of nearly $300,000 on one individual whose functions in this country are purely formal, then I suggest that the Governor General has been very ill-advised indeed in maintaining things on such a scale. I think I can speak for a considerable number of people when I say that we have no desire to set up anything like a feudal state over in this country. I take it that the great purpose of the Governor General's having been sent here is that there should be maintained cordial relationships between the Mother Country and Canada. But if this kind of thing persists I am of opinion that instead of maintaining cordial relationships it will rather work the other way and we shall have very strained relations. I do not think that these burdens should be placed upon people who are finding it exceedingly difficult as it is to obtain the merest necessities of life.

I think I called attention last year to the unprecedented extravagance which Ontario, in my judgment, was guilty of a few years ago in building a palace on the Don river, and to the fact that during a coal famine some time ago, when the citizens of Toronto and the people of the province generally were pretty nearly freezing, a single house for just one functionary consumed about one thousand tons of coal. This sort of thing is bound to excite a great deal of resentment and uneasiness in the country and it must come to a stop some time or other.

I realize that a man is on rather dangerous ground when he undertakes to discuss a subject like this; he is apt to be charged with a lack of patriotism if not something worse. But the time has come, I think, when we ought to protest against such expenditures. I do not agree with the member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth) in attaching any blame in this regard to His Excellency. I think the matter rests entirely with the government; I do not believe His Excellency has anything to do with it; in fact I doubt very much whether he is aware that these votes are in the estimates. The government ought to consider all the circumstances very carefully before asking for these expenditures to be sanctioned.

What is the reason for putting in the Supplementary Estimates $75,000 for the Royal Military College at Kingston?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
For about
twenty years the different governments in office have sought to obtain suitable quarters in London for the High Commissioner's office. The governments of Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa all have suitable buildings there-very much better, indeed, than anything Canada has. I think each government that has been in office has felt that our Dominion was being placed in a false light before all citizens in London at the heart of the Empire. Efforts were made by the late government to secure a suitable building, and when this government came into office the effort was continued. The High Commissioner has gone into the matter very carefully. Last year we thought we had obtained a building that would be suitable, but on giving the matter careful consideration we abandoned the idea of purchasing it.	.
Was that the Cox Bank building?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No; I forget at the moment what building it was. However, this year the High Commissioner did think there was an opportunity of securing the building to which my hon. friend has referred, namely, the Cox Bank building. This building was in course of erection; it was almost completed and there was an exceptional opportunity to obtain it. At one time the government thought it might be wise to secure it, having in mind, of course, the subletting of the greater part of it to different Canadian firms, banks, and so on, that have their offices in London. The High Commissioner went into the question very thoroughly; he felt that if that building could be secured it would pretty well carry itself through the rents to be obtained. However, when he began to negotiate in the matter there were one or two conditions that he did not feel he would be justified in accepting, and he abandoned altogether the thought of taking over the Cox building. He has since been looking at one or two others, but has not yet decided what building he will recommend; and that is where the matter stands. A suitable building in London is urgently required. As my hon. friend has suggested, notice
Supply-Public Works

recently had to be given of our intentions regarding our present offices; unless we took a lease for another term of years it was represented that we would have to relinquish the premises at the expiration of the present lease, about the first of July. The High Commissioner was willing to let the lease lapse rather than renew it for a term of years. As the offices will very shortly have to be vacated and transferred to other quarters until a new building is secured, this item is put in to meet any expenses that may arise in that connection.
I take it from what the minister says that we are abandoning our present quarters; that we have no other quarters in view, and that this sum is to keep the office running for the year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: To cover the period of transition, yes.
Nothing else is being asked for that purpose?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

Has the government
taken an option for the purchase of a building in London?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not that I am aware of. As I said before my right hon. friend came in, negotiations were under way for the possible acquisition of the Cox Bank building. Those negotiations have been dropped, however, and I think the High Commissioner is at present considering the possibility of securing another building, but has not taken any official action upon it.
No option has been secured?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say that an option has not been secured. I think the High Commissioner has arranged that at any rate before a certain building is disposed of he will be given the refusal of it. More than that I cannot say.
Sir Henry Thornton may possibly have bought a castle or two in London, and perhaps the thing may come in that way.

May I ask whether the question will be considered of assembling all the Canadian offices in London? It seems too bad that the Ontario office should be in the Strand, the British Columbia offices in Pall Mall, and the High Commissioner's office in Victoria street. In the Strand one finds practically all the Australian offices combined

in one building, the result being a splendid advertisement for Australia. It struck me as being too bad that a similar situation could not be created for Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend asked that question, because he has reminded me of the fact that last year we tried to acquire the British Columbia building. The federal government would have been prepared to take that building over had the British Columbia government been willing to part with it, but they have found that in that large building, which is so favourably located, they have an excellent investment; as a matter of fact I think they are making money on it. The present situation is that Canada has a much inferior building to that maintained in London by one of its provinces. The federal government rents part of the British Columbia building for offices connected with immigration work. The government has felt that Canada has been handicapped as compared with the other dominions in having its offices scattered about in various buildings throughout London-not only the offices of the different provinces, but the different federal offices that were created during the war. The office which has to do with the soldiers' overseas work is in one part of the city. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has offices for his agents in another part of the city. The immigration offices are in still another part and the High Commissioner's offices are elsewhere. We felt that it was desirable to acquire a building in which all these offices could be brought together and which would be large enough also to accommodate the representatives of the different provinces, but that kind of a building in London is not easily acquired, and rather than make a purchase which would not meet with the general approval of the country we have proceeded slowly in the matter. But the object is to do the very thing my hon. friend has said-to acquire a building that will serve all these purposes in a way that will reflect credit on the country.

May I express my opinion in regard to this voting of money for experimental farms? A great deal of it is well expended; it is good work. But I think a great deal of it might well be saved. I would like to have a re-allocation of the expenditure in connection with the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa. We are often taunted in this quarter of the House with the amount of money spent on agriculture in this country, and these expenditures on farms and such like are all linked together and the whole sum is hurled at our heads. Now a vast sum of money is spent on the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa for a park. It is a magnificent, delightful show place, it is really a credit to the Dominion and affords delight
especially to visitors coming to Ottawa. But at the same time there is no justification for charging up all the expenses of the maintenance of that park to the Department of Agriculture or to its estimates. I would suggest that these expenses be segregated and the money that is spent on the park be charged against the Parks Branch of the Department if the Interior.

I have very grave doubts indeed whether any of these experimental farms are of any practical use to the farmer at all. It is true, they raise some very excellent stock and grow fine varieties of different farm products, but these are all produced at a loss. Now, is it any consolation to the ordinary farmer to exhibit to him some very excellent products that are grown at a loss? I think the minister will agree with me that they cannot be grown except at a loss, and I think it is something we should take into serious consideration.

speechtext: The details are as follows: Division of Botany, field laboratory, $4,500; new botanical building, estimated cost, 830,000; extension to chemistry' building, $22,000; division of forage plants, frame barn 30 x 50, ground floor and root cellar, $2,000; division of horticulture, greenhouse addition, $15,000; poultry division, new buildings, breeding house, $2,500; making a total of $76,000. That is $1,000 more than the amount we are voting, but my hon, friend will understand that in addition there is the difference between $75,000 and $130,000 which is said to be the estimated expenditure in all parts of the country. This $75,000 we are voting is to be allocated among the whole of these farms after a conference between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Agriculture.

The original amount asked for by myself and my staff was $200,000. The amount before parliament is $75,000, and in consequence we shall have to eliminate for the present a lot of the work that can with least disadvantage be done without, though it is all required. This $75,000 will have to be re-allocated to satisfy the most pressing requirements. A lot of the requirements we shall be unable to supply. During the four years of the war no expenditure was made by the late government on buildings for experimental farms. I am not blaming the former

Supply-Public Works

government for that, because they could not very well do otherwise nor in the years following the war could they take any other course. But now the time has come when we must equip these farms with proper buildings or close them up. Is anybody prepared to close them?
Let us close them.
We would like to have some applications during the recess from any province that wants these farms closed. I cannot undertake the responsibility of operating these farms in a half-equipped condition.
Let us close half of them, anyhow.

There is not a single dollar asked to be expended that is not most urgently required. I wish some of my friends would go out to the Central Experimental Farm, it is looking very beautiful now. And look at the accommodation we have for the botanical laboratory. You will find, if you put two or three good-sized beds there, you could hardly turn around without knocking over some chemicals. There are three or four men in a cubby-hole of an office where there should be only one. It is a most disgraceful building for an experimental farm system such as we have. Generally speaking, our experimental farms compare favourably with those of other countries, but some of the buildings are disgracefully out of date. I wish hon. gentlemen would go and see that botanical laboratory. We have just recently moved out of another laboratory, the biological laboratory, that we have had to put up with since 1904. There has been absolutely no extension to it for nearly twenty years and this year we were moved into a private building on Wellington street. So far as the departmental buildings and the buildings on the experimental farms are concerned there is not another department of agriculture that I know of on this continent, or anywhere else, that is housed in such poor buildings as the Department of Agriculture of Canada. To the buildings of the experimental farm system the same remarks will apply. I can assure my hon. friend that there is a clear lack in Ottawa in this respect. There are certain laboratories, particularly the botanical laboratory, which are decidedly lacking in suitable accommodation. The botanical laboratory does not possess the accommodation it should in order to cope with such diseases as lust-one of the most virulent and contagious in the entire list-that affect our cereals. Such

important problems as these are being studied and dealt with, and yet the quarters of the staff are nothing like what they should be. For experimental work intended to evolve a remedy for rust, an equipment and accommodation of the most efficient character should be provided, and yet we have undertaken an investigation of some of these big problems with accommodation which limits you to 50 per cent of efficiency.

I shall not go as far as the hon. member for Mackenzie and say that these experimental farms are of little or no value. I would say, however, that the Dominion is top-heavy with these institutions at the present time. While agriculture is languishing from one end of the Dominion to the other we are lavishly spending money year after year on these institutions, and I do not think it is right. Very much of the work done, we will say at Ottawa, is also undertaken by the provinces and there is a great deal of overlapping. I wish to protest against the lavish expenditure year after year on these farms.

The minister spoke of the need of more extensive offices in order to enable the scientists attached to his department to carry on their experiments. Let me tell the minister that some of the best work ever done in the interest of agriculture in the Dominion was done outside-it was not done in those offices. I have in mind a certain incident which occurred some years ago in connection with cut-worm. An active educational propaganda was being carried on by the department in order to try and combat the ravages of the cut-worm, and a number of pamphlets were issued on the subject. I know a boy, only twelve years old at that time, who collected evidence out in a summer fallow field that entirely upset the theory advanced in these pamphlets in respect to the cut-worm. According to that theory cutworms were supposed to hide themselves beneath the surface of the ground during the hours of daylight. Yet this boy I speak of gathered no less than sixteen different specimens out of thousands, yes millions, of worms, which were crawling all over that field between the hours of eleven and twelve o'clock in the day. At that time the rays of the sun were pouring down with intense heat; I would say the temperature must have been 90 degrees in the shade. According to the teaching of the pamphlet these cut-worms should all have been under the surface of. the ground at that time, but there they were travelling in all directions-north, south, east and west.
Now as to the expenditure on experimental farms. The actual work of agriculture is car-
