We should like to have some explanation of this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
The committee will remember that earlier in the afternoon I referred to the fact that a large number of buildings and a tract of land on Wellington street had been expropriated and taken over by. the government in 1913 with a view of doing away with the present system of renting buildings throughout the city and concentrating all the offices that were not in buildings owned by the government in that particular area. On April 14, 1913, an order in council was passed providing for a competition for designs for a new departmental block on Wellington street to cost from ten to twelve million dollars. That amount seems very large to-day when we look at the proposals for the construction of buildings, but that idea was in the mind of the government of the day in 1913. The Minister of Public Works appointed assessors to judge the designs. Conditions governing the competition were drawn up. The competition was advertised. Plans were received up to April 2nd, 1914. British and Canadian architects to the number of 59 submitted designs. Each set of plans consisted of from 18 to 30 drawings. It is estimated that the draughtsmanship alone cost the architects not less than $177,000. This only takes into account draughting-not the higher wo*'k of designing. Up to the present no competitor has received any return for his labour or expense. The conditions provided that of the competitors six should be chosen. These six were to make any further preliminary drawings required by the assessors. The assessors were then to choose from the six the one having the best design. The one selected was to be employed to carry out the work. The others were each to receive $3,000
Supply-Public Works
The others of the six.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
The others of the six were each to receive $3,000. The assessors out of the designs submitted selected the best six. Beyond this point the competitors did not proceed. The immediate delay was said to be caused by the desire to wait for the report of the Federal Town Planning Commission. Finally the war put an end co the whole thing. The six best designs having been chosen, the other competitors had no grievance. They were out of the race. The only question remaining was the remuneration which should be paid the six architects successful, in the first stage. The six successful competitors asked for settlement, but nothing satisfactory wras offered. One of them, Saxe & Archibald of Montreal then took the matter to the Exchequer Court. Suit was brought to recover $100,000, the amount allowed by the architects tariff for the province of Quebec for preparing and furnishing preliminary plans, being 1 per cent on $10,000,000, the estimated cost of the buildings. The matter was dealt with in the Exchequer Court. The Crown had tendered $3,000, and judgment was given for this amount. Last session $3,000 for each of the six architects was placed in the Estimates. This the architects refused to accept, and they put forward this claim:
1.	The plans called for were not mere sketches. They consisted of from 18 to 30 large drawings. The sum of $3,000 would not pay for the work of the draughtsman alone.
2.	In addition to what the architects had to pay for draughting they had other expenses incidental to studying the problems presented. One of the architects has produced vouchers showing that he actually disbursed over $9,000.
3.	This work was done prior to April 2nd, 1914. The architects have been out their money for nine years. The lowest prize offered, namely $3,000, would with interest now amount approximately to $5,000.
4.	This was no ordinary undertaking. It was the designing of a public building to cost over $10,000,000. The plans represented all the thought and genius these men were able to bring to the work. Other plans would have been necessary, but they would have been a matter of elaboration merely. The conception with all the effort involved was in these plans.
5.	Among the six men was the cue who must have been entrusted with the work of erec^.'ng the building. No one of these architects would have considered com-pet:ng for a prize of $3,000 or of $10,000. What each struggled for was the first prize, the honour of doing the work and the fee that went with it. It is submitted that it is unfair for the government of Canada to set 59 architects or firms of architects working for prizes and then when they have done the largest part of their work to say that there sh?.ll be no first prize-merely consolation prizes. Since it is now impossible to say which of the six should get the first prize the only thing that remains is to divide some part of it at least among the six.
Clause 28 of the general conditions provided that if the government abandoned the work

or failed to give instructions within twelve months from the selection of the successful architect he should be paid a sum equal to It per cent of the amount of the estimated expenditure. The amount to be divided by the government amongst these six architects would therefore have been as follows: li per cent on estimated cost of $10,000,000.. $125,000 $3,000 to each of the five other competitors.. 15,000

The architects think that they should be given at least $10,000 each. This would not do more than cover the ordinary draughting and other expenses incidental to the work. It would leave nothing for the work of the architects themselves. That is the whole situation, and the department submits to the House the suggestion that it is reasonable under the circumstances that these men having done this work should be paid. It is only honest and proper on the part of the government to do that which any individual would have done if he were in the same position. That is the position in which ths vote stands. Among the first six whose plans were approved by the assessors this amount of $30,000 would be divided.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The desire was expressed by some of the hon. members of the House that an opportunity should be given for discussing the Imperial conference and the Imperial Economic conference. I think possibly it would be advisable to take up these items at once so that there may be opportunity for the members to discuss them perhaps at greater length than if we delayed the discussion till another sitting.
Amount required for expenses of delegation to Imperial conference, $10,000.

One would hardly think that this was such an occasion that hon. members had in mind to discuss what should be the conduct of the Canadian representatives at this conference or at the Imperial Economic conference. The House is the place to discuss that, and a day should have been set. This is not doing anything. Of course, we have a right I suppose to discuss the subject on this vote and in committee, but there is no concession here by the government at all. I understood from the answer given to an hon. gentleman on my left-I do not remember who it was-that a day would be fixed for this discussion, and that hon. members would know when it was so that they could prepare themselves for the occasion. This is no time for a discussion of that sort, and for a statement by the government of its intentions at the conference.

Supply-Imperial Conference

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I may say to
my right hon. friend that I stated on two or three occasions when the opportunity would be given. I have before me the remarks I made and which appear in Hansard. On two occasions I mentioned that when the Supplementary Estimates were brought down they would contain an item with reference to the Imperial Conference and the Economic Conference, and that ample opportunity would be afforded members to discuss the whole question when that item was considered. The government as a matter of fact felt there would be greater freedom if the discussion took place in committee in the form in which it is now suggested. The last reference I made to the subject was in reply to my hon. friend the member for Brant (Mr. Good). The hon. member's question and my reply thereto appear in Hansard of June 22nd, as follows:
Mr. Good: When wiU the House have an opportunity of discussing the agenda of the Imperial Conference and the Economic Conference to be held this fall?
My reply was:
I have mentioned, I think, several times, that when the supplementary estimates are brought down, they will contain an item to make provision for the Economic Conference and the Imperial Conference, and that will be the appropriate time, I think, for the discussion to take place. I hope the supplementary estimates will be brought down possibly by Tuesday or Wednesday of next week.
I think it is perfectly clear to every member of the House that this was the time when the discussion would take place.

This is not a discussion
in the House at all, this is a discussion in committee; the main point is not there. It is not appropriate to discuss in committee a subject of this magnitude and character and it has never been the practice to do so. We do not know-

Will my right hon. friend
allow me to ask him a question?
Oh, yes.
What is the difference between a discussion in committee and a discussion in the House? Everybody is present now.
Yes, everybody is present, but if the hon. gentleman does not know the difference I do not think I will take time to explain it.
You will be much freer.

My point is this: No
hon. member of the House knew this item was coming up now. We are called upon without one moment's notice to discuss what is to be the policy adopted by Canada at an
economic conference, and if the government think that is reasonable I am quite sure the House does not. The papers on the subject are not yet down. Some time ago I asked for and obtained what was described at the time as a partial list of the subjects that had been suggested for discussion-suggested from Great Britain. I cannot speak with certainty as to the exact words of the Prime Minister, but I have the impression that he promised to give later any other subjects that were submitted for discussion so that we would have the agenda and have some little time to consider it before the time would be fixed for discussion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps my
right hon. friend will allow me to say to him that I complied with that intention on the 5th June. I then gave to the House such further statements as I had received from the Home government. I would further say to my right hon. friend that there is before the House at the present time all the information that the government has received and which it is at liberty to place on the table. All the papers are down.

Is the full agenda now
ready for discussion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The whole
agenda so far as the government has received it.
Is the government prepared to state what its position is to be in reference to these subjects?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In so far as it is possible to state it. I notice that when my right hon. friend was similarly situated he indicated that he did not think he should be asked'to state what his position would be at the conference, inasmuch as it was impossible to do so until he was in conference with the other parties.

I think that is absolutely the right stand but I did not expect it to come from the Prime Minister because he took the other view. I think the stand I took is right and should be his stand to-day. I was, however, met with a resolution of instructions which the Prime Minister supported, or rather which he moved. I was supposed to go tied round the neck with a lasso on a resolution moved by himself. I am glad his opinions in that respect are now reformed.
No, you needed it.

The hon. gentleman seems to have risen to be a critic on this subject now.
Supply-Imperial Conference
I say no, that you needed it.

Possibly that is the opinion of the hon. member. As to whether it is the opinion of the country or not I will offer no comment at the moment. However, I am glad the hon. member is not to be one of the delegates himself. What I am asking for was a discussion in the House. If the government insist upon having that discussion in committee they will have to carry their insistence, but I do think the House is entitled to a little notification in advance of the time when discussion will take place on such an important matter as this.

Carried.
Mr. Jacobs and Mr. Good rising at the same time.
Are we discussing the item?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are.
I came in about two or three minutes late.
Try and get here on time and save us a lot of trouble.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman if the Prime Minister would agree to bring this matter up to-morrow morning at eleven o'clock.
Not at all.
I am prepared to go ahead with whatever information I may have in regard to the question if the rest of the committee are satisfied.
Go on.

Mr. Chairman, I came down without any notes or papers and, perhaps, the committee will be very glad. In fact my experience this session has led me to believe that sometimes the support which one may expect or get will be in an inverse ratio to the amount of evidence one can bring forward to support his position. At least that might be a logical deduction from our experience in one of the committees.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) has the floor or had.
He thinks he has.
It is usual for the Chairman to decide who has the floor. He has decided against me.

I beg to draw attention to what happened. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier was on his feet and the hon.

member for Brant interpolated more or less on a point of order, wanting to discuss the course being pursued on the same lines that the leader of the Opposition did. When he concluded his objections it appears to me it was then the privilege of the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier to go on with his remarks. The hon. member for Brant having told us that he has not got his notes, he can avail himself of the opportunity to obtain them while my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) is speaking.
I did not know that the hon. member had begun to discuss the matter. I will gladly give way to him.
It will give you time to get your notes.,

Everybody would make
better speeches without notes.

I gladly accept the support of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill). I hope when my remarks are concluded he will still continue to give me support.
At the last Imperial Conference, Mr. Chairman, a resolution was proposed and carried in the following terms:
The conference while reaffirming the resolution of the Imperial War Conference of 1918, that each community of the British Commonwealth should enjoy complete control of the composition of its own population by means of restriction of immigration from any of the other communities, recognizes that there is an incongruity between the position of India as an equal member of the British Empire and the existence of disabilities upon British Indians lawfully domiciled1 in other parts of the Empire. The conference accordingly is of the opinion that in the interests of the solidarity of the British Commonwealth, it is desirable that the rights of such Indians to citizenship should be recognized.
This resolution was supported by the then Prime Minister, now the leader of the Opposition, who was present at the conference; and in passing I wish to say that I commend the conduct of the right hon. gentleman on that occasion. No matter how opposite political views may be, I am glad to bear public tribute to him, putting it in the words of Kipling-
'E's a poor benighted 'eathen,
But a firstclass fighting man
The leader of the Opposition receives a considerable share of support from the people of the province of British Columbia. I do not say they are benighted heathens away out there, but for reasons which I am not going to discuss here, a large portion of the delegation on the other side of the House supports the hon. leader of the Opposition; and notwithstanding that,

Supply-Imperial Conference
he was prepared to back up this resolution, which I understand is not particularly popular in British Columbia. No matter what the views of the people of any particular province may be on a matter of this kind, I submit they ought to give way to the generally accepted views of the people of the Dominion of Canada as a whole and to the views of the Empire of which we are always proud to say we form an integral part. The question of the Hindu franchise is of great interest to this country. There i? no reason in the wide world, so far as I can see, why British subjects domiciled in Canada should be deprived of the franchise. They are British-born. Their skins may be a little duskier than ours, but they belong to the Aryan race, and in all respects they are quite as capable of using the franchise as any person who resides in this country. The franchise is given to the Chinese and the Japanese in eight provinces. I understand that in British Columbia they do not vote, but there is a vast difference between the Chinese and Japanese and the Hindu. The first difference is that these latter people are British subjects and are part of the British Empire.
Does the hon. member think it is right that a lawyer should have the privilege of pleading his client's case in this House?

In answer to the hon. member, I would say that these people are not clients of mine. I would be very glad, indeed if they were because I understand they are a highly moral people, a respectable people, and that they pay legal fees when they are due. I cannot say as much for many of the white clients who come to my office. I was going to remark, Mr. Chairman, that the Hindu citizens have a big claim upon us by reason of the fact that they are part of the British Empire. The Chinese and Japanese come to this country. They have to be naturalized as British citizens. They forswear their allegiance to the country from which they come, and they are essentially a different race from the Hindus. They belong to what is known as the yellow race. I do not want to go into the question as to whether it is well to permit large numbers of people of this kind to come into this country or not because it is not a matter which concerns me just now. This question was urged upon the delegates at the Imperial Conference by the Right Hon. Mr. Sastri, who travelled through the country last year, and made what I consider an irrefutable case for his people who are resident here.
There are, I understand, 1,200 Hindus resident in Canada to-day. These people came here ten or twelve years ago. Hon. members will recollect that there was some question about their landing at the time. But they subsequently were permitted to land, and from that time until now they have been denied the right to which they are entitled; that is the right of the franchise which every person coming to this country ought to be given. It may be argued that if we give these people a foothold in this country they will increase and multiply, and after a time this country will no longer be a so-called white country. In answer to that objection, I say that no Hindus are now permitted to leave India for the purpose of coming to Canada to reside. Before it is possible for any of these people to leave their own country they must obtain a passport and a certificate from the Indian government, and that has been consistently refused in the interests of harmony with this country. No more of these people are permitted to come to Canada, and consequently we are only dealing with a handful of 1,200 people, who are, as I understand, all residents today in British Columbia. Mr. Sastri stated when he was here that he was delighted to know at the time that our government was going to fall in with the views of the representatives and delegates at the conference, but he said he found to his bitter experience that the intellectual acceptance of a theory sometimes was very far from its practical application, and he found, so far as this government seemed to be concerned, that there was no intention of putting into effect the promise given by the then Prime Minister of Canada at the conference.
If that be so, Mr. Chairman, it puts the right hon. leader of the Opposition in a very peculiar position. He found that he was putting his signature to a document which was not recognized, or is not recognized, by the present government. He is very much in the position of Mr. Woodrow Wilson after he had signed the Treaty of Versailles and returned to Washington, and found that the Senate refused to back up the solemn undertaking given by him. Surely, we do not want the present leader of the Opposition to become the Woodrow Wilson of this country. No, I think it is our duty to see to it that this undertaking given by him, properly delegated as he was, should be carried out. Those of us who had the pleasure of listening to Mr. Sastri when he was here were very much struck by his argument in favour of the inclusion of his countrymen in the franchise of this country. He pointed out that
Supply-Imperial Conference

India at the present time was disturbed by sedition. The Ghandi propaganda was generally accepted throughout India, and these people in India were making capital out of the fact that the sister commonwealths were not carrying out the undertaking which had been given to them at the conference.
I submit this is a very serious matter, and it is a matter of Imperial concern. We can understand 300,000,000 of people who are being fed with seditious matter using objections of this kind with the very greatest effect in their own country. Hon. members will recollect that last September,-I think it was September or October-we were nearly drawn into war in the matter of the Angora situation. The people of India, as we know, were practically on the crater of a volcano. It is a very simple matter to declare a civil war in Islam, and if that were done, the fat would be in the fire as far as India was concerned. All those considerations were something to be carefully thought over, and I am sure the statesmen gathered round the board at the Imperial conference did think matters of this kind over before they came to the conclusion, that in this particular matter, the commonwealths ought to listen to the combined reason of those who were present, and carry out the Views of Mr. Sastri and the Indian delegates.
It was also pointed out some time ago that, as regards India nationally and in its relation to the sister Dominions that country stands practically in the same position as any of the self-governing nations constituting the British Empire. It may be-and I concede the point -that as regards the internal affairs of India, they may not have the same degree of constitutional liberty which we in this country have or which the other commonwealths have. But as I said before, with regard to the dominions constituting the British Empire, India is treated in exactly the same way as the other dominions, and consequently when we deal with the inhabitants of India we have to deal with them in the same way as we deal with the people of South Africa, Australia, New Zealand and the other self-governing commonwealths. I should like to learn if it is the intention of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the other delegates who attend this conference, to carry out the undertakings given by our delegates at the last conference, or whether we intend to embark upon some new policy and to deny to those people the right to which I claim they are justly entitled.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What is the
undertaking?
The undertaking as conveyed in this resolution which I read at the opening of my remarks.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: To what extent does my hon. friend read into that paragraph an obligation on the part of the government of Canada?

I think the moral obligation is clearly seen there:
The conference while reaffirming the resolution of the Imperial War conference of 1918, that each community of the British commonwealth should enjoy complete control of the composition of its own population by means of restriction on immigration from any of the other communities, recognized that there is an incongruity between the position of India as an equal member of the British Empire and the existence of disabilities upon British Indians lawfully domiciled in other parts of the Empire.
They say that this was the incongruity and that this was recognized by the conference of which the Leader of the Opposition was a member, and he agreed to the resolution.
As I said before, I should like to learn what will be the position of the Prime Minister on this important question before the conference. It might be well that there should be an expression of opinion from this House on the matter so that his hands may be strengthened when he appears before that body as a member of the conference. So far as I can see, no valid reason can be urged against granting this franchise to those people. I have yet to learn any good reason which can be urged. I am sure the leader of the Opposition still has the same views on this question as he had in 1921. I heard him in a public address in Montreal, at a meeting at which Mr. Sastri was present, declaring that his views had not changed up to that time, and I have reason to believe that they are identically the same as they were then.
It is not a good thing for any country to have within its borders any people or class of people who are half slave and half free. Any person who is permitted to live in this country and who is denied the franchise, although he is a tax-payer of the country, is deprived of some of his liberties and is half free. I would rather keep those people out of this country altogether, debar them at the gates and not permit them to enter, than allow them to enter and then treat them as if they were not the equals of ourselves and as if they were slaves. I know the Prime Minister has certain notions on this matter, and I should be glad to hear them. It might be argued that this rule excluding the Hindus

Supply-Imperial Conference
from the franchise obtains only in British Columbia; that British Columbia is one of nine provinces; that in the other eight provinces or in eight-ninths of the Dominion of Canada they have the same rights as people of the white races, and that they ought to be satisfied with eight-ninths of the bargain and let it go at that.

Are the Hindus debarred
from the federal franchise in British Columbia?

Yes, and debarred also
from the local franchise in British Columbia.
It ought to be borne in mind, and I am sure it will be noted by every person in this House that inasmuch as the twelve hundred of these Hindus are residing in that one-ninth of the country where they are debarred the privilege of voting, the eight-ninths amount to nothing at all; that we may as well bar them altogether as bar them in the province in which they have elected to reside. Therefore,
I claim we would be doing our duty as citizens of the British Empire in granting this franchise to the Hindus. We would be carrying out the undertaking of the leader of the Opposition, and we ourselves would be benefiting by the fact that every person who comes to this country, who has a stake in the community, who pays his taxes and who is an honourable citizen, should be given the same rights as we have, whether his skin be dark or fair. I should be glad to hear the views of the Prime Minister on this subject.

I propose to deal only very
briefly with the remarks of the hon member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), who has expressed the desire to allow Hindus to vote in Canada, and to deal for a moment with the allegations-I will not call them arguments, because that would be sophistical -with which he attempted to buttress his position. I apologize to the House for proposing to take up time at this late hour of the session. It is only the urgent necessity of the case that compels me to do so. I wish the limits of the narrow confines of parliamentary language allowed me to express as the poet says "in language warm as could be breathed or penned" my opinion of the hon. gentleman in precipitating this subject into the political arena at this late hour. I am sorry to see that several of the members for British Columbia either are not in the House or have left. Consequently it behooves the one or two who are here to speak for the province. There is little difficulty m that because we know British Columbia is a unit on the subject. I can well say that this
is neither the time nor the place to discuss this subject.
The hon. gentleman based his remarks up-jn the resolution which he read from the order paper, a resolution which stands and has been standing in his name for nearly five months. We have been sitting through the apparently interminable length of this long weary session, not having accomplished very much either, as some people think, and that resolution was on the Order Paper and it was pasied over again and again either at the wish of the hon. member himself or because he was not present to do his duty in the House, while members from British Columbia have been sitting here in session day and night attending to the business. The hon. member reminds me of a beautiful butterfly; he descends at periods. Or
like a comet he comes along with a very doubtful periodicity and tells the House to do thus and so, and then flits away to some other scene or field of activity, or of rest and repose. Whether it is relaxation in the way of business, pleasure, or passion, I know not.
It is for him to say. But I do know that if he had been doing his duty this matter would have been debated in the proper way by hon. members long ago. The hon. member mentioned the number of Hindus in British Columbia and he was careful to say that he had been "told" there were 1,200. Let me inform him that he has been told wrong; the number of Hindus that came into the country in the years prior to July 1st, 1920, was 5.297. I suppose some of them have gone since then to the country from whose bourne no traveller returns, but not many of them; and there is a long distance between 5,000 and 1,200. But that statement by the hon. member is quite as near the facts as most of his other logic on the subject.
Where did the hon. member obtain his figures?

The statement from which I obtained them is headed "Nationalities of 'immigrants for the fiscal year ended Maich 31st, 1920, and total immigration since July Jst, 1920." It begins with the British and goes through the list of other nationalities. It is a long statement and I will not weary the House by reading it. It was prepared by the librarian and the statistician of British Columbia.
Has the hon. gentleman the census figures from the department at Ottawa?

I got these figures from the librarian and the statistician of British Columbia.
Supply-Imperial Conference
I understand the hon. gentleman to say that they were prepared by the librarian.
And the statistician as well, I said.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman did not observe that the figures do not take account of emigrants, a great many of whom have gone South.

We are told that if we dd not pass the resolution or adhere to the principle suggested by the hon. member there will be a sore spot against Canada in the minds of the people of India. That point was dwelt upon very strongly on a previous occasion. Well, we shall not be alone in that respect, for the same precise conditions prevail, as regards India, in New Zealand, South Africa and Australia, and if you add Canada to the list what considerable portion of the British Empire is left for India to be sore at? She will lave to be sore at the whole Empire and noo against this one particular section of it.
Does the hon. member pretend that Australia and New Zealand were not parties to the understanding that the Hindus should be given the franchise?

I am not pretending anything. The subject is too serious for any pretence, and indeed no pretence is needed to bolster up my arguments; for what I say is true. In New Zealand the people of the Orient, including Hindus, are not allowed to vote, and if the hon. gentleman insists on corrobora-lion I may say that I have the Australian act here from which I can quote if necessary.
I do not want to detain the House however. It will be sufficient for me to observe that in Australia the Franchise Act says that no one born in Asia shall vote. I think that covers Indians. And as regards South Africa, the delegates from that part of the Empire hurried 10 put themselves right on this subject at the conference. They said, "We have no pari, nor lot with this principle and will not countenance it." They spoke right up and said they would have nothing to do with it.
That was the only Dominion that did protest and my hon. friend knows it.

They went further in their opposition, because as late as April 18th in a press cable from Capetown the Minister of the Interior in the government of South Africa is reported thus:
He proposed to introduce a measure providing for residential and trading segregation next session.

That was in reference to Indians and it does not look as though they propose to take the Hindus to their heart and bosom in the matter of the franchise or in any other way:	Tllat disposes of that portion of the
British Empire.
Now my hon. friend drew a pitiful picture of the condition of these poor suffering people who are deprived of something which he represented as being almost as priceless to them as freedom itself, namely, the right to vote. Well, let us see what their condition was in the country from whence they came. The hon. member suggested that India was in the same position as Canada in regard to this matter. I am surprised that he should advance such a statement. Why, it is only since 1921, which is only two years ago-and all these Hindus came to this country long before that, when there was not even the faintest pretence at suffrage in India-that there was any form of popular legislature established in India. I have by me the year book, but I will not Pead from it. But there are 103 elected representatives in India at the present time in addition to a few nominated members; and as against 103 elected representatives there is a population in India of 247,000,000; so that on the basis of manhood suffrage each representative would have a constituency of 2,500,000. That is patently absurd, but it shows how much restricted is the franchise in India; and yet the hon. gentleman wants to give them the full advantage of our Canadian manhood suffrage. A constituency of 2,500,0001 How I should like to be a member there. On the basis of our population and our unit of representation it would mean that one Hindu in 8,000 would vote in Canada, and if the hon. gentleman will whittle down to that proportion the rep-iesentation which he would like to extend to these people in Canada I should not mind that fraction voting. But that is the proportion ; it would be one in 8,000 of these downtrodden people who would have the right to vote in Canada if they were subjected here to the conditions that exist in India-conditions that did not come into being until long after they left their own country.
Surely the association with men like my hon. friend would be beneficial to these 1,200 Hindus in British Columbia?

The 5,927 Hindus in British Columbia do not associate with me. Now if it were thought advisable in any part of the world to give these people the vote or to allow them to have a voice in their government it surely would be in India where they

Supply-Imperial Conference
have lived all their lives and where they would be conversant with all the conditions and all the peculiar troubles that concern them. But no; they are to be transplanted here to a country of which they are ignorant in the extreme. They know not our language nor do they know our customs; and what is more, they do not want to know them. Yet we are to bring them here and give thqm the franchise such as we and our women enjoy, although we deny to the aborigines of Canada, the native sons of the country, brought up and educated here, the very privilege which the hon. member is anxious to give to the same class of people bom in some other country. An effort was made a year or two ago to give to the native Indians in this country the franchise in a limited degree but it proved a failure; but notwithstanding that denial to the aborigines of our own country the hon. member desires to give to the same class, so far as their position in the strata of society is concerned, people of the same standard of intelligence, the right to vote. He wants to give this right to people bom in India, a heathen and many of them a debased class of people.
Would my hon. friend deny entirely the franchise to these Hindu citizens, or would he be prepared to give them a limited franchise?

So far as British Columbia is concerned I deny them that right absolutely, but I will suggest a scheme later on for partially meeting the hon. member's proposal. Now we are told we must give way in this matter to that good old stalking horse "Imperial reasons." I think I am as much an imperialist as the hon. gentleman opposite, and I recall that a few weeks ago I suggested that it would not besmirch our reputations as Canadians if we accepted a title of honour from the sovereign that reigns over us. I cannot recall that I got much sympathy from the hon. members in that respect, but that surely was an indication of my imperialism.

I hope I may be allowed to interrupt my hon. friend in order to explain my position on the question he has just introduced. Notwithstanding the vote of the majority of hon. members on this side, I did my utmost to see that honours should De accepted in this country so long as Canada formed a part of the British Empire. I only desire to make my position clear on this question.
I am glad to find that there is one more intelligent man in the House.

May I tell my hon. friend
that my imperialism and love of Empire is based on something that is sounder than mere ribbons or orders or decorations.

I could not help thinking
the other day, when we were passing the annuity to Dr. Banting and seeking in that way to do him honour, that that was one occasion on which perhaps' it might have been well if Dr. Banting had been able to receive a title of honour from the sovereign and the people he has so well served. It is said that we are asked to lay on the altar of imperialism this right. Mr. Chairman, we are not asked to do so by imperialism at all; we are asked by Mr. Sastri and a few amiable faddis-ts who follow him-that is all. Their audacity in asking is equalled only by their ignorance of what the granting of the request would mean. Amiable they are,
I admit it; faddists they are-the class of people that send bouquets to the cell of the condemned prisoner. Faddists they are from beginning to end, not imperialists. But Mr. Sastri, with his beautiful and flowery language, captivates their shallow minds, and they are following him.
Is the hon. gentleman referring to the members who compose the Imperial Conference when he speaks about shallow minds?

No, I am not. Did the hon. member think I was? Now, let us pause for a moment and see how the Imperial authorities regarded this question. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier says they promised -"promised" was the word he used a few minutes ago-the Hon. Mr. Sastri this concession; and in speaking to the Prime Minister he used the word "undertaking;" he said that an undertaking had been given by the leader of the Opposition. 9 p.m. ist; he was Secretary of State I think, or Secretary of the Colonies at the time. Here is the report of the conference that the member alludes to at which this question was brought up, and this is what Winston Churchill says-I will quote only two sentences:
I think there is only one ideal that the British Empire can set before itself in this regard, and that is that there should be no barrier of race, colour, or creed which should prevent any man by merit from reaching any station if he is fitted for it.

Does the hon. gentleman not see a difference between being hopeful of obtaining the franchise in a municipality in British Columbia and obtaining the franchise from the parliament of Canada? There is surely some difference.

The hon. gentleman tells us-and here I may be treading on dangerous ground, because he is a skilful lawyer-that the reason the Hindus do not now come to Canada is that they have to get a passport which is not obtainable from the Indian government. the franchise and that would be the end of it. Well, that would not be the end of it. Five thousand voters in British Columbia would have a very powerful influence on the electorate and on the result of the election. Would it be the advancement of Canada as a whole or of British Columbia as a province, or would it be to secure some advantage for that colony of Hindus? Would it not be the latter ? Would it not be a case of those five thousand votes going to the candidate who would undertake to let these people bring in their women, their relations, or their friends? These votes would go solidly for the man who would do that or the party that would do that, and five thousand votes, especially in a provincial election, would cut an important figure. Moreover, the voters would soon cease to be only five thousand in number; they would increase very rapidly.
Another point is this: If you grant this privilege to the Hindus, can you deny it to others under similar conditions? But Japanese and Chinese are born in British Columbia, which is far more than the Hindu is. He too is a British subject, I admit; but when the oriental is born in British Columbia of naturalized parents how can we logically and with any sense of decency withhold the vote from him when he attains the age of twenty-one when we have given it to the Hindu, a worse fitted man, a man untrained, unaccustomed to our language? If we grant it to the Hindu how can we deny it to the oriental bom in British Columbia who speaks the same tongue as we do? It follows as the night the day that if we grant it to Hindus we must grant it to the other orientals.

Is it not a fact that a
person born in any part of the British dominions, whether of British parentage or not, is regarded as a British subject? Japanese who are bom in a British dominion are British subjects, whether their parents are naturalized or not.

Certainly they are; I was
not dealing with that aspect of it. I was saying that if we give the Hindus, who are British subjects, the vote, we should have to give it also to Japanese British subjects born in British Columbia. It is logical that we

should do so. Let me quote from what the Bishop of London said at a big meeting at London-I saw it in the paper only yesterday. He evidently had been over here, and this is what the report says:
He had been preaching in London, immigration to Canada, but he found it very unpopular, for the following reason: There were, he said, 38,000 Chinese in British Columbia and 5,000 Japanese babies were born every year on the Pacific coast. He gave it as his opinion that unless Canada was populated to a larger degree by people from the British Isles, the white inhabitants would eventually become extinct in the Dominion.
That is an exaggerated statement, as we know, but it indicates the influence that these conditions have upon the point of view in England. I would not for the world-in fact, the rules forbid me-reflect upon the hon. member's motives. But this resolution is what I might call a chart which guides his course to the goal he has in view. If you will look at the next resolution on the order paper following the one upon which he has based his remarks, you will find that it is also by him and it embodies a proposal that all the bars should be let down and that wholesale immigration into Canada should be permitted. I wonder if these two resolutions could have anything to do with each other? I wonder if the one is the doormat leading to the door of the other? I saw the other day in a medical journal that a new alkaloid had been discovered; I believe the name of it is scopolamin; I cannot pronounce it correctly. It has this peculiar quality that if it is administered in small doses it prevents, to put it in the medical sense, the inhibition of will, or to put it in plain language it compels a man to speak the truth without removing from him his ability to speak. I wonder if we applied a small dose of this to the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier whether we would find that his motion was actuated by the imperialism of which he talks or with a desire to reach the next motion on the order paper and open the door to practically every kind of immigration. In case the hon. gentleman should be upset by my suggestion I would inform him that I would only prescribe for him a very small dose because I understand that if too strong a dose
is given the effects are permanent, and I know he is a lawyer and might find that awkward.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me if he has any large quantity of that drug on hand and if he is able to spare a little of it?

Just one word more and I am done. I said at the beginning that this was not the place to discuss the question, and it is not. It is not a Dominion matter. It is a British Columbia problem. Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's. Let us settle this problem in British Columbia. It has no more to do with the other provinces than if I were to interfere with some of the local customs and traditions of the province of Quebec. It is a British Columbia problem for this reason: the franchise invariably originates in the province. It is entirely a provincial matter. I would quote Sir Wilfrid Laurier who in 1917 laid down in most emphatic language in paragraph after paragraph that the true basis of our Dominion franchise under the British North America Act is the provincial franchise. He used the word "originates". The franchise originates in the province and then has to be translated into the Dominion act. The right hon. leader of the Opposition last year is on record in Hansard to substantially the same effect. He said that where prohibitions existed in the provincial franchise we carried them into the Dominion franchise, and if that is correct, and here we have two of the ablest men of our time on this subject, then the thing for us to do is to take this subject up in British Columbia and deal with it there, and the province of British Columbia would know how to deal with such a subject in the best interests of Canada as well as the best interests of the province. I would ask this House, therefore, not to force upon us in British Columbia a thing which is unconstitutional, and is against our customs and bitterly against our desires. There is no precedent for it whatever. Talk about creating a sore spot. Do this and you would create a canker in British Columbia that we as a nation would never recover from.
Let us go back to Quebec. I use that province as an illustration because it is the most united in its population and in its characteristics. If the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier is so enamoured of this proposition of which he has talked to us let him go to Quebec and get Quebec to pass a franchise law giving the Hindus and all kinds of orientals the right to vote there. Let him try that out for a while in the province of Quebec, and if these people value the franchise so



Supply-Imperial Conference
highly British Columbia will gladly send them down to Quebec. We will wish them Godspeed and pay their fares. We will be delighted to see them go, and see how the hon. member will get on under those conditions. Is it not fair to use the hon. gentleman's own argument against himself? He wants to give them the franchise. Then let him give it them in his own province. Then such a wave of reform will spread from Quebec that perhaps we in British Columbia may follow his example-perhaps. But let him begin with Quebec. Let him ask the Trench race, those men who have maintained for scores of generations the purity of their race, of their language, and of their religion and traditions to give up all that and. to take on the same plane of equality as themselves the lower strata of these orientals such as I have described, take them on the same level of political equality, take them on the same level of business equality, for the one follows the other, and take them on the same level of social equality for you cannot stop at business equality. Take them on the same plane of domestic equality, for you must go the whole length if you make a start. Ask the people of Quebec if they want to do that, and see what the answer is. I am sure they would repudiate the suggestion with scorn and indignation, and therefore I ask these Frenchmen, of whom our hon. Speaker is such an illustrious type, courtly eons of a courtly race, to give us in British Columbia only the same privilege that they would ask and demand for themselves. We ask no more and demand no less. We only ask that they shall treat us as they themselves would like to be treated, and therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope and trust that our representatives at this conference will go there with a determination to see that they preserve at that conference the right of British Columbia and of every other province to prescribe its own franchise, a right which I venture to suggest is the free right of a free people.

It is not my intention to take up the time of the House for the ground has been fully covered by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I say this though, that we in British Columbia want no more Hindus. Never did I value Canada and the laws of Canada more highly than when a boat-load of Hindus came from India to the port of Vancouver and was refused admittance to this country and sent back home by the previous government. I hope this government will maintain that stand. We have on the coast of British Columbia, Chinamen and Japs running our stores. They are running

the white people out. We have the Greeks there running our hotels and we have the Jews running our second-hand stores, and now some people want to bring in the Hindus to run our mills. We have had enough of that in the past, and if this government wants to cast British Columbia adrift let her cast it adrift and let her east it adrift before any more orientals come in. If they do, we white people out on the Pacific will prevent any more orientals coming to British Columbia.

It is not my purpose to answer the wild harangue of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. It would be impossible for me to do it. It does not require an answer. It is not susceptible of an answer. I notice that these gentlemen from British Columbia as soon as any subject is brought before the House see in it danger. They see in the Japanese, the Chinese and the Hindus something which they have reason to fear. So far as I know these people, they not only work but they seem to be the only men who do the work in that part of the country. But it is not for me here to criticize British Columbia. I am looking at this matter from the wider, from the national standpoint. I do not care what franchise the British Columbians have for their provincial legislature. That is a matter that does not concern me. But this is a matter which concerns the Dominion of Canada, and that is the reason why I raise it here in this House.
My hon. friend referred to the fact that I had had this resolution on the order paper for a considerable time and only brought it up in the last hours of the session. Well, he knows very well, and I need not tell him, I think he is a victim like myself of the fact that private members' day was taken away somewhat early in the session and consequently private members could not discuss the resolutions standing in their names on the order paper. There were all kinds of resolutions placed on the order paper, some of them by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.
The hon. member's resolution is dated February 21st.

It is dated February 23rd, and I did not have an opportunity of bringing it before the House before private members' day was taken away. I will admit as the hon. member has referred to it that I did not attend perhaps as assiduously as he did. and it is very possible that when the resolution was called I was not here to go on with it, but that ought not to be a reason for not

debating the matter when it can be legally-brought before the House. The hon. member seems to make a point of the fact that some British Columbia members have left for their homes, and he insinuated that I had taken occasion to bring this matter up in the absence of these members, but I can assure the hon. member that he is a host in himself and it is not necessary for any British Columbia member other than himself to be here when the subject of oriental immigration or franchise is brought up. I want to put upon Hansard a despatch from Simla, India, which has appeared in the daily papers. It is dated June 26:
Indians would retaliate against the Dominions
Simla, India, June 26.-In connection with the problem relating to the status of Indians overseas, there is a growing demand here for retaliatory legislation imposing on subjects of the dominions anti colonies similar disabilities to those imposed on Indian settlers in those countries. A leading democrat has given notice of a private permissive bill in the legislative assembly and three unofficial resolutions have also been laid on the table urging the government to legislate in the direction of reciprocity.
The adverse decision by the United. States supreme court regarding the naturalization of Indians has strengthened the elements favoring retaliation.
What is the date of that?

It was dated June 26, 1923 It is a despatch from Simla, India. May I also refer to an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of this week which is quite favourable to British Indians.
Fair play for British Indians
During last winter Rt. Hon. Mr. Sastri, a member of the King's Privy Council, visited Canada for the purpose of impressing upon the government the right of British India subjects resident in Canada to exercise the franchise. The request was so reasonable that on every hand Mr. Sastri received sympathy.
Is my hon. friend going to give the name of the writer of that article?
I can assure the hon. gentleman that I did not write it nor did I inspire it.
The House would be interested in knowing the writer.
This is an editorial in the Montreal Gazette.
I thought it was not customary to read extracts unless the writer's name was given?
Editorials from the Montreal Gazette have been read in this House. With tome of them I agreed, with others I did not. This is one with which I agree.
Perhaps Sastri wrote it?

Let me continue:
Yet no action has been taken. The parliamentary session is now drawing to a close, and it may be too late to initiate new legislation despite the apothegm that it's never too late to mend. Yet it is disappointing that the government has not moved to the end of justice, regrettable from both Empire and Canadian standpoints. Chinese enjoy and exercise the franchise, but East Indians are deprived of the right. Why? Surely not because the latter are British subjects? The larger question of opening the door to admission to Canada of all races is not involved in this matter. What Mr. Sastri urged was the fairness of granting to Indians domiciled in Canada the same political rights as other classes of Canadians enjoy, and it is difficult to understand the delay of the government in granting the concession. There is more than moral right involved, and more than Empire interest. Canada does some trade with British India, and desires to extend the same, but if the East Indians conceive the notion that Canada is a country of prejudices, narrow views, and illiberality, it may easily happen that British Indians will turn from trade with it, and look askance at the pretence of Empire solidity. Antipathy to Canadian business agencies in India is already being cultivated. A straw serves to show how the wind blows. The Parsee Chamber of Commerce recently adopted a series of resolutions of which the preamble was as follows: "Whereas the treatment meted out to Indians in the colonies has been unsatisfactory and has continued to be so in an acute form notwithstanding the efforts of the Indian public and the government of India to get the situation altered, this Assembly now resolves that the government of India should henceforth, and until the matters complained of are fully remedied, adopt the principle of retaliation towards the nationals of the colonies."
The spirit of that resolution does not make for Empire unity, nor give hope of increasing connection commercially between Canada and India. It may be that the larger question of an open door to Indian immigration may be referred to the coming Imperial Conference, though that is debatable, but of this there is no room for doubt East Indians domiciled in Canada should be given the right of franchise on the same terms and conditions as are applied to other residents. That was the request of Mr. Sastri, and it ought to be complied with.
If my hon. friend had a daughter would he want her to live and associate with the Hindu?

I would say this: I have
three daughters, and I would rather see them associate with respectable Hindus than with some white men I know. But that is not the question which comes up here to-night. It is not a question of the association of white men with the duskier races or anything of the kind. The question-
That is exactly what it is, Mr. Chairman. It is forcing these coloured races in among white people, and making the people of British Columbia associate with them.

Let me remind my hon.
friend that the people of British Columbia are associating with them now.

They are associating with them and would not associate with them any more if they had this right than they do now. I trust this parliament will rise above these narrow considerations which have been mentioned by the member for Comox-Alberni and do its duty. I think it will be generally admitted that my hon. friend (Mr. Neill) is perhaps not the best person to speak on this matter without prejudice. He is one of the most prejudiced members in this House-

-from British Columbia on the question

-of orientals. He positively glories in it. He says: "I am against orientals in every form; I am against their immigration, I am against their franchise." We perhaps are
somewhat in the dark in entering upon a discussion such as this, because of not having placed before us any very definite agenda as to the subjects that are likely to come, before either the Imperial or the Economic conference. A great deal will depend on the general intellectual background and attitude of

our delegates there. When we had the discussion the other day on the Halibut treaty I am sure a great many of us must have been very much pleased indeed at the attitude of the Prime Minister with regard to the relationship which should exist between Canada and the Empire; and I feel very confident that if he can retain that position, in the midst of the surroundings in which he will find himself placed on the other side of the water, Canada will be comparatively safe.
It is, perhaps, rather fitting in a way and yet somewhat of an ill omen, that accompanying the Prime Minister there should be the Acting Minister of National Defence. Unfortunately, in the past imperialism and militarism have been very closely associated, but I trust that this appointment does not mean that the matters chiefly to be discussed are military in character.
Just in passing I have often wondered as we have sat here during these last months, as to how long it will be before the appointment of the Acting Minister of National Defence shall be endorsed by the people. It has seemed to me that it is of the very essence of our British institutions that a man should not become the head of an important government department without his appointment being definitely endorsed by the people.
I could think of no better development that could take place in international affairs than that we should have the whole question placed on some other than a military basis. Ideally, I have no doubt whatever that the appointment of the Minister of Justice is the best that could be made. From a practical standpoint, I wish the Minister of Justice were not so closely associated with the big financiers of this country. Some of us believe that the big financial interests ought not to dominate the Imperial or Economic Conferences. I wish that in some way it were possible that the great producing classes of this country, the farmers and the labouring people, could be represented on the Economic Conference. I do not propose to-night to discuss the legal and constitutional aspects of our relations to the Empire. These have been dealt with by our constitutional authorities and our legal friends. A great deal of stress has often been laid by them upon precedent. It seems to me the time has come when we shall have to make new precedents, when we shall have to view the situation as it actually is to-day, and act, having regard to the developments which have taken place in recent years. We all recognize that there are certain sentimental attachments-I do not use that word in a disparaging sense at all-

Supply-Imperial Conference
which unite Canada with the Motherland. We remember our common origin. We remember that we have a common language, that we have common traditions and common institutions. These things, after all, are the most fundamental in maintaining the ties that unite this country with other countries composing the British Commonwealth of nations. But I should like to emphasize that loyalty does not in any way mean subserviency. Too often we have people on the floor of this House and elsewhere throughout the country deprecating any criticisms of policies which are regarded as British, or which are named British. Rather it would appear that in the effort to decide our own policies according to our best lights, we are preeminently British in spirit. Some people have still the colonial mind. They think of themselves as inferiors. They have what I suppose the psycho-analysts would call inferiority complex. I cannot conceive that we can take our real place in the British Empire until we outgrow that and remember that we in Canada are just as fit to discuss the affairs of the Empire as are the people in any other part of the Empire.
I should like to endorse a great deal of what has been said by the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). It seems to me he has placed the whole situation on a proper basis. I cannot but deprecate the attitude taken by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) with regard to the orientals. He has tried to disparage almost every other nationality than our own, the Chinese, the Japanese and the Greeks and the Jews. No, I think it was the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) who enumerated these particular groups. I cannot see that we	are going to	getvery far by	a	narrow bigotry	of
that kind. The member for Comox-Alberni, in referring to the fact that the orientals have no vote, said he was afraid that if the Indians should be given a vote it would result in a vote being given to other orientals. I should like to ask why not? I admit that I do not believe in admitting large numbers of these people at the present time because we are not in a fit position to take care of them. I do not believe we can have an intermingling of these races under existing conditions, but it is one thing to say to the orientals "it is not well for you to come in at the present time," and it is quite another thing after we have allowed them to come in and they are citizens with us, rate-payers with us and all the rest of it, to deny them
the fundamental rights of citizenship. Last summer when I was walking through Stanley Park I could not but think of the member for Comox-Alberni. At one spot I stood before a beautiful monument erected to the memory of the Japanese soldiers who had fallen during the great war in the cause of what we were told was British liberty. I cannot quite see just where is the British justice in accepting the sacrifice which these people made for the British Empire and then refusing them the common rights of citizenship. The member for Comox-Alberni spoke of the Indian people as a heathen and debased class. Any one who has had the most elementary knowledge of the great philosophies of India must realize how far the member is from at all correctly representing the situation. Even out in British Columbia several years ago, when I visited the Sikh temple in Vancouver, where several hundred Indians were met, and heard one educated Indian speaking to his fellow countrymen, and holding before them the very highest ideals, I could not help but realize our narrowness. I believe that, in dealing with these matters, difficult as they are-and I know they are difficult-we should rise above narrow prejudice and look at them from a little bit more of a world point of view.
There are several principles that have oc-cured to me, to which I would like to refer very briefly, which it would seem to me we ought to adhere to at this Imperial Conference; the first, clear understanding that from this time on Canada must be essentially autonomous. We need not worry as to our exact relationship to the other parts of the Empire. I suppose in time some arrangement will develop, through a series of conferences or something of that kind, which will enable us to keep in touch with other parts of the world, but the biggest thing we can emphasize is our own autonomy. I do not know that the position of labour on this point has ever been closely defined, but I would say that, on the whole, labour in this country echoes the thought of labour in the Old Country, and hence I should like to read a paragraph or two of the famous draft programme of the British labour party, as published several years ago.

Let us hear from British Columbia.
Mr. W7OODSWORTH:	There are other
parts of the world than British Columbia. The paragraph 1 refer to reads:
We desire to maintain the most intimate relations with the labor party overseas. Like them, we have no sympathy with the projects of "Imperial Federa-

tion," in so far as these imply the subjection to a common imperial legislature wielding coercive power (including dangerous facilities for coercive imperial taxation and for enforced military service), either of the existing self-governing dominions, whose autonomy would be thereby invaded; or of the United Kingdom, whose freedom of democratic self-development would be thereby hampered; or if India and the colonial dependencies, which would thereby run the risk of being further exploited for the benefit of a " White Empire." And we carry the idea further. As regards our relations to foreign countries, we disavow and disclaim any desire or intention to dispossess or to impoverish any other state or nation. We seek no increase of territory. We disclaim all idea of "economic war." We ourselves object to all protective customs tariffs; but we hold that each nation must be left free to do what it thinks best for its own economic development, without thought of injuring others. We believe that nations are in no way damaged by each other's prosperity or commercial progress; but, on the contrary, that they are actually themselves mutually enriched thereby. We would therefore put an end to the old entanglements and justifications of secret diplomacy and the formation d*f leagues against leagues.
I would not urge a narrow nationalism in this regard. There are some who have even on the floor of this House suggested that we should cut ourselves almost entirely free from either the Motherland or international councils. The world has developed past that stage. There is such a close interrelation between its different parts to-day, such an essential unity, that no one nation can any longer live to itself. Canada cannot possibly turn the clock backward. Canada canot possibly play the role of an independent nation. We must meet with the other nations throughout the world; but let us meet with them recognizing that we are full grown and free to co-operate with them in all that will make for the common welfare.
We have been very frequently told that we in this country have nothing to do but to endorse what has been called British policy. I should like to pause for a moment to ask: What is British policy? Surely we do not have to read history very closely to recognize that British policy is as changeable as the policy of any other country; that it changes with each successive government; that it changes from year to year. I suppose we might talk about Canada's National policy. That, perhaps, is the most stable thing that I know anything about, because the Liberal party may come or the Conservative party
I Mr. Woodsworth.l
may come, but there is little difference-we have the self-same protective policy as we have had it for many years. At the same time we remember that there are considerable changes of policy from year to year. We cannot speak definitely of a British policy. It was the British policy a few months ago to bring Great Britain to the verge of another great war. A few months later the particular group that advocated that policy was discredited, and we had a new British policy. So I would suggest that the policy called the British policy, to which we have often been asked to subscribe, has been a policy simply of a little group of militarists and imperialists. I would venture to suggest to the Prime Minister and others who go in this delegation, that possibly they would be a great deal more nearly in line with the fundamental sympathies and ideals of the Canadian people if they followed not so much the representations of some of the old-time diplomats of Great Briitain, as the representations of the more humble people represented by the British Labour party.
With regard to our international relations, there are several points, I think, that ought to be held before us clearly at this time. I should like to quote a few paragraphs from a recent debate in the British House of Commons and to put forward the positions taken on the floor of that House as fairly representing the positions taken by many of us in this country. On May 10, in the House of Commons, Sir John Simon raised the question of a certain decree issued by the commission which is governing the Saar, or rather misgoverning it under the League of Nations. Mr. Asquith supported Sir John Simon. Lord Robert Cecil broadened out the debate and raised the general problem of Franco-German relations. In the course of that debate Mr. E. D. Morel gave utterance to some sentiments which I should like to place before this House. He said:
The real issue in this matter is not reparations. It never has been reparations. It is not security. It never has been security. The real issue in this matter is whether or not the present rulers of France are going to succeed in their fixed determined aim of disrupting Germany. That is the real issue. It is an issue of very great importance not only to France and Germany, but to the whole of the continent of Europe and to ourselves. All these discussions about reparations and security are really completely artificial when you are faced with a situation such as you are facing to-day-when a French army is paralysing the heart and lungs of industrial Germany, when the Saar valley is being virtually annexed to France under the cloak of the League of Nations, when the whole of the civil administration of the Rhineland is being ruthlessly stamped out and the whole country is being gallicized. Deportations to-day amount
