to over 23,400 persons, including 33 editors, 5 Roman Catholic priests, 10 Protestant clergymen, and 150 teachers. This, I repeat, is the real issue-whether France is going to succeed in disrupting Germany. This country can no longer afford to ignore the real issue. The interest of our working classes, the interests of our commercial classes, and our national security are being more and more affected, and French policy is threatening more and more the peace, the immediate peace, of the world	
What is the truth? Put bluntly-and I shall make no reference whatever to French armaments as to which a great deal has recently been disclosed-the truth is this: The French General Staff is organizing the new Europe for war.
And he goes on to give in some detail the conditions which warrant him in making that statement. With regard to the Saar valley, Mr. Charles Buxton stated:
Here is a great miltary occupation going on, not by the League of Nations at all, not under the Treaty at all, because the Treaty says that you have to have a force formed of the population of the Saar itself. There is nothing of the kind. The French troops began, I think, speaking from recollection, at 2,000 or 3,000. They rose to 4,000, and have now risen to 10,000 men, for a wretchedly small district as regards size, and for a population, as I have said, of considerably under 1,000,000. Moreover, as I am reminded, they have their wives and families with them quartered on the country.
With regard to the Ruhr he said:
The hon. member for Thanet (Mr. Harmsworth) has said something about the smooth and easy working of this-occupation of the Ruhr.
I would like to know what bearing this has on the Hindu question.

It is hardly necessary to remind the House, although it might be necessary to remind the hon. member, that the Hindu question is not the only question that has to be discussed at the Imperial Conference.
He has ignored the fact that there prevails a reign of terror among the workers. He did not even pay any regard to the fact that a very large number of them have been shot down. The number amounts, if I have added up the figures rightly, to 52 who have already been killed, the majority of them working men, generally on the way to or from their work, suspected for aught I know of some evil intention or other, but in many cases with no overt act proved against them whatsoever, but simply shot as they were going about in the ordinary course of their business.
From what paper is my hon. friend quoting?

From the Official Debates of the British House of Commons. With regard to the Russian situation, too, I desire to give another brief quotation as to the attitude taken by those whom we labour people in this country regard as essentially representing our position in the Old Land. Mr. Ponsonby said:
The bottom of the trouble is our refusal to recognize The Russian government. The question, of recognition
is one of very great importance. Recognition of a government does not depend on its quality or its methods but purely and solely on its stability. That is the only point that ought to be taken into account in recognizing the sovereignty of another nation. I would refer the hon. gentleman in charge of the vote to the books on international law, and he will find there is no instance in history of so long a period elapsing in which a government- which has shown stability from the fact that after five and a-half years it is more firmly established'-has been denied recognition in the way we have denied it.
Who made the speech in the British House of Commons from which lhe hon. gentleman has quoted?
The first quotation was from Mr. Morel, the second from Mr. Charles Buxton, and the third from Mr. Ponsonby.
I thought you mentioned Lord Robert Cecil and Sir John Simon.

I mentioned them as taking part previously in the debate, but the quotations I gave were from those whom I have just mentioned. Without going at all mto the details of these great questions which are before Great Britain and Europe I would suggest that the representatives of this country urge upon the Imperial Conference the necessity for a modification of the Peace Treaty of Versailles, looking towards getting a little bit nearer the terms of the Armistice. I shall not weary the House to-night by quoting from that standard book of Mr. John M. Keyne's, in which he shows the iniquity of the Peace treaty and how far It is from the terms under which our enemy laid down his arms. I would refer anyone seeking information to (hat book by an expert.
We have all read it.
I am sure it is sufficient to convince anyone who has read it.
Did the hon. member lead Tardieu's answer to that book?
I have read a number of them but not that one.
You have a one-sided view of the situation if you have not read it.

I would also urge
upon our representatives that they insist upon the fixing of reparations in some form that will allow for the reconstruction of Europe and the bringing about of those stable conditions on which alone permanent peace depends. With regard to the League of Nations, I would point out, as I did in a previous discussion, the importance of making the league inclusive and democratic in its character.

Supply-Imperial Conference
The whole world has looked forward to some sort of institution, some super-national assembly, that would be a meeting place for the various nations for the interchange of opinions, where relations could be explained in order better to be understood, and where in some wajr discussion would be substituted for war as the arbiter in every dispute. I cannot see how this can be accomplished so long as any nation is excluded from what purports to be a league of the nations of the world; nor do I think it can be brought about until such a league has become more democratic than the existing one. It should be clearly recognized that the old policy of regarding armaments as a guarantee of pease has absolutely failed; and instead of fortifying Singapore, as I believe is being done at the present time, with the consent of, if not under pressure from some of the other dominions-instead of going still further on the road towards the preparation for war by air, we should recognize frankly that war has been a failure so far as the establishment of international peace is concerned. If these principles could be successfully maintained at the conference and some progress made in the direction of having them implemented the conference would serve an eminently useful purpose. Undoubtedly at the present time there is need for a better understanding between the various peoples of the world. But that is not sufficient. As the editor of a farm paper wrote me only a few days ago, until definite economic reforms are achieved war is inevitable; so long as the condtions making for war remain there can be no escape from it. I would urge upon men who have the great responsibility of representing Canada that they carry these ideals with them across the waters. We know that when President Wilson crossed to the great conference in France he carried with him the ideals of the majority of the people of America, and I think of a very great many other countries. Unfortunately, owing to a series of circumstances, he seemed to have been unable to impress his ideals upon that conference so that we find the treaty altogether different from any instrument which would really express those ideals. The result has been the disturbed condition that has existed in Europe since that time. 1 I should like our representatives in going overseas to carry with them some of the ideals that are so common among the ordinary people of this country. We are longing for' peace and for economic justice. We are a people whose forefathers came to this country prepared to 
work hard in the hope that they might be able to found homes for themselves and their children. We are a people who in the pioneer days knew a great deal of neighbourliness. We are not anxious to interfere with other people's affairs; wei are anxious to live and let live; and if we can only carry out these homely virtues in international relationships then the coming conference will be of value not merely to us, but as well to the world at large.

I would call the attention
of the committee to the conditions that existed in pre-war days. Europe at that time was an armed camp. Large nations were arming one against the other, and the onlv epoch in history to which that time can be fittingly compared' was the Napoleonic era. But conditions have changed considerably since then. A conference was called in 1909 when the different communities comprising the British commonwealth assembled to discuss some very important questions. I believe that Australia undertook at that time to establish the nucleus of an Australian navy, while Canada undertook some naval contributions and New Zealand gave a promise of cash. Then came the war and all the concomitant conditions of war, and we find today an entirely different world from that which we knew before 1914. The great nation of Germany has almost, if not entirely, disappeared from the face of Europe as a military power and Russia is practically beyond the pale df international co-operation. In fact in Europe to-day we have about twenty-five nations in a more or less disorganized condition, each of them trying to maintain an army, all of them, perhaps, weak economically and in almost every other way. It seems to me to be one of the tragedies of the time that instead of getting together to hasten the day of peace and goodwill, the countries of Europe to-day are engendering quite a different feeling by hostile armies and hostile tariffs. They are building around themselves; they are shutting each other out; they imagine they are going to bring about prosperity in their own respective countries by having no communication with their neighbours. What is the world's greatest need at this time? I think it can be best expressed by the word that Bonar Law used when he came into power-'"tranquillity." What the world needs is tranquillity, stability, in order that men may devote themselves to the work of rebuilding, to the work of bringing back a condition of contentment and prosperity.
I would like to say just a word here in connection with the position that the United

States occupies. We all realize the great power and influence that the United States of America can have for good or for evil in the world. The United States occupies a position that has never been occupied by any other country. We speak of the United States as a nation; in reality it is a galaxy of nations, almost self-contained. They could almost build a fence around themselves and be complete in themselves. I know they require certain commodities that are necessary to civilization; yet the United States more than any othgr country can stand upon its own feet, can carry on almost without entering into communication with other lands. I do not believe, however, that anything like that is ever going to happen. I know there is a movement in the United States the purpose of which is to have that country live unto itself, to look only to its own welfare and its own prosperity. But it is only a passing phase; it will soon disappear and the United States will come back to the great position she should occupy in the world's affairs. Now, what is the view that the United States takes of the British Empire? I know we always speak of ourselves as a community of nations, each of which is complete in itself. Yet I venture to make the assertion to-day that outside of the politicians and the diplomats 10 p.m. in the United States, the general impression there is that Canada is little more than a colony of Great Britain. The great masses of the people of the United States do not, I believe, understand the position that Canada and the other nations occupy in the British Empire. The war has changed the whole aspect of our national life. I think I am correct in saying that during the war the supreme executive was composed of the British cabinet and the prime ministers of the different dominions. Canada during the war, through her sacrifice and the price she paid in that conflict, reached what may be called the status of nationhood; we realize that from the part she took in the framing of the Peace Treaty and the formation of the League of Nations. Conditions have entirely changed, and at the coming conference many important questions will have to be discussed and at least partly settled. Lloyd George's famous telegram with regard to the Chanak affair brought us very quickly to our senses and made us realize that some day we shall be forced to come to a rapid decision bearing upon the question just what position we occupy in the British Empire. I think the sentiment that was expressed in a great many quarters by a large number of the people of this Dominion in that connection was that no action should be taken by the government
of Canada without the consent of parliament. But that has not been settled; nothing is definite. These questions all remain to be settled in the future and I hope that when the decision is taken they will be settled rightly.
Will the hon. gentleman repeat that? What question is it that is not settled?
I was speaking about that famous telegram that came from England during the Chanak affair.
The Chanak affair?

The Near Eastern question.
I think I am correct in that.
I was just asking what question it was that had not been settled.

That is the question that is not settled: What position was Canada going to take when the requisition came from Great Britain? Or should war arise and assistance be sought from Canada and the other nations of the Empire, what position should we take? That is the question that is not settled. Does my right hon. friend understand my point?
No, I do not. I do not know any question that is not settled.

I imagine that a great many
questions have not been settled. If the right hon. leader of the Opposition has settled the exact position of Canada in the Empire I hope we will get the benefit of his views when he speaks on this question.

I thought the hon. gentleman said there was some question as to who decided what we would do in case of requisition. I do not know of any requisition. I certainly do not know of any question as to who decides.

Perhaps we will leave the
question, because the right hon. gentleman does not understand me, and I do not understand him; we will call it quits.
India has been mentioned several times tonight. In discussing these questions we can hardly take India into consideration. India occupies a different position from that of any of the other nations making up the British commonwealth. We speak about India as a country; in reality India comprises many countries. There are eleven distinct languages in India, to say nothing of a great variety of dialects, and I suppose for the time being at least we shall have to leave India out of

consideration. I wish only to dwell for a few moments on certain conditions affecting the position occupied by the British commonwealth as a whole.
We are all a little disappointed, perhaps, at the extent of the influence the League of Nations has had upon the world's history during the last few years. I believe that in that same league is the germ of something that will in the years to come be of inestimable benefit to the civilized world. I like to think of the British commonwealth, or of the British Empire if you will-because it does not make any difference what phrase you use to express the same meaning-I do like to think of the British Empire as being in itself a League of Nations, a beginning of that wider and better league that we hope some day will embrace the whole civilized world. I only hope the day is not far distant when the United States will enter the League and thereby lend its great influence to the cause of promoting the peace and welfare of humanity.
As to what will take place at the conference, let me say a word. While retaining our own individuality as a nation, working out our own salvation, I wish to see no slacking of the ties that bind us in that Empire, the ties of sentiment and loyalty to the British Crown. I believe, however, that any attempt to bind the ties more tightly by any agreement will perhaps have the worst effect possible-will, in fact, have results that are not anticipated. I believe that nothing can bind us with stronger chains than those feelings of loyalty and those ties of sentiment that are the strongest feelings within the human breast, and I would warn those delegates who go over to represent Canada at that conference to be very, very careful in entering into any agreement that will be binding or constitute a legal tie of any kind that might be irksome because I do believe that there is no question of the loyalty of this country to the British Empire or of our remaining an integral- part of that great Empire. The world to-day is in need of a partnership of nations. That is its greatest need, to live down the feelings of hatred and envy that are so rampant everywhere. If we need a commonwealth of nations I come back to where I began and say, shall we do anything that will lessen the ties that bind the nations of the British commonwealth into one? I say no. By every means in our power let us strengthen those ties by those feelings of affection and loyalty that I have already mentioned.
What of the future? There has been some little misunderstanding about what I have

said to-night as to our future not being settled. Our future is not settled. Our position is not settled. We claim that we are a nation, that we are, as was quoted the other night, "daughter in our mother's house but mistress in our own." That is a very good phrase and perhaps it explains our position. But, Mr. Chairman, there are a great many things to be taken into consideration. A great many difficult problems will have to be solved, and I would only hold out this idea to those who go over to Great Britain to represent Canada, and that is to be careful, to go slow, to make no rash promises. I know the temptations will be great. I have read something about those conferences that were held during Chamberlain's time, when every influence was brought to bear to tie up the daughter nations a little more firmly than they were at that time. But it came to naught and I believe that any such attempts along the same lines at the present time will work nothing but evil. I have faith in the loyalty of the people of this country. I have faith that they will do the right thing when the occasion arises, that they will be loyal. Should the Mother Country be ever in necessity I know that this country will be ready to rise to the occasion. But there is danger in making an attempt to fix hard and fast lines. I believe the safe thing, to quote again, would be "to go on from precedent to precedent" until finally the stage has been reached when we shall know exactly what our destiny is to be.
I shall not take up any more time. I have not uttered anything I know that will help those who go over to represent us other than this, that they should be very careful in making any binding promises that may be irksome, and which would perhaps do more than anything else to disintegrate this Empire that is founded upon feelings of affection and reverence and love for the Mother Country.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention to broach the subject of the Hindus and Japanese or of any other people in the world. I rather wish to speak in behalf of the Canadian people. You are not without knowing, sir, what have been my views in the past and what they are to-day.
In the last war, the Great War as it is known, I was in favour of participating within the limit of our means. I was, however, against taking part to the extent of bringing ruin upon us, as we did. That is why I rise this evening to again warn, inasmuch as my humble voice can he heard, the right hon.

Supply-Imperial Conference
Prime Minister and his colleagues who will soon cross the Atlantic to confer with the statesmen of England. My sympathy accompanies them, for British diplomats have a way of outwitting all others. Therefore, let us pray God that our own statesmen may hold their own.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) sailed across the seas in 1921. He took part in an Imperial Conference. A report of this conference was tabled in the House; however, before laying down reports of that nature, it seems that great care is taken to withhold anjdhing that one does not wish the Canadian people to know. I might ask the right hon. leader of the Opposition if he understands what I am saying. If not, let him say so, and I shall repeat it in English. I might ask him if it is not a fact that we never have an exact report of the Imperial Conferences? I wish to know what took place; not only for myself, but for the electors whom I represent in this House, the whole country wants to know whether he has pledged himself to build naval stations here and there with a view to participating in future wars of the Empire ?
For my part, sir, I Shall not oppose those who wish to go and fight for the British Empire, so long as they do so at the expense of that Empire that they follow the example of the Frenchmen who were in our country when war broke out, and fought for their flag but always at the expense of the French government. I, myself, wish to uphold the British flag, but I want to do so within the limit of our means and no more; for one must not go beyond such means.
I do not think that the present Prime Minister, in whom I have faith, is the greatest advocate of imperialism in this House; on the contrary, I believe he has somewhat of my ideas on the subject, for I have read a little the biography of the Prime Minister's grandfather and I am led to believe that he is not an Imperialist but has at heart the interest of the Canadian people.	.
When I listen, very attentively indeed, to the right hon. leader of the Opposition who always shows ability as a debater, besides being very entertaining, when I witness his attacks against the government in regard to moneys voted here and there on wharves amounting to very little, when I note that he has become close, I might say like a Jew, I then ask myself how a man like him can still think of going to England to pledge Canada to the extent of hundreds of millions even billions of dollars. I cannot understand my right hon. friend's actions, at present, because we, the citizens of Quebec, those bad people to his mind, know fully well that he is one of those who ruined our country. Every one admits it. The ex-Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, as well as the late Prime Minister, the present right hon. leader of the Opposition, declared time after time that they would sacrifice our last man and last dollar to win the war. Just as if we had been left alone to win the war! But, Mr. Chairman, I have often stated and I do so again, we were not alone in this war; there must have been people in the British Isles, in the other colonies, in Belgium and in Italy. We were three against one German, at the beginning of the war. There must have been some people who did not take seriously to the war. I have reason to believe that the colonies were wiser than the remainder of the British Empire, at the outbreak of the war. However, let us change the subject.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition, as I previously stated a few moments ago, does not want any wharves; he says we are spending too much; in fact, I admit it. However, last year, he told us that we were spending only 17 cents per capita for the navy and that we should be ashamed to spend so little for such an object. I put the question to the right hon. leader of the Opposition: Why this navy ? With whom shall we go to war to-morrow? With our neighbours, the Americans? We do not need to make preparations to fight them, we are beaten in advance; they are 12 to 1. Now, if in the near future, war breaks out in Europe, and that England is still more interested than we are in these wars, I wish to tell the right hon. leader of the Opposition, For heaven's sake, let England first fight; and if she cannot do so alone, let her call upon our men and let her pay them to fight. At the present moment, England is paying off part of her debts While we are accumulating deficit after deficit, from year to year. Would it then be fair that we should take part again in European wars? I say no.
Why all these trips to the Imperial Conferences, if it is not to trap the Prime Ministers of the self-governing colonies, to make them take on responsibilities towards the Empire, like when the question of the Near East cropped up, when the late Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Meighen) wanted us to immediately declare ourselves in favour of participating in the mix-up. The right hon. leader of the Opposition seems to think that the moment Canada will enter a war, the enemies will say: We will fight no more, because these Canadians wipe out everybody and we are

Supply-Imperial Conference
afraid of them. If that is his opinion, such is not mine.
Does England need a navy? She certainly does need a navy to protect her trade over the whole world. Her existence is dependent on that trade 1 That is why she fought against Germany, for she feared Germany might displace her in the world's trade. England needs her merchant marine and her navy is absolutely indispensable to protect the former; but that is her business and I do not see what we have to do with it. Let us not disturb our mother-in-law, England, and let us go about our own business in this country. That is all I ask. During the last general election, in 1921, I proclaimed before the people of the county I represent, that I had not, so to speak, any recognized leader and I state in this House, in the presence of the leader I recognize to-day, that if I were again candidate in my county, and should the Prime Minister be in favour of taking part in the Imperial defence, either by a contribution in money or by the building of a Canadian navy in peace time, but for the defence of the Empire in war time, I declare now that I would not be that Prime Minister's candidate and that he would hear from me, should he blunder to that extent. I wish to always be consistent with my past and faithfully represent the electors that have sent me to parliament.

Inasmuch as the right hon. leader of the Opposition was a delegate to the conference of 1921, and took part in the deliberations with respect to the Hindu franchise, would it be unreasonable to ask him to let us have the benefit of his views on this important question. If the discussion were to close without any expression of opinion from him it would be like playing Hamlet without the melancholy Dane.

I was not aware that I still was Hamlet. I observed when the hon. member spoke first that he asked that the Prime Minister state what his position was, that he already knew mine. He repeated his appeal two or three times, but I do not see that it has been very successful. Since that I notice he has been down sitting with the Prime Minister. Now he has decided to ask me to state my position. I will answer him in one word: I stand just where I did, and my words are fully on record in the conference.

I do not wish to prolong this discussion in any way. I wish to say, however, that I associate myself with the remarks made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), particularly as one of the representatives of the province whose population is largely composed of industrial workers. These workers are fully in accord with the views that have been expressed by my colleague from British Columbia to-night.
I should like to refer for a moment or two to one or two remarks made by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). That hon. gentleman stated that the representatives from British Columbia are opposed to oriental or Hindu immigration, or words to that effect. I should like to assure the House that the members from British Columbia are a unit on this question with which they have been identified to a greater degree than the members from any other province. You will understand, Mr. JUNE 29, 1923
Supply-Imperial Conference
Chairman, that the climatic conditions in British Columbia are such as to appeal to immigrants from the Orient. In the eastern provinces the climate is such that it is hardly likely to attract any very great number of the immigrants, and therefore those provinces will not be troubled with the problem that confronts us on the Pacific coast. Some few years ago a test case was made in British Columbia in regard to the admission of Hindus into Canada. The stand then taken by the people of the province was not based on any narrow ground. They did not look upon the question from the point of view that it was going to interfere with the industrial workers of the province, or with industrial activities carried on there. The stand they took was with the desire to reserve the province for the people for whom it was meant. The position that the people of British Columbia took at that time was very sound, and they have carried out that position from year to year. Some few years ago certain regulations were made which restricted the immigration of Hindus to this country, and if it were not for those regulations we would have in British Columbia, not 1,200 or 1,500, not 5,000, but we would have at least 500,000 or 1,000,000 Hindus. That, in a few words, is practically the situation, that is why the people of that province have taken this firm stand, and that is why the members from British Columbia are a unit on this question. At the present time there are only some few hundred, perhaps anywhere around 1,500 or 2,000 Hindus there. But the people of that province have expressed themselves very forcibly in regard to extending the franchise to these Hindus in reference to provincial and federal questions, and it is our belief that that expression of opinion should still be maintained. It is only through necessity that we have adopted that opinion and taken that firm stand in the past, and that we wish to maintain that attitude on it in the future. I can only add my few remarks to those expressed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) in saying that we can only urge the Prime Minister to keep in view the sentiment of the province of British Columbia and the position that we have taken in the past. We respectfully urge that at the coming conference the Prime Minister give every consideration to the views of the people as they have been expressed in British Columbia, and to the views that have been expressed in this House by members representing that province, particularly upon the oriental and Hindu question. I might
also add that the people of British Columbia do not take any second place with the other provinces in respect to their loyalty or the broadness of their views.

When I rose before I was
under the impression that we were discussing item 563. I perceive, however, that we are discussing the Imperial Conference vote, and I shall confine my remarks at the present moment to that question, and reserve what I had in mind before for the subsequent vote on the Economic Conference.
I think the question under consideration is one of the most important that we can possibly give attention to. I am reminded of a statement which H. G. Wells makes in, I think, the concluding chapter of his Outline of History where he says that modern civilization faces three great classes of problems; those pertaining to property, those pertaining to currency, and those pertaining to international relations; and if any one will read his war novel Mr. Britling Sees it Through, I think he cannot help being convinced, if he had not been convinced before by his own observations, of the intimate relations that exist between what we might call foreign policy or international relations and the life and welfare of the individual. It seems to me that our citizens do not generally attach sufficient importance to the question of foreign relations. Sometimes I think of a little group of what we have called German junkers, sitting down prior to the great catastrophe, and, like a couple of men playing chess, figuring out how they were going to play the game of war. Little did they think at that time of the awful misery, bloodshed and loss that was to follow. Little did the people of the world think that those few men could plunge the whole world into such chaos. However, Mr. Chairman, unless the rank and file of the people of the world wake up, and take an interest in questions of this sort, at any time we may be plunged into the same sort of disaster. Our children may be slain, our fields devastated, and our cities razed to the ground. Therefore, I think it is of extreme importance that at this Imperial Conference, where the issues of war and peace and other matters of great importance will be under consideration, our delegation should keep in mind, not the playing of the game, not the old kind of diplo-mancy, but the interests and welfare of the rank and file of the masses of the people. I suppose most of the hon. members present, some at least, will have read that eloquent passage in Carlyle's Sartor Resartus, where he speaks of the twenty Britishers going
Supply-Imperial Conference

to meet the twenty Frenchmen, who had no quarrel with them, and each blowing out the brains of the other. This awful tragedy is something that statesmen will have to grapple with, that those who elect statesmen to office will also have to grapple with.
In regard to this matter, which no doubt will be considered at the conference, I would like to endorse what the member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) has already said in that connection. The condition in Europe at the present time is an object lesson to us, and we ourselves have suffered, and are suffering at the present time, from that condition. We are suffering directly and indirectly. Our farmers are suffering at the present time from dislocation of trade, from the loss of Europe as a purchaser of our commodities and I hope that the most serious consideration will be given at the approaching conference to some amendments of the Treaty of Versailles which would look towards the restoration of normal conditions in Europe.
In regard to questions which we might call domestic, I want to suggest to the Prime Minister and to the House one very definite matter which might possibly be taken up, and which I think ought to be taken up at the Imperial Conference, and that is the question of the right to amend our own constitution. I do think that this is a matter of prime importance. I was going to say it is a disgrace, but at all events, it is an ana-cronism, and an anomoly that Canada should not have the right to amend her own constitution, and if there were any way of submitting the matter to the House to be voted on, I would be only too glad to test the feeling of the House in regard thereto. I know these things have to develop gradually; but I submit in all earnestness that our delegation should take up with the British government, this question of obtaining the right to amend our constitution. I wonder whether some resolution could not be drafted in that direction. Perhaps this is premature; but may I at all events earnestly urge the Prime Minister and our delegation to discuss the matter, and when he comes back next session, to have something definite to report to the House in regard to ways and means and prospects of getting through such a constitutional change? I presume this would be simply an amendment to the British North America Act enabling us to change the act without the consent of the British parliament.
Now with regard to the question of the Hindu franchise, I should like to offer just one or two brief comments. We have not yet

fathomed this question. I think the discussion has been, if I may say so, without offending honl gentlemen who have spoken, rather shallow in respect to that matter. I sometimes think of the old and well-known statement "God hath made of one blood all nations of men." We will at some time or another have to recognize that truth.

He put the sea between
them to keep them apart.

Perhaps so, but the sea at
the present time is not something that keeps nations apart. It is rather a well-travelled road, a pathway between nations, and we have arrived at a stage in the history of the world when we have to think a little deeper than we have in the past in regard to these relationships between nations and races. I recognize full well the difficulties, but I would submit to the House that this is a matter that we ought to consider with the greatest possible degree of sympathy for those whose skins do not happen to be of our colour.
I venture, in conclusion, to ask some definite questions of the Prime Minister. I hope he will pay attention to those questions because I want him to answer them if possible as definitely as he can. I will ask the questions in order so that he can answer them. Have any recent proposals come to this government from the British government in connection with these conferences?

That the House, while recognizing the propriety of Canada being represented at any Imperial Conference or conference of the Prime Ministers of the Empire that may be called, desires to record its opinion that at the coming conference no steps should be taken in any way involving any change in the relations of Canada to other parts of the Empire.

I wish to say a few words on the Hindu question, a subject which has been pretty well ventilated in this House tonight. I hardly agree with many of the sentiments enunciated by hon. members who have spoken about those people, and who have prated about the brotherhood Of man. If they lived in British Columbia, they would have different ideas with respect to the oriental races.
With respect to the Hindus, it is generally understood that there are between 1,000 and 1,200 Hindus in British Columbia. If they were all of the caste or calibre of Mr. Sastri, the question would be a different one entirely; that gentleman seems to have hypnotized people throughout Canada by his brilliance. As regards the 1,200 or so Hindus we have in British Columbia, I should judge that about 1,000 at least were low caste Hindus. If they had a vote, they would not know what to do with it; they would simply be voted as a unit by the other 200.
Is there not a chance that they would vote for the Tory party?

The hon. member might believe that such might be the case, if they were enfranchised, but I do not think the Tory party would want them. We do not need their votes in my constituency, in which there are many of them. They would vote when they got the promise that something would be given them in return. That is the way with the low caste Hindus. But the question of caste is too complex a one for me to enter into to-night, even if I were familiar enough with it to do so. Hon. gentlemen must realize this important fact, that these Hindus are not men such as we are; they have the mentality of children without childhood's innocence. You cannot comprehend the eastern mind unless you have lived among the people. They are shack-dwellers, men who do not make any effort whatever to improve the country, and they live under conditions that we could not tolerate for a moment. The Hindus will not work for us for any length of time, and they cannot adapt themselves
Supply-Imperial Conference

to our methods. In their natural community spirit, they club their funds together and erect a sawmill or engage in other undertakings, and it is impossible for us to compete with them. Those of them who go into the dairy business can live upon 10 or 15 cents a day. Our old fellows who are about ready to cross the divide used to be able to exist by means of market-gardening and from the sale of milk which they got from the one cow or so they kept. But that day has gone by, as a result of the intrusion of these orientals. I think it would be unwise on our part to grant the franchise to the Hindus. If they were all of the type of Mr. Sastri the question would be somewhat different, but as a broad principle it should be definitely laid down that we cannot afford to admit to the full citizenship of Canada any people with whom or their descendants we or our descendants cannot intermarry. On the Pacific coast we have only a strip of land, and yet we are the melting-pot for these orientals. The question is becoming a very grave one for us indeed. Since the advent of the Japanese, whose mode of living is like that of other orientals, it is exceedingly difficult for the poor white man to get along on the outskirts of any of the cities in British Columbia. The disability of the Hindus, so far as their not being allowed to vote is concerned, is a matter that is by no means so serious as some people would lead us to think. The fact that 1,000 low caste Indians in Canada have not the vote should not be a matter of grave consequence to India, for if these Hindus were in India their vote would not amount to anything, if indeed they would have any vote at all. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has pointed this out quite clearly and I need not emphasize this particular point. Most of these people at home would be subservient to some native prince, and without the vote in Canada they are very much better off and a great deal more satisfied than they have ever been in their lives at home. I have never heard any one of them express a wish to be enfranchised. They are getting along perfectly well without the vote they are living within their means and are prosperous. If they had the vote they would simply become tools in the hands of unscrupulous politicians of one party or another and in all probability the very first thing they would ask is that their families be brought out to this country. We have no room for them. If the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) lived in British Columbia I am sure he would not father any such resolution as this. But he does not understand the question as we do; indeed, he cannot understand it because he is living

apart from the facts. I claim to be absolutely unbiassed in reference to my attitude towards oriental people, whose economical virtues I quite recognize, but I repeat we have no room for them; and for the Hindu of low caste we have still less room than for others of the oriental races.

I regret that on account of the short notice which was given of the debate any remarks I may have to make on this important subject must necessarily be fragmentary. The prospective Imperial Conference seems to follow the lines laid down at prior colonial and imperial conferences. These conferences have, I think, quite frankly had in view one definite purpose, namely, of co-ordinating as far as possible the naval, military and air forces of the Empire for purposes of common defence. It has not always been expressed just in that language but I believe it will be admitted that this has been clearly the object since the first colonial conference was held. In the development of these conferences it was soon realized that the meetings could not ultimately result in the greatest success unless some method were devised by which each of the component parts of the Empire secured adequate representation. In other words, the various communities constituting the Empire were not prepared to spend their money without having control over the objects for which that money might be used. And so to-day we have developed a system of consultation, so-called, by which -usually subsequent to the event-the various component parts of the Empire are notified as to what has taken place, and are kept informed to some extent at least as to the progress of affairs. This problem will undoubtedly receive consideration at the Conference, but it is going to be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to evolve any system of consultation which will be adequate to serve Canadian purposes. Let me suggest that the consultation by the prime ministers of the various dominions, even during the period when the conference is in progress, is not adequate; and I want, if I may do so, to cite an incident of the last Imperial Conference in support of what I am stating. The conference in 1921, at which Canada was represented by the present leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), approved of a certain policy which Lord Cur-zon had given effect to with regard to Egypt. Subsequently, so far as we aTe informed, after the conference had given its approval to Lord Curzon's policy and had disbanded, Lloyd George, in consultation with Lord Allenby, completely reversed the policy of the confer-

Supply-Imperial Conference
ence with regard to Egypt and set out upon an entirely different tack, the dominions not being consulted.
Will the hon. gentleman say to what resolution he refers? I cannol recall any action by the conference respecting Egypt.

That point I shall come to in a moment. The information with regard to this conference is so inadequate that one finds it difficult to get at the facts. But I am judging only from a statement made by Premier Hughes in Australia when he said that the conference had given consideration to the situation in Egypt and had come to a conclusion in connection therewith.

Perhaps I should say that there is no conclusion of the conference that is not embodied in a fitting resolution; none whatever; it does not matter what anyone says. The report of the conference speaks for itself.

Well, the report of the conference as it is presented to us is very inadequate indeed; that is all I can say. We [DOT] have little information as to what purposes invited the various resolutions that were before the conference. Unfortunately I have not before me the proceedings of the conference itself, but I state that the Egyptian policy as presented by Lord Curzon was approved of by the conference and subsequently after the conference had disbanded, the policy was reversed without any reference to the various dominions of such a vital and material change.
Not only that, but I suggest that if the policy approved by the conference had been maintained, this country and the other members of the Empire would probably have found themselves in the position of fighting Egypt. Now, if this difficulty prevails in regard to consultation when the conference members are present, what must the difficulty be when the various representatives of the dominions are scattered about the four quarters of the earth? I just want, in that connection, to point out what Premier Hughes of Australia said, speaking at this 1921 conference:
But the position in regard to policy in the future is very difficult. Every day a new situation arises, or may arise. How is it to be dealt with? We shall be scattered to the four quarters of the earth. How are the dominions to have an effective voice on foreign policy when, as things stand, they can only be told after things have been done, and are not consulted beforehand.
I may say also that the Prime Minister.
Lloyd George, said in a reference to consultation :
Communications by cable are not a means by which you can have real consultation, because you may have a particular point in view, and may alter it after hearing what is to be said on the other side.
Lord Milner apparently was of the same opinion, because he js reported to have said:
Experience has shown that the consultation which is necessary in order to keep the different interests of the Empire in line cannot be properly effected by telegrams and despatches, between half a dozen different governments.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier many years ago refused l- have any part in consultation, because, he said, consultation meant responsibility. I suggest that if we are going to take part iin the foreign policy of the Empire, then we must have a hand in the framing of that policy and in its execution. But if this prevailing system of consultattion is the only part we are going to have in that policy, the method js not only ineffective but absolutely dangerous.
Does the hon. gentleman say that Sir Wilfrid Laurier never took part in consultation on foreign policy?

No, I make no such statement. I simply say that Sir Wilfrid Laurier laid down the principle that consultation meant responsibility. I think he was correct in making that statement. Whether or not he adhered to it fully is a matter for argument. A question of foreign policy may, of course, be a question of peace or war. We realize fully in Canada to-day the significance of war, we realize what result it may have so far a< our own people are concerned. We realize it is dangerous, not only to the manhood of our country but also to the wealth of our country. Canada must know, before she engages in any future war, several things. She must know whether or not the cause is a just one. She must know whether or not it is a war in which Canada should properly be involved and in which Canadian interests are involved. In the third place, she must know whether or not the war is unavoidable These things can only be determined by Canadian representatives having a voice in the formation of the policy which may ultimately lead to war, and in addition, in the execution of that policy. I suggest that the
11 p.m. Prime Minister has laid down the proper principle for this country to 'ollow with regard to peace or. war, namely that there shall be no commitments, no declaration of war involving this country, unless the parliament of Canada first gives its approval to such a course. That, I think, is solid ground upon which to predicate our future.

Supply-Imperial Conference

I wish to speak very shortly about another matter which has been referred to by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) and that is whether or not it is proposed to discuss at this conference the advisability of subsequently holding a constitutional convention. I was very much interested in listening the other day to the remarks of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) during the discussion on the Halibut treaty, and also to the remarks of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Morin). We hear many expressions of gratification at the status which Canada has achieved. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was not in his place at the time, otherwise I think he might have taken issue on that question of exactly what is Canada's status to-day. I remember reading last summer a statement reported in the press of that distinguished Canadian, Sir Allen Aylesworth, who suggested Canada was still a colony. Well, I suggest to hon. members of this committee that an important question is, what is our status? It is variously defined -sometimes as a partnership, sometimes as one of a league of nations within the Empire, sometimes as a component part of the Empire; and various other glittering terms are used to describe our present position. Sir Clifford Sifton, in a statement, claimed, and I think with much justification and truth, that we were allowing ourselves to be flattered by the language of the stump, and that really these terms did not correctly disclose our real status. In 1917 it was deemed advisable that at an early day a constitutional conference should be called for the purpose of defining, as far as possible, the exact status of Canada and the other dominions. In fact, it was on the programme for the 1921 conference that preparation should be made for such a constitutional conference, but, for reasons that I am not aware of, the conference was postponed. I think that was a very regrettable circumstance, and now early steps shouid be taken to hold a constitutional conference in order more adequately to determine the exact status of this country. That is a matter of importance for us, because when the distinguished statesmen in this country, as I have indicated, disagree, what can we expect statesmen in other countries to say? We may call ourselves a nation as much as we like, but unless foreign countries are prepared to take us at our own valuation it is simply a case of trying to lift ourselves by our own bootstraps. So I suggest the urgent need for that constitutional conference, and I trust that the Prime Minister will see to it that steps are taken in that direction. I know Premier fMr. Shaw.]
Hughes of Australia has stated that it would be a very dangerous thing to do; that all sorts of catastrophes would be invited. I am not sure whether that prediction is justified, but I do know that the opposite is, in any case, equally true, namely, that if we proceed in the vague and indefinite course we are pursuing we may ultimately come to disaster.
I think the time has arrived for the appointment of a Canadian ambassador to Washington. Whatever misunderstanding there has been in the past with regard to that appointment, I think the Prime Minister should make it part of his duty at that conference to state our position frankly and clearly and to indicate that we as Canadians desire to have a representative at our neighbour's capital. Our interests are largely interwoven with the interests of the United States, and it is important that our representative should be there at the earliest possible date. I need only refer in proof of that to the latest instance we have had, the Halibut treaty. There is a case in which a triangular correspondence resulted not only in delay but in embarrassment, and in many cases in the future it might even result in disaster. I suggest that we want in Washington a Canadian who is thoroughly conversant with our conditions, who is familiar with our problems and who can speak authoritatively on behalf of the government of Canada. I trust that the Prime Minister will take adequate steps to see that whatever difficulties there may be in the way of that appointment are promptly removed in order that this much to be desired end may be accomplished.
One would think in listening to the members from British Columbia that this problem of the Indian question was a very simple one, that exclusion was the only adequate remedy, and that the question could be justly settled by that quick and easy method. May I suggest to the Prime Minister that this question will be one of the most serious problems that will confront the Imperial Conference? The question has been raised in the colony of Kenya in East Africa and is there to-day a vital problem. Representatives I believe of the various conflicting interests in Kenya colony are now in London and propose to take this matter up before the Imperial Conference. It is important that this matter be decided not on narrow, sectional lines but in a broad spirit of fairness and of justice, and I have no doubt that the Prime Minister will give to that problem the sincere and deep study that it merits.

Supply-Imperial Conference
I have just one other suggestion to make and it is this. We have heard much of late years about secret diplomacy and its perils. I trust that steps will be taken in order that the fullest publicity may be given to the proceedings of this Imperial Conference. I see no reason at all if peace be the object of that conference why the whole proceedings should not be made public. I know no reason for keeping from the Canadian public at least the full facts involved in all the problems and in addition the remarks of all the statesmen who may attend the conference and the conclusions at which they arrive. If we ever hope to get anywhere in this country it is by a full, frank and fair statement of the facts and by an equally frank; and candid discussion of those facts. I therefore trust that the Prime Minister will leave no stone unturned to see that the fullest publicity is given to the proceedings of this conference.

speechtext:
'Just before the resolution carries I would like to say a word in regard to the granting of the franchise to the Indians which has been referred to. Perhaps I cannot do better than to state to the House just what I said to Mr. Sastri when he was in Ottawa. As hon. members will recall, Mr. Sastri made a trip through the different parts of the British Empire, visiting the several dominions, and came to Canada, I think, last of all. While he was in this country he was the guest of the country, and when he came to Ottawa we invited him to meet the members of the government in cabinet council. We discussed with him there very freely and openly the situation as we view it in Canada, pointing out the difficulties which we have in endeavouring to solve that problem, and seeking to gaiD from him the difficulties with which India is confronted through the situations that may arise in other parts of the Empire. When Mr. Sastri left I sent him the following letter expressing the government's attitude in the matter:
Ottawa, September 5, 1922.
The Right Honourable V. Srinivasa Sastri,
Chateau Laurier, Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Sastri,
In reply to the representations made by you at the interview with my colleagues and myself on Friday of last week, and which were the subject of further conference betwen us yesterday, I desire to assure you that, at the earliest favourable moment, the government will be pleased to invite the consideration of parliament to your request that natives of India resident in Canada be granted a Dominion parliamentary franchise on terms and conditions identical with those which govern the exercise of that right by Canadian citizens generally.
297i
The subject is necessarily one which parliament alone can determine. It will be submitted to parliament for consideration when the franchise law is under revision.
In conveying to the government of India an expression of the attitude of the government of Canada in this matter, we hope that you will not fail to make it clear that at the present time, in eight out of the nine provinces of which our Dominion is composed, the federal franchise is granted to natives of India resident in Canada, on terms which are identical with those applicable generally to Canadian citizens.
Your sincerely,
(sgd) W. L. Mackenzie King.
I might say that the point on which particular emphasis was laid in conversation with Mr. Sastri was the fact that our Dominion is a federation of provinces, that in the distribution of seats in this House regard is had primarily to the provinces, each province being allowed a certain proportion in relation to the others, and that at all times the provinces of the Dominion have had regard for each other's problems, that nothing could be more unfortunate than that an effort should be made on the part of any province or group of provinces to coerce, so to speak, any other province in regard to any matter which was of great concern to it, that the federal government could not afford to ignore the prevailing sentiment in any province. 1 pointed out to Mr. Sastri that when the Dominion franchise law would be under review, mentioning in that connection that it would come up for review in all probability before any general election was held, doubtless it would be referred to a committee of the House to consider and that the representations which he had made would be presented to the committee, but that what was of most importance was how the members from the province of British Columbia themselves would view the matter. I said quite frankly that if the members from the province of British Columbia regardless of political party were to be favourable to having the franchise granted to the Indians in British Columbia, the rest of parliament would fall cordially into harmony with their view, that on the other hand if there was no agreement among the members of the province of British Columbia on this question, if it were clear to the members of this House that so far as British Columbia was concerned instead of being in favour of granting the franchise they were all pretty much the other way, it was hardly probable that the members of parliament generally would seek to impose any view upon them which would be contrary to their wishes. In other words, that it was very doubtful how any situation of unrest in one part of the British Empire could be improved by creating a new condition of unrest in

another part. That was broadly the nature of the representations made to Mr. Sastri. I believe it is the true situation. I cannot see unless there is among the people of British Columbia themselves some general agreement as to what is wisest and best in regard to this matter, and that after all is best attested by the members for the province of British Columbia in this House, that the rest of the Dominion would be helping the situation materially by forcing a view contrary to that which is entertained by its members in that province. If, however, the members of the province of British Columbia are divided on the matter and there is any preponderating view one way or the other, I think that is a circumstance of which parliament would take account, but the important factor is that the question of whether or not the franchise is to be granted to the Indians of British Columbia is a matter, so far as I can see, not to be determined at any Imperial Conference, but to be decided by this parliament in settling the franchise for membership in this House.

When I rose before to speak on this question I remarked that I had left my notes upstairs. I continued to leave them there because I think the House is not deirous of hearing any long speech from me, or from anyone else, at the present time. I will be very brief. I simply want to suggest to the House and to the government that one matter of prime importance be submitted by this government to the Economic Conference-I refer to the question which we had under consideration in the committee on Banking and Commerce: that of the stabliz-ing the purchasing power of money. I do not suppose there has been any economic question or any economic problem which has been more serious, in recent years at all events, than that problem. We had before the committee Professor Irving Fisher, of Yale University, who has made a special study of this matter for some twenty years, and he gave us his assurance that a solution of the problem was quite within the realm of possibility or probability. Now, I have given some little thought and consideration to this matter, particularly since Professor Fisher was here and I want to state to the House that all authorities which I can find on the subject are agreed that the problem is one of tremendous importance-that the stabilizing of the price level, or in other

words the stabilizing of the purchasing power of money, is fundamental to prevent succeeding periods of what we call business booms and business depressions. Moreover, through the fluctuation in the purchasing power of money, great injustice has been done and is being done to our citizens. Dr. Fisher stated when he was here, that one of the economists in the United States had figured out that during the war years and shortly afterwards there had been an unjust transfer of wealth- what he described as wholesale pickpocketing-in the United States-to the extent of 40 billions of dollars; and he enumerated at considerable length the	continued misfortunes, disasters, difficulties and miseries that follow upon the	fluctuations in
the purchasing power of money. Dr. Fisher has written a number of books on the subject and recently, I presume owing party to his influence, the matter has been brought to the attention of the congress of the United States. Indeed, a bill was presented during the last session of congress dealing with this particular matter, a bill providing for stabilizing the purchasing power of money or, as Dr. Fisher puts it, "stabilizing the dollar." Now, in the course of the discussion which we had in the committee, it developed that there were two ways of doing this highly necessary and important thing. The first method was to regulate the amount of gold in the dollar where a country was on a. gold basis, or, to use Dr. Fisher's phrase, to standardize the gold standard. The second method was to control the volume of credit instruments through the regulation of the interest rate. This matter was referred to by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) the other day, and has received a good deal of attention from modern economists. When Dr. Fisher was here he. suggested that probably the most feasible means of stabilizing the purchasing power of money was through international action. The question was indeed considered to some extent at the Genoa Conference, and he suggested that at any future conferences this matter should be further considered. I should like to suggest therefore-if I were permitted I should like to move in the committee, although I do not know just in what shape we can put a motion through-that this question be sent forward from this parliament to the Economic Conference at London for consideration; because if something could be suggested in the way of joint action between the constituent parts of the British Empire I think it would be very easy to enlist the co-operation of

the United States, particularly in view of the fact that the matter has already entered the field of practical politics over there. Therefore, it is not unlikely that we might get all the English speaking nations of the world to take the matter up, and thus a very great gain might be secured in a relatively short time. I wish I were fully able, I wish I had the time-if the House was in the mood to listen-to submit evidence in support of the suggestion and recommendation that I make. But I will simply leave it at that. If the House will support the suggestion I shall be very glad; but if the matter continues to be ignored I shall at least have done my duty in bringing it to the attention of the House.

In connection
with the increases we have here I observe that while there are a good many departments in which increases are made all of them do not appear in the list. I observe, for example, that the Department of Customs is not there. Nor is the Department of Agriculture there. I do not know why it is; because my hon. friend justly claimed that there was a great volume of work done there,

I would like to get some idea as to the lines on which the government is proceeding, and also as to whether the government really think, irrespective of the merits of these deputies, that in a year like the present, with a budget such as has been presented, it is advisable to advance salaries that are already as high as $6,000 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With regard to the particular deputies mentioned, I can assure my hon. friend that there is no desire to discriminate. The Deputy Minister of Customs, to whom he referred, is a most faithful, able and efficient officer, and I would be the last to permit any discrimination against him. The salaries of the deputies is a troublesome question at all times. We have adopted a rule which, when I mention it, I think will be accepted. It was felt at first that the salaries of the deputies were not high and that there was fair claim for consideration. Then it was argued with some force that regard must be had to length of service, and the decision we reached was that in the case of any deputy in active service at the head of a department who had a service to his credit of ten years or more, we would consider that he was entitled to an advance; but those whose term of service were less than ten years were left out, not because they were not capable or efficient, but because it was held, and I think with reason, that some regard should be had to the term of service. At all events, that is the explanation. In every case where a deputy has served for ten years or more, and is in active service at the head of the department, he receives the increase, unless he already has the increased salary; but as to the others there is no discrimination, except that which arises from the term of service.

The Minister of Finance has stated that it required ten years of service in order to get the increase. I have only to say that I happen to have had the honour of serving for five years under one of the best deputy ministers in any of the departments at Ottawa, Mr. Alexander Johnston; and I want to say there is not a man in the Dominion of Canada more capable of presiding over a department than Mr. Johnston. He happened to have had the extreme privilege of being born on the Atlantic seaboard, and he had received a good education which is backed up by good common sense. Mr. Johnston is a man who is capable of earn-
Supply-Civil Government

ing money outside of the department to a very much greater amount than he is receiving here. I believe that on one occasion he was offered a position at $20,000 a year, but he is in love with his present work. Being a maritime man he knows the work, and knows what is required of a man in the position of Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries; and I believe if ^he government of Canada never did anything else than to give Mr. Johnston a salary of $10,000-and it is only one-fifth of what he is worth-they would be doing sufficient to justify their being returned to power in this country. His salary should be $20,000. I know what I am talking about, because I served in that department and I have had practical knowledge which is more than most of the members of this1 House have had. I have this knowledge from having been born on the seaboard, having been a sailor, and having served under Mr. Johnston.	,

I am not one of those who would refuse to give faithful servants adequate pay. I think that the move of the minister is a desirable one. I think if we are going to get competent men to handle these big departments of the government service, we must pay them adequate salaries. I desire to make it clear that I have no objection to the proposed increases. I do not know that I would go to the extent the government indicate in applying the increase after ten years to every officer of the standing of a deputy minister. There are some of these departments which must be more or less insignificant, when compared with large departments like the Departments of Marine and Fisheries and the Interior; and I do not know that I would apply the principle that far. I also want to make this suggestion: The deputy ministers in charge of large departments can, if they so desire, save thousands of dollars annually to the country. I do not know whether they are doing it or not. I think steps should be taken to see that the public services are properly co-ordinated, in order to ensure our getting the greatest possible efficiency. One can realize the tendency of deputy ministers. They are human as well as anybody else, and as soon as they get control of a large department, I suppose there is a desire to secure by accretion, other services, regardless of whatever services may be carried on of a similar nature in other departments. I have had occasion to look into this matter to some extent and when one finds that dredging service is carried on by three separate departments, apparently without much justification,

when one finds surveying services are carried on by three or more departments, it makes one wonder whether these deputy ministers are themselves co-ordinating the services. They apparently have not done it. I think the government should make it one of its first duties to see that these services are coordinated, to prevent overlapping and overmanning, and in this connection I am sure that if they do not secure, they will at any rate demand, the hearty co-operation of the ministers concerned.

The hon. member (Mr. Martell) suggests that Mr. Johnston, the deputy minister, did have an offer a good deal bigger than his salary. That is true and Mr. Johnston did go with the British Steel Corporation but now he is back again, to take his $6,000. I think the manner in which the government is going about this matter is simply to follow the line of least resistance, and the worst line it can possibly take having any regard to efficiency or economy. Work ought to be paid for having regard to its importance. We have some departments here where the work is only a multiple of the work of other departments. There is no question about it. Everyone who knows anything about the matter knows that is perfectly true. That whole question of efficiency and of results is to be absolutely discarded for the purpose of adopting some safe and easy road, which will enable the government to increase the salaries of some picked deputies. That is being done. Merit has nothing to do with it at all. It only depends upon how long the man has been drawing his pay. Merit has absolutely nothing to do with this particular increase, which is merely on account of length of service. I would like the Finance Minister to tell this House what possible justification there is for the consideration of the increases in the Supplementary Estimates brought down now. What excuse can be given that would satisfy the most credulous that these matters ought not to have been considered in the Main Estimates instead of the Supplementaries? I am going to ask my hon. friend whether he does not think efficiency should have something to do with it, and whether he does not think that the weight of work ought to have something to do with it. I do not want to pick out a department here or a department there. I need not do it. He knows them just as well as I do and better, but he knows that some of the heaviest departments are not represented here. He mentioned Customs. I mentioned Customs myself. What about Agriculture?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Suppose we admit, for the sake of argument, that it would have been wiser that these things should have been brought down in the Main Estimates. Having dealt with that point, let us now consider the merits of the question. If we need a deputy-minister in this country and if a man is capable of filling that office, a salary of $8,000 a year is not too much to pay him. If he has had long service added to his merit and strength of character, $8,000 is not too much. The trouble is, I think, that in our higher positions we do not pay men enough, and men are therefore being drawn away from the service of Canada and taken into private service because we cannot pay them enough.
I have a case in mind of a man I should very well like to have had in the service of my department. I could not keep him because the ordinary custom of the House would not allow me to give him a proper salary, but he went to another place and received twice as much as he could get here. We must pay some regard to the dignity of this office, tc the importance of the duties. But my hon. friend must have found in his day that it was exceedingly difficult to distinguish. The law fixes the salaries of nearly all the deputies at one figure. When I came into the department first the deputies, with one or two exceptions, received $3,200 a year. Their salaries have been advanced from time to time and, I think, with regard to the changes that have taken place, the increases in all lines, $8,000 is not too much to pay a deputy if he is competent and has had ten years' service. Length of service is entitled to some consideration. I do not know how you can discriminate. You cannot make the minister of any department believe that the position of his deputy is inferior to that of any other. We all magnify our offices a little. The minister magnifies his and the deputy magnifies his. I know there are differences; I know there are some departments which are much heavier than others, but it is by no means an easy thing to distinguish between them. As regards the increase, I do not know any deputy who is getting $8,000 a year who is not deserving of that amount if he is capable of filling the office.
I rise to ask a question: Are there any perquisites attached to the office, for instance, rent-free houses, motor cars, chauffeurs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nothing that I know of. I think in the Department of Agriculture some (.f the officials are provided with houses on the farms, but I think that is taken into consideration. As regards the deputies concerned in this vote, they have no perquisites whatever.
In the case of the Deputy Minister of Agriculture the amount, $500, is taken off his salary.

I do not often agree with my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) but I think he has improved so much tonight that I can almost agree with some of the things that he has said. I find it difficult to understand on what principle some of the deputies receive $8,000 a year, some $6,000 and some $10,000. There are in the service four deputy ministers receiving $10,000 a year. At least two of these gentlemen have not been in the service or have not held the position of deputy minister for anything like ten years. The Commissioner of Taxation, I understand, receives $10,000 a year and he has not held that position for anything like ten years. I have nothing to say against the increases which are being proposed to-night. I think, as a rule, the higher civil servants are underpaid; but I wish to say a word on behalf of the deputies of two of the departments, who are not receiving this increase. I refer to the Deputy Minister of Agriculture and the Deputy Minister of Customs and Excise. Both of these departments are very large and the work is very heavy and important. Both are manned by men of exceptional ability and particularly suited for their positions. Doctor Grisdale, Deputy Minister of Agriculture, is a man of very great ability, a man who has devoted all his life to the work of that department and of the experimental farms. He has been in the service of the government for some twenty-three or twenty-four years, and surely that length of service should be taken into consideration when we are considering raising the salaries of deputies. I do not wish to delay the committee at this time, but I would strongly urge the Minister of Finance to consider the work that these gentlemen have to do, the importance of their services to the country, the length of time that they have given to the service of the government, and that he grant the increase, a well-merited increase it would be, to the Deputy Ministers of Agriculture and of Customs.

I agree with the Minister of Finance that it is always difficult to do the right thing. Of course it is difficult to discriminate. It is always difficult to pick who is right and who is wrong. It is always easy to do the opposite.
