speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What does my hon.
friend think would be right?

To pay the
salary where it is earned. My hon. friend is discriminating. I have discriminated; but when I became Minister of Finance, if I remember aright, the Deputy Minister of Justice was getting $10,000 a year. I increased the salary of the Commissioner of Taxation to $10,000 a year. I did that for very specific reasons.
What were they?

I could not lose him. If there was one man who had heavy responsibilities in an almost unchecked position, it would be the Commissioner of Taxation. A man, who, as the present Minister of Finance told us the day before yesterday, has handled $200,000,000 of taxation under regulations which had to be fixed and determined by him under the most intricate act, and who has collected everything except $8,000,000 to date, was a man who was worth keeping, and he was kept. My hon. friend comes in, and he in his turn does some discriminating. The present Deputy Minister of Finance was appointed three years ago, I think, say three and a half, certainly not more than that. My hon. friend makes his salary $10,000. My hon. friend did not deal with the matter on a question of a ten-year service. He dealt with it from a question of merit. What has been done here is merely to apply an arbitrary rule of length of employment, with absolutely no regard to the volume of work or to the importance of the department. The reason for the adoption of this plan, we are told, is the difficulty of making a selection. I think that the whole idea is entirely wrong. The increases ought to have been brought down in the Main Estimates and we should then have had an opportunity of looking into the various departments. But there is very little chance of doing that now. Were we not told that generally speaking these were votes that could not. have been put in the Main Estimates? Yet here we have something that has stood for so many years when the cost of living, according to my hon. friends, was higher than it is to-day and when the financial conditions looked as well as they do now, if, indeed, not better. If the government are determined to put this matter through in this way I do not want to delay them, but there is neither fairness nor any business idea in what they are doing. One would suppose that they would be anxious to economise, but if they insist that the salary of 
$6,000 paid to certain persons should be increased they can increase it. If they want to deal with an important question of this kind in the Supplementary Estimates, a method that deprives one absolutely of all opportunity for consideration, and of any means of answering the arguments advanced by my hon. friend from Missisquoi (Mr. Kay), they are, I suppose, at liberty to do so. But again I say, the responsibility is entirely theirs; and we have the spectacle of a party that prates about economy adopting this attitude in connection with this important matter.

It is rather regrettable that this increase must be made at this time when the financial condition of Canada is so appalling. I can understand the difficulty of the government in retaining really good men when other concerns are willing to offer them more than they are now getting. But my mind goes back to two instances that came to my notice, one of which no doubt the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) will recall. An able deputy minister left the service on a question of salary alone. He was a very good man and I well remember that it was not very many years after he had left the service before he discovered, when he went to s*ell his labour in the markets of the world, that his experience with the government had imbued him with very little appreciation of the value of money, and for that reason he did not make a success. The result was that he was very ready to come back; I think he was one of the most willing men to enter the service again. Another case I have in mind is that of a gentleman in the employ of the late government managing one of the farms. He was offered a large sum elsewhere and he thought he was going to be able to make twice as much as he was getting from the government. He left the service and after six or seven years-in fact, last fall-he was eager to return. I am not sure that he is under this government, but at any rate he is in a similar position to the one he held before. Both gentlemen, I am sure, were able in their respective fields, and I am convinced that from their experience neither of them would now think for a moment of leaving governmental employment. In my opinion, if any of the deputies contemplate taking such a step they would do well to consult these gentlemen to whom I have referred. If they did, and they acted on the advice they would no doubt receive, I believe they would reconsider their decision. It depends, I suppose, on the comparison you make in deciding whether deputies are receiving what they

are worth when they get $6,000. When you compare a salary of $6,000, as paid to a deputy minister, with salaries ranging from $15,000 to $20,000 paid to men engaged in occupations with big interests, the discrepancy would of course suggest that the deputies are being underpaid. But compare their salary with the salaries paid to the thousands of men in their own walk of life who are equally efficient and whose remuneration is by no means $15,000 or anything like it,-as a matter of fact, not a quarter as* much in many cases as the deputies receive-and you will realize that the deputies are not so ill-paid after all. It is difficult to say just what a man is worth, and we have nothing but the bald statement that gentlemen who fill these positions efficiently are worth $8,000. I believe that a deputy would be worth this sum if he were willing to save the thousands that he could save by standing firmly against the pressure brought to bear upon him by his staff in urging larger salaries for themselves. But I fear that in some departments, particularly in the Public Works and the Interior departments, there has not been anything like a firm stand against such pressure. It is apparent that in some departments there has been a considerable practice of economy; but in others this has not been true. All things considered, it would have been well had the government tried to get along for the present without raising the salaries in the way they propose, because there is no possibility of getting them down again. Not only will the present recipients get this extra $2,000, but it is altogether likely that the increased sum will stand for all time as the fixed salary for the office. It is very easy to raise salaries but not so easy to lower them. Not only that; the mere raising of the salaries of the deputies will have a tendency to excite an agitation for increases on the part of those subordinate to them. As soon as the deputies get $8,000 the employees will want their salaries raised, and it will mean on the whole a very much larger expenditure for the Dominion than if the government could get along with the salaries at present paid.

Personally I think this is a
wise move that should have been made long ago. On the second page of the Supplementary Estimates there appear certain names the first of which I read is that of Sir Joseph Pope, to whom it is proposed to pay $8,000. Here is a man who has been forty years in the service of the country. He has been the trusted and loyal deputy of ministers of different political faiths and is probably the best in-
Supply-Civil Government
formed man in Canada on external affairs. Yet he is being paid just $8,000.
Six thousand.

I am referring to the new
estimates. On the other hand there are men employed in most inferior positions in big houses in the cities of the country that are drawing fifty per cent more than this proposed salary to this excellent officer. Take the next name, Mr. Alexander Johnston.

One of the best fellows
in Canada.

He is not only a good deputy, but is probably one of the ablest men we have in the Dominion. Does anyone say that $8,000 is too much for this man who protects the interests of the Marine and Fisheries department as if he owned the department? I think he devotes not eight hours a day, but eighteen hours a day to his work. Take the third man, Mr. J. B. Hunter, of the Public Works department, an extremely able man with an experience in the department extending over twenty-six or twenty-seven years. Mr. Hunter is a very competent official who never thinks of the hours he devotes to the service of the department. Then, take Mr. Thomas Mulvey. There is no doubt that Mr. Mulvey could go out of the Department of State and secure a position as counsel in any legal firm in Canada at a salary of $20,000 a year.
Is Mr. Mulvey the author of Mulvey's Company Law of Canada?
He is the same man.
He would be knighted if we had titles in Canada.
The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) has contended that we should pay deputy ministers according to the extent and importance of the work of the department. Does that apply to ministers?
It ought to.

It does not; it has never been claimed that it did. Ministers are paid the same, whether Secretary of State, or Minister of Public Works, or Minister of Justice. There are two reasons why these men should receive adequate compensation: First, as a return for faithful and loyal service, and, second, as an inducement to them to remain in the service. Take the Deputy Minister of Justice. Why, not long ago there was a discussion about certain legal charges made in connection with the Grand Trunk arbitration.

Supply-Civil Government
Is my hon. friend seeking to delay this estimate? There is no suggestion of increasing the salary of the Deputy Minister of Justice. He is already getting 810,000.

I am saying a word on behalf of men who are deserving and I am also objecting to the inference made by the hon. member in reference to my friend Alex. Johnston of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Do you mean to tell me that Mr. Newcombe could not have left the Department of Justice years ago and have received, not 810,000 a year, as he is paid now, but 850,000 a year, or, at the rate of remuneration given in the case of the Grand Trunk arbitration, 8100,000 a year? He has remained there not for the money that is in it, but out of loyalty to the department and to the service of this country. I believe in paying a man a worthy wage.

Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that these officials are very much underpaid. You cannot get a good man in the Civil Service to-day unless you pay him well. Any of these deputy ministers could go into the outside world and earn twice the salary they receive in the service. As a matter of fact, Jhe whole civil service is underpaid. I hope the government will next session bring down the cost of living bonus and make it permanent. There has been a period of high prices for five or ten years now. This increase of salaries is very well merited; it is but a small return for the service rendered.

Before this vote passes I would like to point out that the men who are listed here are all rendering excellent service. We as members have more or less to do with them, and we find them competent and obliging and quite capable of filling their positions. But I regret that one of the most important deputy ministers in the whole service, the Deputy Minister of Agriculture, has not received an increase in salary. No industry in Canada is more capable of improving the business of the country or of bringing about prosperity than agriculture. In my opinion there is no more important industry from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and in the office of no deputy minister is a greater or more varied knowledge required of the work in hand than in that of the Deputy Minister of Agriculture. As minister in charge of that department for about two years I had an opportunity of working with Dr. Grisdale, who had already made a reputation for himself as Director of Experimental Farms and who as a deputy minister speaking both French and 
English was acceptable to the farmers in all parts of Canada. He rendered and is rendering most excellent service. I regret that he has not been included in this increase and I hope that the government will take the earliest opportunity of seeing that he is included.

Does my hon. friend not believe that a man who is capable of being the deputy minister of any department should start on at least 88,000 a year? I agree with all he said about Dr. Grisdale. There should be a minimum of $8,000.

It has been stated that the higher paid civil servants are underpaid. I should like to call attention to the fact that the lower paid civil servants are very much underpaid. I have stated here before that in Winnipeg postal employees are receiving a smaller wage than the amount that it has been found necessary to give for the sustenance of people who are accepting municipal relief. It seems as if we ought not to advance the salaries of these higher
12 m. officials, however much they may deserve it, until there has been a general revision of salaries and the lower paid employees are looked after.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 438 carry?

In regard to the proposed
salary increases for the various deputy heads I wish to place myself on record that I am not opposed to paying adequate remuneration where merit and competence is shown.
I have since being honoured with this position looked upon the deputy ministers both in the capacity of supervisors of their respective departments and advisers to the ministers at the head of the departments. So far as supervision is concerned I have no criticism to make or any comments to offer, but in their capacity of adviser to the minister I have frequently drawn to the attention of this committee that I would like evidence placed before it as to their interestedness in showing why these huge sums of money are being asked in the estimates from time to time. I have made these representations to the committee from time to time simply because I have not been satisfied in my own mind that the deputy ministers themselves have appreciated the value of a one dollar bill or the importance of getting one hundred cents for a dollar, and as a result of that inappreciation they have presented large amounts in the estimates to the ministers, who in turn present them on the floor of this House and ask parliament to vote them. It seems to me that another word reiterated not alone by myself but by other members of the House that the deputy ministers show greater interest in that phase of the question might
be a very good thing at this time when these increases of $2,000 for the deputies are before the committee. This is just another word that I have to offer on the subject at this time, and I think it is a word that should meet with serious consideration on the part of everyone concerned.

I do not think we ought to
be niggardly in paying our deputy ministers, but I do think that this House ought to consider the financial situation at the present time. We are going behind every year and the Finance Minister does not hold out any hope of our catching up next year. There are a lot of people in this country who are paying this money who are not getting $6,000 nor S2,000 a year. I do not want to say anything in disparagement of these gentlemen, but it does seem to me that this is an inopportune time for increasing their salaries. Item agreed to.

Item agreed to.

Canadian Government Railways-Prince Edward Island Car Ferry Terminals-to pay claim, $196,417.63.

I do not think I can let this vote go through at the rate we have been going. As I am instructed, the vote ou^ht never to go through. I had a file sent over to me exactly three minutes ago. This is the size of the file, as hon. members can see. I have not been able to assimilate much information out of the file in that time. Has the Minister of Finance gone into this matter? I have been told-and I am speaking from partial memory-that this matter was entirely settled, that there was an agreement which covered the whole matter, and that this is something which need not be considered. If it should be considered, I submit Mr. Chairman, it ought not to be considered without some chance of going into it. I do not think it should have been put in the Supplementary Estimates. If the claim be a just one, I can see no reason in the world why it could not stand. I am going to ask the minister whether it may stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not read the file but I have heard the case explained by the Minister of Railways, and supported by his officials. I was satisfied from the information furnished that it was a fair and just claim, and I consented to having it put in the sup-plementaries. I am sure the Minister of Railways will be prepared to explain the matter to the hon. member.

This is a claim that perhaps will not be understood unless you know the men in connection with the claim. The government wished to do this work at Prince Edward Island which was a very difficult work to do. The gentlemen in question are Roger Miller and the late Mr. Caudel. The word of each of these gentlemen was as good as his bond. Because of the relationship of Mr. Roger Miller, the contractor, to the department and the confidence the department always had in him, whenever I became embarrassed or in difficulty over a contract, although he was a contractor, I called him in for consultation, and I gave him work to do that I felt could not be reliably done elsewhere. This difficult work at Prince Edward Island had to be undertaken. The minister advertised. He got one tender, I think, and the tenderer did not accept the contract.
What was the nature of the work?

It was the building of the terminal for the Prince Edward Island car ferry, and a very difficult job.

Supply-Railways and Canals
What is the date of the contract?

It was started in 1913. The first contractor that tendered did not take it. Then Mr. Roger Miller was called in, as I often called him in, to discuss with Mr. Cochrane the difficulties of this contract. There is no doubt in the world that Mr. Roger Miller was not looking for the contract. He was induced to take this contract by the minister. When I was minister I often induced him to take contracts for which he was not tendering. Tenders were called for in the regular way, and Roger Miller, as I absolutely believe, was asked to tender low, so that he would get the contract. In addition to that he was told by the minister that any loss he sustained would be made good, but he wanted him to tender and get that contract. Any person who has been at the head of the department can readily understand that attitude in a work of this kind when one contractor has backed out. He proceeded with the work. The legal gentlemen will say that when there is a written instrument it is the bargain, but not in this case. Roger Miller, whose word was as good as his bond, somewhere in the documents has made an affidavit pointing out that he took the contract with the distinct understanding mentioned and I can understand it thoroughly. He was to go on and do the work, and if it cost more than the contract he was to lose no money. He went on and did the work, and I think it ended in 1917 or 1918. His affidavit is in the file. I may be told that it is an old contract. Well, it is, but in 1917 under the contract, if this be taken as the bargain-which it is not	at	all in
my mind; I am absolutely certain it was not -he could not perhaps be allowed anything. The chief engineer thought so, under the strict terms of the contract, and he emphasized in his report the words "under the contract". Now the reason the matter was not settled before was this: It was necessary to purchase a special plant for this work, and as with all the contractors, a contract cannot be finally settled until the plant is disposed of or valued. From the conclusion of the contract until this spring there was no opportunity of disposing of the plant, and the department had sent auditors to find out, not any profit of Roger Miller, but what the absolute loss to him on this contract was, and this is the amount the auditors returned to me as the amount of loss. The affidavit of Mr. Miller, whose ability as a contractor and whose integrity are above reproach, points out that he did the work under these conditions, and I absolutely believe it to be true, knowing the man and understanding how under the circumstances he took the contract under the conditions stated. We have had the books audited to find out what the loss was, and this is the result.
I would like to find out one or two facts. I cannot get anything out of this maze of documents. The contract was in 1913. When was the work done?
I think it was completed between 1917 and 1918.
What was the date of the final certificate?
I might say the contractors would not at any time accept any payment as final.

Here is a letter at the commencement of the file. The file I am interested in is the file with the contract in it, to show something about the inception of the matter. On the 29th January the Department of Railways forwarded the cheque of the Finance Department for $6,728.72 in payment of the final estimate, and then it is quite true that this letter of receipt from the Roger Miller Company shows that they do not accept it as a final cheque. The letter says:
We do not admit the validity of the claims amounting to $1,631.26, nor do we accept the cheque in question as a settlement of our final estimate, owing to the fact that there are matters pending between us and the department which will have to be gone into before the amount of the final estimate can be arrived at. We are sending you this intimation now, so that there may be no misunderstanding on the subject.
I point out that the final estimate and cheque were forwarded January 29 last. I wonder if the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister are at all serious when they say that they want proper consideration given to these items. This is just a little bit of the file. Surely my hon. friend must see that this is a farce, and that the only proper thing to do is to transfer this item to the main vote of next year.

I try to run my department just as I would run my own business, and no person has accused me of doing anything else. It is a matter of straight business between man and man, and I think no government ought to do anything else. I have investigated this, and I am as convinced as I am living that the Department of Railways and Canals owes Roger Miller this money under the arrangement he made with Mr. Cochrane. If we were to go at the matter technically and work it out, I believe Roger Miller would have a bigger claim.

Supply-Railways and Canals
In fact, he claimed more than this, and we sent an auditor down for the purpose of going through his books; Mr. Miller threw all his books open; the auditor went through them from one end to the other, and he brought in a report. It is on the basis of that report that I am asking that this settlement shall be made.

Where is the
contract?
The contract would be in the law branch. I thought I had the whole file.
I told my hon. friend this afternoon that this was a matter which I thought ought to be looked into in the interest of the country.
A synopsis of the contract is in the order in council on the file.

It may be a
synopsis. Are there two contracts?
No.

Was the work
done as originally proposed?

No, it was much more
expensive than originally proposed. They put in concrete instead of wood.

There was a
change. Was a contract entered into after the change was made?
No.

I have been
told explicitly that a contract was made for a specific sum.
I am informed that there was nothing of the kind; that there was only the original contract.

Then if the
appropriation passes in this way that these files will be all open for our investigation, and that an investigation will be given into the whole of this matter, I do not propose to take up any more time.

My hon. friend has a
right to get these papers at any time he wants them.

The only time
that they are any good is now, unless we have an understanding that the whole of this is subject to re-opening.

What does my hon. friend mean by "re-opening?"
("Mr. Graham.]
I mean an investigation at the time the next House sits.

My hon. friend would
have a perfect right to do that.
No, I could be and would be voted down easily.

Our majority is not so
big.
It might be big enough then.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the vote carry?
I am not saying that the vote carries until I get information on the subject. Of course if we are to get no information, all right.

I have given my friend
all the information.

I asked for
the files this afternoon. I get part 7 at exactly twenty minutes past twelve. The item was called at twenty-three minutes past twelve, and what I started with was the final certificate. That looks like giving full information, does it not?

My deputy tells me that
the entire file is there. I did not expect this item to come on to-night. I gave the file to my hon. friend just as soon as I got it.

Might I
suggest that the item stand until the hon. gentleman has time to peruse it? I think that would be satisfactory to the committee. I should like further information on the subject, and if he can find it for me that would be very satisfactory.

Then it will stand until
Tuesday.

It can stand until next
session. I see the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) laughs. He is the author of the bill that was so described in this House this session that I would have thought he would withdraw from his party after the description given of it by the Minister of Justice. I do not know what he knows about this matter.

I would like to ask the leader of the Opposition if it is a crime for any hon. gentleman in this House to Iaugih?
I was not laughing at the right hon. gentleman. I do not know what bill he refers to. If he would be more specific, perhaps he would do me the honour of giving me a definite answer instead of the uncalled-for insinuation on his part.

Supply-Railways and Canals
The bill transferring land in Nova Scotia.

I was not the author of that
bill.

My hon. friend was
chairman of the committee that put it through.

My right hon. friend has been
long enough in this House to know that a gentleman who is chairman of a committee is in no way, because of his occupying that position, the author of a bill.
He is just as responsible.
Not a bit of it.

Can a chairman of a
committee be shown by parliamentary procedure to be the author of a bill?

It is sufficient responsibility to be chairman of the committee. These are simply settlements being made out of court of claims that should not be paid unless established in court. They have been attempted to be settled in this way time and time again, and they have been refused, but now they have been yielded to by this government at the expense of this country. If there are estimates that are fitted for Main Estimates alone, they are these. Perhaps the minister would remember-he was not in the House-how in a Supplemenary Estimate brought down in 1921, an item was included to pay some $40,000, a judgment of the court of Quebec, taken to the Court of Appeal in Quebec and affirmed, taken from the Court of Appeal in Quebec to the Supreme Court of Canada and affirmed. Then an item was put in to pay that claim after it had gone through three courts, judgment being given.
I think, in every court unanimously. But a terrible row was raised because this was put in the Supplementary Estimates. When it was raised, I withdrew the estimate because there was an allegation of wrongdoing. I promised an investigation and appointed a judge to investigate, and then those who rais-ed the row ran away and declined to give any evidence. Here are three cases that have not been proven, that are simply being paid out of the public treasury without any attempt to establish them before courts of law.

I think the suggestion made
by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) is reasonable. I understand from the minister that this claim of the contractor mentioned for this particular sum rests only on a verbal contract. That is a rather strange thing at

the outset. It seems to me it is only reasonable that he should be asked to prove his claim in a court of law, and then the country would be justified in paying it. Short of that, I must oppose the item.

I explained fully to the
committee that as a matter of law-the hon. member as a lawyer would raise the point-if that were upheld, many cdaims that are settled could not be settled in court, and technically that is not the ground on which I put this thing. The hon. member would know that in a court of law, under this contract there would be no case. I pointed that out. I know if Mr. Cochrane were alive this question would not be asked and the claim would be paid. I have not the file as I sent it to my hon. friend, but on the file there is a long affidavit from Mr. Roger Miller pointing out how he undertook this work; that he was sent for and asked to undertake it under those conditions. He makes an affidavit to that whole statement and we owe him the money just as much as I should owe a board-bill if I stayed at an hotel.

My hon. friend (Mr
Shaw) is a lawyer of years' standing and he knows that often a person is unable to go to court because there is no written memorandum in reference to the contract. There might be a perfectly good verbal contract that could not be enforceable at law but there would be a claim in equity. My hon. friend knows that in many cases no action can be brought unless d note or a memorandum signed by the party can be produced. Nevertheless there is recourse in equity. As I understand the situation, the minister is not taking advantage of a technical objection, but is accepting what in equity would be a claim of contract.

I am not suggesting for a
moment that the statute of frauds should be raised in defence of this action; the minister need not raise that defence unless he wants to. Certainly it should be established to the satisfaction of the court that there had been made some sort of verbal contract or arrangement. The mere affidavit of the individual should not be sufficient for the purpose in a matter of this kind, however reputable he may be. Let the finding of the court on that issue be the determining factor, and in addition let the court ascertain the exact amount due.

Whether there is a
verbal contract or not-

This is not a court of
law.

46S0
Supply-Railways and Canals

-in many instances no
case can lie unless there is a note or a memorandum producible.

My hon. friend is mistaken
in his law. The statute must be pleaded before it is taken advantage of.

Why argue points of law
here?
There is a report from the chief engineer-
I quoted it.

-dated April
30th, 1919. It reads:
It is true that in connection with this work there existed some unusual hazards, but the contractor is in error in implying that the department encouraged tenderers to accept the hazards at a lower cost than wTas warranted.
The whole claim was that he was coaxed into it.

I did not use the word
"coax."

The report goes on:
These hazards like all other parts of the work were subject to competitive tender and a comparison of the bids received shows that the bid of the Roger Miller * Company anticipated the risks that would be encountered.
There wore three offers.
And this was the lowest.

The chief engineer states further:
During the progress of the work, certain changes were made which necessitated the construction of an additional piece of cnbtvork. This was ordered and paid for on the basis of cost plus 10 per cent as provided for in the contract. Such payment to the contractor for this additional piece of cribwork does not involve us in any liability for the cribwork constructed under the lump sum in the contractor's tender. The claim presented for the contractors by the Hon. Charles Murphy cannot be entertained as a claim under the contract.
That is what I said.
It appears that in 1919 the claim was not admitted.

Under the contract. My
hon. friend is basing his argument on the legal right of the man under the contract. The minister has explained that such is not the view that is taken of the matter.

If my hon.
friend desires to discuss that phase of the question I think I can with perfect justice claim that apparently the Postmaster Gan-

eral (Mr. Murphy) has more influence today with the present government than he had with the last one.
That would be a fair insinuation.

Here is the claim presented and here is the report of the engineer. This is all I have been able so far to glean from this exhaustive file. If the government are determined to press the matter through without our knowing anything about it I will not hold them up. It is idle to talk about postponing it until Tuesday; it is not fair to hon. members, and I do not think they should be detained when it is evident that the government are determined to put the thing through. Will the government concede this much? Will they decide to take no action on this vote until we have had some opportunity of going through the files and of satisfying ourselves as to the fairness of the transaction?
That is childish. The government is responsible.
I am submitting a perfectly fair offer.
The hon. member is not. Never in his time did we ever ask that the government should not assume responsibility for anything of this kind. We never asked that we be allowed to decide.
In our time reckless charges of graft were made and the government promptly withdrew the item. If my hon. friend is referring to us to support his contention then he should withdraw this item.

We never asked that we
should be the judges of what should go through.
We never attempted to push things through.
You probably felt guilty.
Then I am not to have an opportunity of reading this file?
Carried.
There are some 200 pages which we are given three minutes to read. If the government are determined to press the matter through, then all I can say is that they will have to take the responsibility.

Item agreed to.
Hudson Bay railway-construction, $350,000.

I am rising not to criticize this vote, because if I had any criticism to

Supply-Railways and Canals
offer it would be that the vote is not as large as it should be. We had hoped that a vote would be brought down which would indicate that something was going to be done towards the completion of this project. However, I feel that the government intends to carry out the statement made in the House when the resolution regarding the Hudson bay project was discussed, that the portion of the line on which steel was laid would be brought up to standard this year. I assume that this is the amount figured on for the work. Am I right in that assumption, and can we rest assured that work will be undertaken in the near future?

I cannot give the assurance that this amount will complete the work we have on hand. That cannot be decided until the engineers are on the line. It might take more, but this is all we can spend this year. My instructions are that the work of reclamation will be proceeded with.
In view of the rumours we have heard to-night in regard to the branch lines in the West, may we take it for granted that there will be plenty of opportunity for men and equipment for this work?
I should think so.
We might also hope, I think, for more than the completion of that portion of the line on which steel has been laid being brought up to standard.
We can only spend this amount of money.
Has this item been recommended by the Canadian National Railway Board?

The amount, as I outlined last year, was recommended by the board. About 114 miles of the road have become dilapidated and the board has recommended that that portion be repaired. That is what this money is for.
I understand that within the last two years certain of the rails were ordered taken up.
It was proposed that some heavy rails should be taken up on this portion of the line, but the line was in such bad shape that they did not even get in to do that.

The construction of the
Hudson Bay railway has been a political proposition from start to finish. I am sorry to say that the two old political parties have had a hand in it, and now the Progressive party
298i
is taking part in it as well. Canada has had too many political railways, and before any more money is spent on this project I think an account should be taken. The Board of Directors of the Canadian National Railways have not had time to consider this matter, notwithstanding what has been said in that regard. I say this is a political matter and it becomes very active around election time. One reason why the taxes of the working classes have been so heavy is that an extravagant railway policy has been pursued in this country. Before any further expenditure is made on this road the following considerations should receive attention:
1.	The navigability of Hudson straits.
2.	The probable volume of eastbound and westbound traffic available.
3.	Local conditions and prospects for colonization.
4.	Operating revenues and expenses.
5.	Storage at Hudson bay.
6.	The linking up of the Hudson Bay railway with the transportation systems of the West.
The minister should be able to answer these questions before we pass this item. Ontario has a railway similar to this, the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario. They applied to the federal government for a subsidy, and what did the federal government say? They said it was not a work for the general advantage of the Crown as a colonization road, and of Canada. It was looked upon by the officers of the Crown as a colonization road, and Ontario is extending that road right up to James Bay. The condition is the same in Manitoba as respects the Hudson Bay railway; it is a colonization road, and if the federal government has regarded the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario as a colonization road, as a work not for the general advantage of Canada, then the same should apply to the Hudson Bay railway. In the first place, the Hudson bay route will not get the grain trade. I venture to say there are some seasons when the channel there is not open two months in the year. Grain which is sent to the head of the lakes can go out 365 days of the year-in the summer months via the lakes, Buffalo, and the St. Lawreence, and in the winter months via Chicago and New York and Montreal. This route was reported upon by a royal commission appointed by the government of Canada. That commission made a very extensive examination of the feasibility of this project, taking into account all considerations affecting finance, the movement of grain, the 1 a.m. probable volume of traffic, and so on. I am sorry the two old political
Supply-Railways and Canals

parties have not heeded the report of that commission, because it is the report of experts. We have enough deficits to meet now -Grand Trunk, Grand Trunk Pacific, Canadian National. Roadis whiich were built under private ownership have had to be taken over by the people of Canada. Public ownership is not responsible for this condition. Now, let me read one paragraph of the report of this commission, which consisted of the present member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), Mr. W. M. Acworth, and Mr. A.
H.	Smith, president of the New York Central. It says:
We understand that construction work on the Hudson bay line has been suspended. We think that the work should not in any case be recommenced till more urgent needs have been met and money is more easily procurable. And if work on the line is begun again, we think it should be done in the most economical manner possible, and only up to the standard of a local line, bearing in mind that it cannot be expected for many years to come to be selfsupporting. Considering the small advantage in rail mileage from the grain-growing areas, which the Hudson bay possesses over the existing routes to Port Arthur, and that from many districts it possesses no advantage at all; considering further the short and uncertain period of navigation in the bay, and that grain consigned to port Nelson will consequently always be liable to be detained there for nine months till navigation is again opened; considering that higher ocean freights may be expected to absorb, if not more than absorb, any possible saving in rail rates,, we cannot believe that this route will ever secure any serious share in the export trade. Still less can we think that it will handle an import business. Unless considerable mineral wealth should be discovered in the territory which this line will open up, it must we fear, continue to be almost indefinitely a burden upon the people of Canada. And everything that can be done should be done to make this burden as small as possible.
I may say further that since the Hudson straits are open for specially constructed vessels between July first and the end of October, only the crop of the preceding year could be counted on for traffic. A good deal of that traffic would have to be at Port Nelson by the opening of navigation, so that there will have to be immense storage facilities at that point. But who would think it wise to lock up his export wheat at Port Nelson knowing that it could be shipped through only between July first and the end of October? The question answers itself. Now, let me quote further from an article on the subject:
Wheat is always somebody's property. It moves at the direction of its owner, and the owner wants it where he can be sure of making delivery by a specified date. The very essence of the export wheat business is time of delivery, and it is precisely that condition which, practically every year, from October 20 to December 5, forces nearly 70 per pent of Canadian export wheat out by way of Buffalo and New York, although the St. Lawrence route to Montreal offers from 2 to 5 cents per bushel lower carrying charges. There is nothing more definitely established than that 
our export wheat does not follow the cheapest channel or shortest channel, all economic theories or assertions to the contrary notwithstanding. It does the reverse, and that astounding fact cannot be ignored in considering the possibility of finding enough traffic to load one train per day, for six months in the year, for Hudson 'bay. People who merely look at a map and then become dogmatic about transportation have thus far done all the talking about this Hudson Bay railway.
We have wasted money enough on this project, money that the old central provinces have had to pay as well as the rest of Canada. The railways of the United States have also got into a deplorable condition; they have gone on making extensions against the reports of experts. Where is Sir Henry Thornton on this proposition? Has he had a chance in the short time he has been here to go over this district and find out if the route is feasible? Talk about giving the board a free hand, if this is how the government is going to do it I have no hope of the railways being a success. At this late hour I do not wish to detain the committee any longer, but I wish to protest against this expenditure on the Hudson Bay railway. I think it is a waste of money. I think the road will never pay the fixed charges on the investment. Talk about navigation. Why, you have not considered the question of terminals, the type of boats and many other questions from a navigation standpoint. If this road is to be built it should be built by the province of Manitoba just like the province of Ontario built a similar road to James bay.

Has the minister the
report of the Railway Board on this construction?

This is not construction. Although the Hudson Bay railway is under construction, this is not for new construction. As I explained to the House last year, 114 miles of the road already built is being put 'in operating shape. There is nothing being done in the way of new construction.
It says "construction" in the item.
The line is under construction until it is completed.

I understand that the
Railway Board have recommended this construction. May we have their report?

I have not that report with me. I thought I went into this matter pretty fully last year. Before any further work is done there will be no other reports. The boards, if for no other reason, but this is not my reason, felt that even if only to take out

Supply-Railways and Canals
these rails my hon. friend has spoken of they had to put the road in shape to the end of the steel to bring them out. All that material would be wasted if the road was not put in shape.

The minister gave the
impression when he spoke earlier this session that the decision to take up the rails on the Hudson Bay railway had been made prior to the arrival of Sir Henry Thornton, and that the reversal took place afterwards. I looked over the file immediately afterwards and found that the impression given by that language was entirely wrong. The recommendation of Sir Henry Thornton came to that effect. The recommendation to council, and I think the order in council itself by which the government decided to approve of the taking up the rails includes a reference to Sir Henry Thornton as agreeing thereto.
Oh no.
Oh yes, it does.
I think my hon. friend is absolutely wrong, because Sir Henry Thornton was not here at the time.
He came here afterwards.

My deputy was then
acting chairman of the board.
If the file is here I will show the minister. I went into it carefully. I have it upstairs. The government approved of it and the file shows that Sir Henry Thornton approved.
I do not agree with that.
I wish the minister had the file. I know the impression he gave before, and it was distinctly wrong.
I do not agree with that either.

It does not matter whether the minister agrees with it or not. I do not know why the minister is objecting because if he looks at the correspondence ne will see what changed the decision of the government. What changed the decision of the government at least, whether it changed the decision of the board or not I will leave hon. members to conjecture, were the appeals and protests from Liberal associations 'n northern Manitoba and northern Saskatchewan. When they arrived the opinions of both the government and the board changed.
I do not want to argui with my hon. friend but he is absolutely incorrect as to why the decision was changed.

I want to add my protest against the expenditure of another dollar on the Hudson Bay railway. I want to tell the minister that the whole of eastern Canada i.3 opposed to the expenditure of another dollar on this railway.
The hon. member foa-Grenville is not.
I cannot help what the hon. member for Grenville thinks. It does not bind my conscience in this matter.
He represents the East.
And you cannot bind that of the East.

All the expression we hear from eastern Canada is directly opposed to the expenditure of another dollar on this road, and the government might as well appreciate the force of public opinion in the East on this matter. At this late hour I am not going to say anything more about it, but eastern Canada will vote against this an i against any government that spends any money on that road.

I want to know if this vote is simply an attempt to carry out the pledge given by the Minister of Agriculture in a recent by-election in the West that the Hudson Bay railway would be completed before next Christmas. I agree with the hon. member for York-Sunbury who has just spoken that eastern Canada is absolutely opposed to this railway, and the common sense of all Canada is equally opposed to it. I would say further that I understand, and I am not going to quote my authority, which hesides is excellent, that Sir Henry Thornton himself started the operation of taking up the rails on this bit of road, which in my judgment should never have been built as it was nothing but a wildcat enterprise built to satisfy a demand from -western Canada, which was absolutely misled as to the purpose that could be served by the construction of this road. Sir Henry Thornton as a railway man started to take up the rails, my informant said, when "they" stopped the operation. When I asked who "they" were 1 was told, "Oh, there was a Mr. Stewart who was a director." I do not know who he is, but he was a director and was in touch with western interests, and apparently political influence was more powerful than the business aspect of this question. As far as I can see it, with the ice-bound bay, with the shifting sands and the danger of the route, it would be far more sensible to direct the trade of Canada in some other direction. Other parts
Supply-Railways and Canals

of Canada which could be vital to the carrying on of overseas trade are being absolutely neglected, and in the hope of getting somehow or other the support of certain members in this House who never will give their support to either party because they think themselves superior to both, the government is prepared to waste $350,000 more to get that which will never be delivered and they are willing to do it at the expense of all the rest of Canada. I want to put myself and the part of the country from which I come as absolutely and definitely on record against the flagrant misuse of the funds of Canada in building a railway that cannot serve either the farmer or any other interest adequately.

Would the minister give the committee an explanation of this point? It was stated that it was the decision of the Railway Board to remove the rails to make use of them in other directions, and a certain number of rails were removed to be used in other portions of the country the view being taken that it was a useless railway. Now the vote here for $350,000 is to restore that railway. What I wished to ask the minister was if he would inform the committee of this change of attitude?

As a matter of fact the Canadian National Railway Board, with Major Bell in the chair, passed a resolution not to abandon the Hudson Bay railway but to secure these rails for the time that were not being used and use them on branch lines. But when they came to discuss the question practically they found they could not rescue these rails or ties without first virtually reconstructing the road or repairing it for about one hundred and some odd miles. If my hon. friend knew the locality he would understand thoroughly what I mean. Now, even if the road were not to be proceeded with to Nelson or Churchill, this money would have to be expended to put the road in shape out to the end of steel to bring in the material to rescue the rails and ties. I suppose there is a million dollars worth of material there. I am not saying this is to be done, but even if it were to be done this money would have to be expended before a yard of rails could be brought out.
Is it proposed to bring any of the rails out after this is done?
That will be a matter for further consideration, but at present no. It does not look from what has taken place that we will need them for branch lines in the West.
I record my dissent to this vote.

Did I understand the minister to say that we are asked to vote $350,000 without being assured that it is the government's intention, or the intention of the board that apparently advises the government, to take up the rails, or that this money is not to be spent for the completion of the line? Are we asked as sensible men to vote this money without knowing what we are voting it for? I cannot grasp what is contemplated from the statement of the minister. He says it may be necessary to spend it in order to save another million dollars worth of property and yet he says in the same breath it may be advisable to extend the railway to completion. I cannot follow his statement and I want to know what I am asked to vote this money for. If it is for the completion of the railway I am unalterably against it. It is one of the mad fancies the people of Canada have gone into, and the sooner it is abandoned the better.
There is not a dollar of this for the completion of the road.
What is it for?

I pointed out three or four times that for 114 miles the line is absolutely in such a condition that the trestles have rotted down; there has not been anything done on it for years in the way of operation. The first thing the government must do before it can either take out the material or start the completion of the line for the last ninety miles is to put this portion of the line in a state of repair.

I ask the minister to tell me whether the government have resolved to build the line or take the rails up. I want to know which course they are going to pursue. Surely the people of Canada are entitled to know what is going to be done with their money.

If a vote should be asked to complete the line that will be proof that the government intends to do it. This is the commitment the government agreed to last session in this House and that is what this vote is for. Whether the line be completed or not this vote, and more too, will be necessary to put the line in a state of repair that will permit the taking out of the material.

What is the object of putting this portion of the line in a state of repair if the railway is not to be completed ultimately?

Supply-Railways and Canals

I have just given the reason. There is approximately, I am told, a million dollars worth of ties, fish plates, and other material which cannot be brought out unless this road is put into a condition for operating.
Is the vote necessary to complete the line, or is it just to move this material?
This vote is necessary no matter what may be done.

Surely we are not to
be asked to vote $350,000 without having a definite statement from the Railway department that they are going to carry the line to completion, or that they are going to take up the rails? Let us know which it is. They must know now which object they are going to carry out, unless we are going to have a repetition of the Hotel Scribe incident in Paris, and the government does not know what is going to be done by superior authority. If we are to be asked for an endorsement by somebody who has not yet indicated his views to the government, tell us even that, but let us know along what line we are asked to vote the money?

I have fully informed
my hon. friend of the reasons for the vote.

We have not got any
reason yet; I do not know what is going to be done.

I wish to say that I object
most strenuously to some of the statements that have been made here by the hon. members for St. John. I think the statements come with a very bad grace from either of these hon. gentlemen considering the amount of money which has been voted for harbours on the Atlantic coast from which we expect to get no revenue whatever. My hon. friend (Mr. Baxter) in his superior way told us this is purely a political matter. I wish to assure him that it is not a political matter in the West; it is a matter of bread and butter to the people out there. Because, unless we will get something that will enable us to get our produce on the markets of the world a little cheaper than vre are doing at the present time I do not know what the future of the West is going to be.

Will the taking up of
these rails help?

We are not taking up the
rails.

The minister will not tell
us whether they are being taken up or not; we do not know.

I presume some of my hon.
friends to my right would like to see the rails taken up, judging from the way they are talking. I wish to assure them that the West will not stand for anything of the kind.

Reference has been made
to the position of the members for St. John. I think I might point out that the hon. member who has just spoken cannot possibly know from the cryptic utterances of the Minister of Railways whether the rails will be taken up, or whether they will be nailed down. Of course, it is only in keeping with the attitude of his party to which I referred earlier in the day. He is quite prepared, if he thinks he can get anything in the way of expenditure, no matter how useless, that will be directed towards his particular section of the country to follow the government with perhaps the hope of something more tangible than that. But for the rest of us, we want to know most definitely whether these rails are to be taken up, or whether the railway is to be extended. I would not expect a member from the West, that is from the Progressive party, to be at all interested in whether there would be at the end of the railway any machinery by which grain would be taken care of. I would not expect him to care whether it was a single track or a double track railroad. I would not expect him to care anything about the question of a possible congestion of cars at the end of the line. I would not expect him to care anything about the conditions of ice in Hudson bay. From what I have seen during this session I would not expect them to require anything but the expenditure of money in a fanciful attempt to carry out their purpose without regard to the uselessness to Canada of that expenditure. But the rest of us have a different idea. We want to know what is going to be accomplished by this expenditure. We want to know whether the government has decided to take up the rails or not, or whether the government has decided to build this railway to tide water. The hon. member, however, does not care so long as money is spent. The rest of us do care and we want to knew what the government proposes to do?

The Minister of Railways was very direct and not any too considerate in his denial of my statement that
Supply-Railways and Canals

Sir Henry Thornton had agreed with the government's decision to take up the rails, he could scarcely have been more specific than he was. Although some months had elapsed since I had read this I felt sure of my ground, and can as surely confront the minister with a most definite confirmation of what I said. The government's order in council authorizing the taking up of the rails was passed on the 24th November. That order in council cited a report dated 22nd November from the Acting Minister of Kail-ways and Canals, representing in connection with the operation of the Hudson Bay railway that the vice-president and general manager of the Canadian National Railways had presented a report relative to the advisability of lifting the rails between miles 214 and 334, consisting of 120 miles of No. 1, eighty-pound rails the same to be used on the main line subdivision between Vermilion and Edmonton to replace sixty pound rails urgently requiring renewal.
There are certain other recitals not necessary to refer to, but this is the end-
The minister observes that until such time as the financial condition of the country would warrant the completion of the Hudson Bay railway project the using of the lifted rails on another portion of the system would appear to be an economical procedure, as if left where they are they would in short time deteriorate to such an extent as to become of no value.
The preceding paragraph reads:
The minister, upon the advice of the said board, concurred in by the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, accordingly recommends that authority be granted to take up the track on the Hudson Bay railway from mile 214 to mile 334, and to use the material therefrom at such points upon the Canadian National Railways as the said board may deem expedient.
That is the order in council which decided the matter dated 24th November. To be brief, I will pass now to a document which is on the file dated 19th December. This order in council refers to a resolution, a decision, come to by the directors on the 20th October. The directors decided to the 20th October to take up the rails. That was included in a report in November, and the whole thing was given effect to in an order in council dated 24th November. On the 19th December the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals wrote the following letter to James Stewart, who at this time was director of the roads, and who had written the letter protesting against this policy: The letter reads:
In reply to your letter of the 11th instant, I may state that following meeting held by the Directors of the Canadian National Railways on the 20th October while inspecting the western lines, a communication

was addressed to the Acting Minister of Railways, pointing out to him the views expressed by the directors at this meeting, and requesting him to submit the matter to the Governor in Council for approval. This has been done, and an order in council has already been passed, authorizing the Board of Directors to proceed with the taking up of the rails between miles 214 and 334.
Since the arrival of the chairman, Sir Henry Thornton, this matter has been discussed with him at some length, and he has expressed his approval of the action taken by the Board of Directors during his absence. In view of this, I do not see that any good object would be served by having the matter brought up for reconsideration at the present time.
I hope the minister will now accept the situation.

I accept it absolutely.
My right hon. friend and I were discussing two different things.
Oh no.

My right hon. friend will
take an hour to straighten out a thing that needs no straightening. The decision to take up the rails was made before Sir Henry came here. That is what I had in my mind, and I pointed out to him-

I said that Sir Henry
Thornton had agreed to it, and the minister distinctly contradicted me. That is all there was to it.

He would not even let
me agree with him if I wanted to. He would interrupt me if I were trying to agree with him. The decision to take up the rails was passed by the board before Sir Henry came here. I never heard anything of this letter between the deputy minister and Mr. Stewart. It never came to me and as far as my connection with it is concerned Sir Henry Thornton was not present when the decision was arrived at. If he agreed to it afterwards that is another thing.
I said he had agreed to it and that is what the minister contradicted. I do not say he knew he was wrong but he should not have contradicted me unless he knew he was right.

I have had a chance of going through the next file while the matter is being discussed and I think I can tell hon. members what the government's policy is in connection with the Hudson Bay railway because I see that the next item is a refund to J. D. McArthur & Co. of 890,000 and I find from the file that under the contract and the arrangements that money can never be paid him until the railway is completed. I think the minister will agree with me.

Supply-Railways and Canals
I could not tell until I had read the file. That is not the way I read it.

If the road is not to be completed the money can be paid, but if the road is to be constructed the country has no right to give up the 890,000. Mr. McArthur states that the $90,000 is in the hands of the Department of Railways and Canals and is held pending the completion of the Hudson Bay line. I know that. Then I note that he got impatient about it, and made application to the late minister, the Hon. W. C. Kennedy, on August 9, 1922. Mr. Kennedy handed the letter over to the deputy, and this is what Major Bell says:
Your letter of August 9th to the minister is now before me. With reference to the agreement of the 5th April, 1919, you will note that the use of the word "temporarily" is relevant only to the suspension of the work at the time your contracts were in force. The agreement cancelled these contracts and provided for the retaining of $90,000-*
"until such time as His Majesty shall complete the works-
The word "temporarily" is not found in this latter connection, and I am advised that the time for completion of the work is entirely within the discretion of His Majesty. It is not necessary, nor in order, for me at the present time to deal with the contingency suggested by the expression in your letter-"if the government decides not to proceed with the work at all".
If your legal advisers entertain the opinion that a petition of right to obtain a refund now of the above sum will have any profitable result, this department will not, I apprehend, interpose any objection to the granting of a fiat, but, in the opinion of our legal department, such a proceeding would be absolutely futile. Under clause 8 of the agreement the Exchequer Court would have no jurisdiction, as the chief engineer is the sole arbitrator in all disputes.
In looking upon this $90,000 as an asset to be hypothecated, regard must have been had to the fact that it really was the payment of an estimated loss if the contracts were completed under conditions such as then existing, even though coupled with a prospect of some refund if construction costs were lower at some future time when the government might decide to complete.
The whole thing is that if the man. had not been let off his contract he would have lost $90,000. As a matter of fact, I think it would have been more. It is quite obvious that this refund never should be given unless the government lias definitely abandoned the Hudson Bay project. If the Hudson Bay railway is to be completed, in granting this refund the government is adding just that much to the cost and the country's expense.
I will make a statement of the other side of the case. My hon. friend has a little advantage of me in all these things, because he has the files.
The minister has had them a long time. I have only had a chance to skim over them.

The hon. member has done pretty well. This is the situation for the committee to decide. McArthur had a contract to complete the Hudson Bay railway, and the late government had paid him so much money, but retained $90,000 as stated clearly in settlement to pay any loss that might accrue to the government if they proceeded to complete the road. That is, if the government in completing the road were compelled to pay more money than McArthur had contracted to build the road for, this $90,000 was to meet the loss. The engineers, under the estimate of that time, thought the loss could not be more than $90,000. If in completing the road, a greater cost was not incurred than was included in McArthur's contract, the whole $90,000 would come back. As a matter of fact, this $90,000 is McArthur's by the settlement, retained by the government as against the completion of the road. The only question is this: This has been retained for five years, perhaps, nearly six years. Is it fair for the government to sit down and keep McArthur's $90,000 for all eternity? It is his money.
Is that when this road is going to be built?

You cannot compare time with eternity. It is his money retained by the government in case loss was incurred in connection with the completion of the contract. We cannot go on with the work this year. It does not look as if it would be gone on with next year. How long should the country retain this $90,000 belonging to McArthur? If the committee thinks five years is not long enough, my opinion is that if this had been a matter between private individuals, this $90,000 would have been handed back to him. When the matter comes up again, the contract will be made under new conditions and new terms; a new contract will be entered into. McArthur cannot get the money unless we vote it for him; but it is his money, as I say, retained by the government. Does the committee think it is time to give him back his $90,000?
That is not quite the way in which the matter should be put.
What is the right way? I want to be fair about it.
In 1919 he wanted to get rid of his contract and he got a good, big settlement. He got a just settlement. He got a settlement which he should be absolutely satisfied with.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Was Mr. McArthur prepared to go on with the contract, or did the government stop it?
Supply-Railways and Canals
He certainly did not want to go on.
Did the government not stop the contract?
The deputy is there and he can give the minister the information.

The deputy informs me
that the work was stopped earlier than this time.
Certainly, and I think the deputy will say something else too.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon.
member has not answered the question. Did the government not stop the contract?
I am trying to get the information from the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The item before the
committee is the Hudson Bay railway construction, and the discussion is proceeding in connection with the McArthur claim.
We can pass the other one if the committee is willing.
All right.

No. I do not wish to detain the House more than a few minutes, but I desire to add a word of protest to those uttered by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) against the spirit of opposition manifested towards this western aspiration by one or two hon. members to our right. I trust that spirit is not widely shared by the members in any corner of this House. It would be very regrettable if a spirit of that kind prevailed in this House. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) seems to be obsessed by twin antipathies, one to the Progressive party and the other to the western part of Canada. Usually his judgment is to be relied upon. When his mind is working in a sphere with which it is familiar, we delight to listen to his utterances; but when he is under the influence of those pet aversions of his, his judgment seems to wander far from sound logic. I want to say, as I have tried to say before in this House, that the Hudson Bay railway transcends a mere political matter. It is an aspiration of the West and of the whole of the West. When hon. members stand up and say with superficial finality that the East will not do this and the East will not do the other, we can do what we regret to do, what we think it is always inadvisable to do, we can stand up and

say that the West will do this and the West will do the other. That is a spirit that ought not to be engendered in this House by responsible members. It is a spirit that ought to be avoided if possible. Where will this Dominion arrive at if hon. members deliberately on every occasion take the opportunity to stir up that kind of spirit of blind, unreasoning opposition between one part of Canada and another? I would not mind, no hon. member would mind, if that kind of thing was supported by facts and reasons; but the hon. member for St. John and the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) have had ample opportunity in this House to array their facts upon this question, to stand up in a reasonable manner and to meet argument with argument previously in this session and in the last session. Did they do that? At this moment, in a totally unsupported manner, without a single fact, without the least suspicion of acquaintance with the facts, they stand up and deliberately tell this House and the West that the East is forever and for all time opposed to this aspiration of western Canada. One trembles almost to think what the repercussion in western Canada will be of a recent act of the Senior Chamber of this parliament. We want to know how far responsible statesmen in this country are going to go with matters of that kind. If some of these hon. members were a little better acquainted with the sentiment that prevails in western Canada, they would be a little more careful before adding fuel to fires that are already burning pretty briskly. Hon. members will stand up and proclaim their love for this wide Dominion of ours, speaking in superlatives, and yet when it comes to practical matters wherein all the sympathies of all parts of Canada may be legitimately sought these men will deliberately try to drive in the wedge and make it impossible for the country to work harmoniously and in a practical way I would advise these gentlemen to make their patriotism a little more practical. Let them use their imaginations in trying to visualize what the future of Canada can only hold if the communities in all parts of the country will co-operate under some form of reasonable compromise.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would recall the
attention of the hon. member to the fact that he has already dealt rather fully with the question of the failure of certain hon. members to appreciate certain things. There is a definite item before the committee, however, and I would ask him tc confine his remarks thereto.

Supply-Railways and Canals

The item is an important
one, but the issue raised by the hon. gentleman to my right is of still greater importance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It does not happen
however to be the item before the committee. The hon. member must confine his remarks to the subject matter under discussion.

Perhaps I am taking hon.
gentlemen too seriously.
You certainly are.

If that is the feeling of the
committee I am prepared to let the matter go so far as that particular aspect of it is concerned. With regard to the vote itself, what is provided now is a very small start, but I must be grateful for small mercies. I cannot understand just how this $350,000 is going to put that 300 miles of line into anything like its original condition. I understand the minister to say that it is to be applied to the northern 100 miles, but I gathered from the deputation that was down here some weeks ago that the whole of the line was in very bad repair. The first 200 miles, although it had been in partial operation some time, appeared to be in very poor condition, and if that is the case I can see that this $350,000 will not go very far.

Does the hon. member
not think that $350,000 is sufficient for the purpose of taking up the rails?

So far as I can understand,
the question is not of taking up but of putting down rails, or rather of repairing the rails that already exist. Now this should not be a political matter but it seems to me that there is a strong attempt being made to use it for political purposes. With regard to the original intention of the board to take up these rails, it was by accident that I was instrumental in making that fact generally known to the public, and from the knowledge I have of the circumstances I am of the opinion that Sir Henry Thornton's acquaintance with the question was subsequent to the action of the board. Even if he did approve of the board's action, that can be easily explained. Sir Henry Thornton was newly arrived in this country, and he would naturally know little of the necessities of western Canada; and had he been here before and been acquainted with the conditions that have existed so long it is inconceivable to me that he would have approved of that action of the board, which I will not begin to explain. I am not going to offer any criticism; probably the board considered themselves justified. No doubt
the desire was to get out the material; and so far as my knowledge goes, whenever Sir Henry Thornton knew the state of public opinion in the West concerning this matter he must immediately have disapproved of what had been done. Has the minister any expert advice as to what this amount of money will accomplish, and to what extent this 300 miles will be restored to its original condition? The first 185-not 200-
