Item agreed to.
Refund to J. D. McArthur & Co., $90,000.

The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) asked me a question, but I see he is' not in the House. Let me read from a letter on the file. It was written in September 1918 from McArthur to the Minister of Railways and it shows how the matter in question came about:
As you are aware, it is impossible, owing to war conditions, to proceed at present to build at schedule prices the Hudson Bay railway referred to in contracts between myself and the Dominion.
Then he states what is being done. In September, 1918, the man found that he could not go on with the contract owing to increased prices. About that time, perhaps a little later, the government had on hand of his moneys $400,000 odd. They let him out of his responsibilities; they merely held back $90,000 as against the losses which they will have when they come to build the line. I think the

Supply-Railways and Canals
deputy would tell his minister, if his memory is at all good-and I think it is-that Mr. McArthur at that time was very much pleased to receive the money; that it was a very good settlement. He has no right to this now at all. There is the deputy's letter of only last year, there is the action of Hon. Mr. Kennedy only last year. It is absurd to bring down in a supplemental estimate a claim like this: Surely the government do not want to put themselves in the position of forcing a thing like this through at the present stage of the session. It is idle to say that the government will only have the House sit when hon. members want to sit; that is nonsense, piffle of the purest kind. The government know that hon. members want to get away. They know that members have made their arrangements. They know it is wrong to keep this House sitting longer. It is a first-rate foundation for a reputation of forcing through in the dying days of the session-yes, in the dying seconds of the session-claims, settlements which have no basis in law, which have stood for years, and of forcing them through in this way because it is the only way of getting them through.

There is no desire to do that at all. I have sat up until four or five o'clock in the morning when Sir Robert Borden's estimates were being put through and when there would be only three or four members behind me

sat up two nights before the closing of the session-
I do not object to that at all.
Then why make a fuss about it?
There is nothing to be accomplished by misrepresenting my position. I am objecting because this is not a proper vote to be considered in the Supplementary Estimates.

I have not much objection to what my hon. friend says about the contract. The only question is that they made a contract, McArthur accepted it, they kept $90,000 of his money-have we kept it long enough? An arrangement of that kind would not be tolerated five minutes between men in business.
No, the claim would not be tolerated.

Ninety thousand dollars was to be handed back when there was no work being done and no prospect of it in the immediate future. Contracts must be construed in the light of reason. Is five years a 
sufficient time to withhold a man's drawback as against some loss you may make in construction when there is not even a proposal before the House to build the road?
The order in council went through in 1919. When my hon. friend says it is five years he is a year previous.

It js strange that this is just the right time to decide that the $90,000 is to go to Mr. McArthur. Why is it not in the Main Estimates this year? Why can it not be held over for the Main Estimates of next year? This kind of estimate should not be in the Supplementaries which are considered in the last few days of the session, and the minister knows it. Let him wait and just see what investigation reveals. Let him watt and see what will be said about this vote if it appears in the Main Estimates when hon. members will have a real opportunity, as he knows they have not now, to look into it and discuss it. Let the minister hold this one a3 the one was held at the end of the session of 1921; let him have an investigation-and 1 will guarantee we will not run away from it.

If I understand the arrangements correctly, the $90,000 is held by the government against any possible loss when the line is completed. That is the definite arrangement between the government and Mr. McArthur and it seems to me the first thing for the government to do is to determine whether or not they are going to build the railway, and then, in the light of that fact, make the arrangements with Mr. McArthur. I do not think Mr. McArthur is entitled to the money under the circumstances; the people of Canada should hold it against any possible loss that may be incurred in the completion of the railway. If the government had decided not to build the railway, then it would be proper to consider whether or not the money should be returned, but that not having been decided, I say there ,is no reason why the right of the people of Canada to am' portion of that money should be forfeited.

Item agreed to.
Trent canal-improvements-roadway north of Buck-horn lock, $4,000.

As I have not had an opportunity earlier this session I might on this item, as it is for a roadway, bring to the attention of the minister and the House the needs of a town known as Depot Harbour, which is the terminus of the Ottawa line, the
old Canada Atlantic. This town is situated on an island, an Indian reserve. It has no connection with the mainland and these people are absolutely isolated. It has a population of from 1,000 to 1,500. The engineer of the department has made an estimate of the cost to provide a short roadway one and a half miles long to connect with the mainland. The difficulty in the past has been that the Ontario government had no right to build a road this being an Indian reserve, and there is no authority for the building of it except by the Railway department. While it was under the jurisdiction of the Grand Trunk Railway we had a difficulty in another way,, but now that the government has taken over the Grand Trunk I think there is absolutely no justification for withholding a small grant for this purpose in order to give these people access to the outer world. It is not a boomer town; many of the inhabitants have resided there for many years. Many of them have to send their children forty or fifty miles to a continuation school, whereas if we had a road they would have only a very short distance to travel. This matter has been brought to the attention of the department, and I am only repeating now what I have said before in order to impress it on the minister. I trust that before another session a grant will be made to give these people some relief. It would be justifiable in every way.

I should like some explanation of this item. In the Main Estimates there was a vote of $10,000 for re. pairing the Governor General's cars. I cannot conceive at all what this item may involve.

Item agreed to.
Surveys and Inspections-railways-including expenses of Advisory Fuel Committee-additional amount required, $5,000.

May I ask what amount of this is attributable to the expenses of the Advisory Fuel Committee?
Supply-Railways and Canals

One cannot tell just what their expenses will be, as it depends on what travelling they will have to do. Last year they did very important work, and did it very quietly and unostentatiously. Mr. Magrath and Mr. McCourt made many trips to Washington and other parts of the States trying to protect Canadians against a coal shortage, and they succeeded admirably. They work for nothing. This is merely to provide for their expenses. If they do not travel the money is not used. They would not accept any remuneration whatever.

I would like to take the opportunity on this item of making a few remarks with regard to that very question. I am more convinced than I was even before the Fuel Committee took up the question of Canada's fuel supply, that this is a national question of practically the first importance. At the present time we find that the American anthracite supply is rapidly running out. It will run out within man's age at the rate it is now being used. The visible supply of anthracite in Wales is reduced to a very low amount, about 5,000,000 tons a year. Over half of this amount is at the present time consumed by Great Britain, and the balance goes to Norway, Holland and to some extent Denmark. We can never rely upon even Welsh coal for an adequate supply of fuel. We cannot rely on Pennsylvania coal in the future for very long, and the time has come when this country must turn its attention towards the establishment of an all-Canadian fuel supply. That ought to be the aspiration of hon. members of this House who are true Canadians, as I hope we all are, to develop the hope of an all-Canadian fuel supply. Few hon. gentlemen can conceive the vast amount of money we are spending in the United States annually for coal. In the last ten years we spent $580,000,000 or a little better than that in the United States for coal. Had that amount of Canadian money been spent in this country one does not need to exert his imagination very much to see what the result would be. We have in the province of Alberta, it is estimated, over 17 per cent of the world's total coal supply. Great Britain, famous for many years as one of the greatest coal producing countries in the world, has only 5 per cent, and that will perhaps give Canadians some conception of the potentialities of our coal supply. We have recently established definitely that in the northwest portion of the province there is an area of 100 square miles of almost exposed semi-anthracite higher in heating value

than the Pennsylvania anthracite, and 80 miles of road would bring that into the markets of the Pacific and possibly as far east as Winnipeg. We have in that deposit of coal the power to practically control the coal supply of the west coast. We have in that portion of the country every known form of coal adaptable for every known purpose, domestic, industrial and shipping. We could coal every boat on the Pacific ocean and every householder from the Yukon to San Francisco, and it is a practical proposition. It would be a national question to open up these coal fields and develop them as a national industry, and I submit that it is in the interest of Canada that that should be done as speedily as possible.
Many recommendations have been made by the Advisory Fuel Board whose estimate we are considering. Some of them are of great value and some of minor value. The one of greatest value I think is that our attention should be turned to the solution of our transportation problem in connection with the coal supply. There is no coal problem in Canada. We have so much coal that one cannot form an adequate conception of it. Think of it-1,234,269 millions of metric tons. That is the calculated coal resources of Canada. I hope hon. members will realize from the little picture I have given the necessity of solving the transportation problem. We have the coal and all we need is transportation, and that problem we must solve. I hope the government will digest the report that was made by the Fuel committee the other day, and just here I want to pay a tribute to the excellent way in which the chairman conducted that committee, and to his extreme courtesy to both witnesses and members. I hope the government will take that report into very serious consideration, and more than that, put into active practice the recommendations of that committee.

I have perused the statements supplementary to statement No. 1 set out on page 3790 and following pages in Hansard. from?

I am reading
from a letter written to you on the 15th June.

Never.
-to table his little black book.
Never.

I said I only did it to save the hon. gentleman's time. I pointed out to him at that time that I 'had written for this information. I have not yet got it.

The matter is in the
Exchequer Court.

The transaction is not
completed yet.
Well, I suppose we will be told about that next year; we shall get the details then. Now, this $1,500,000 is for the 2,000 ears is it?

Yes.

cars?

been ordered yet.

Where is it
proposed to order them?

Tenders will be called
for in the usual way.

If my hon.
friend does not know his deputy may be able to tell me, whether it is in Canada or the United States?

ordered in Canada.

My hon. friend is trying

I wonder if the hon. gentleman would ever get round to giving me this information. I suppose I may hope to get it some time after the House is closed.

This information will be

I should

Will the

Mr. GARLAND Bow River): I am under the impression the government has the power

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: That is a different thing. You require to bring down a further estimate.

speechtext: You want to amend this.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
The hon.
member knows why.

I do not know why. If the hon. member thinks he can elighten us, let him do so. Item 139 appears on page 31 of the estimates and it covers about a page, and it reads:
Amount not exceeding $73,000,000 to meet expenditures made or indebtedness incurred (where amounts available from net operating earnings may be insufficient by or on behalf of the Canadian National Railway Company, hereinafter called "the Company", or any Company specified in the first schedule to the act incorporating the Canadian National Railway Company, being chapter 13 of the Statutes of Canada, 1919, or by the Company in respept of any railways, properties or works entrusted to the Company from time to time under the provisions of section 11 of the said chapter 13 of the Statutes of Canada, 1919, or by or on behalf of any Company specified or referred to in chapter 13 of the Statutes of Canada, 1920; or any one or more of them, on any of the following accounts:-
(a)	Operating deficits whenever incurred or ascertained.
(b)	Acquisition of property, materials and supplies.
(c)	Interest and sinking funds on notes, securities or obligations.
(d)	Principal and interest of maturing or matured, loans secured or unsecured.
(e)	Construction and betterments.
(f)	Co-ordination or consolidation of railway lines and facilities.
(g)	Guarantees of securities.
Then it goes over on the next page and reads:
The amount herein authorized may be applied from time to time, in the discretion of the Governor in Council:
(a)	To meet expenditures made or indebtedness incurred by the Company in respect of railways, properties and works entrusted to the Company as aforesaid.
(b)	By way of loans in cash, or by way of guarantee, or partly one way and partly the other, subject, however, as follows:
If by way of loans, the amount or amounts advanced shall be repayable on demand, with interest at the rate fixed by the Governor in Council, from time to time, payable half-yearly, secured if and when directed by the Governor in Council by mortgage or mortgages upon such properties, in such form and containing such terms and conditions, not inconsistent herewith, as the Governor in Council may approve. [DOT]
If by way of guarantee, any such guarantee may be of the principal and interest of the notes and obligations or securities of one or more of the said Companies specified by the Governor in Council, and may be signed by the Minister of Finance, on behalf of His Majesty, in such form and on such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may determine to be appropriate and applicable thereto.

Therefore, all the government needs to do is to bring down an estimate, which it can do in a few hours, and just simply add what it wants for construction purposes. The government knows that the severest attack on its own conduct comes from its own friends.
Would the hon. member be willing to support such an amendment?

Yes; as to the action of the other House there is no question whatever judging from the speeches made there.
Mr. GRAHAM; We must not discuss the other House. The hon. member says the only reason they did not pass the other bill was because it was not brought down in the way he thought it should be brought down. If he says this item is not in proper form-

My right hon. friend
should not try to confuse anybody else.

I never try to confuse
anyone.
Not me in particular. As a matter of fact, this estimate is exactly according to the method adopted by my right hon. friend.

It is perfectly right. I
am not objecting to it.

Yes, and my right hon.
friend said twice:	"Why should you not put
the whole amount in the estimate?"

If you are guaranteeing
it, yes.

We did not guarantee

My hon. friend's friends in another place

That may be until the

I know it just the way
the minister knows it.

As a matter of fact, the
Upper Chamber objects to many of the lines on the ground that they are not needed.

They were chiefly of
a minor character.

I have been endeavouring for some time to call the attention of the committee to a condition that exists with regard to equipment on the government roads and which, I think, might obviate the necessity of building so many cars. I believe there is an arrangement between the railroads of Canada and the United States that if either
retain cars of the other beyond a certain number of days, they pay one dollar rental a day for those cars. I think this is a very unwise arrangement for Canada for this reason: In a time of congestion when freight cars are badly needed, they are -worth more than a dollar a day. During the season we are shipping a large amount of produce to the United States, and they retain our cars while the rush is on. I may be wrong in this, and if so I am subject to correction. I understand they are able to retain them by paying a dollar a day rent for them. I think our railroads realize that this is no rental for a car, because if a Canadian occupies more than the 48 hours which is allowed for either unloading or loading a car, he is charged demurrage of one dollar for the first day, two dollars for the second day, and five dollars a day after that. If some such arrangement as this were made with the United States, they would return our cars much more promptly. I am informed on very good authority that hundreds, yes thousands of our cars arc retained by the United States during the grain-moving period, while our railroads are starved for cars to haul grain.

This matter is in charge

I realize that in a
charge of one dollar a day, there is nothing to induce the railways to send those cars back. I understand this is an international matter. During the grain movement, we send far more cars to United States' ports than we receive, so that they have a great advantage over us. The management of our government railroads would be well advised to endeavour to get some new arrangement in this particular, because this would help us out in the car shortage.

The Minister of Railways and the leader of the Opposition have very successfully placed this whole question in a state of confusion so far as I am concerned and, I think, as regards most of the other hon. members, if not all of them. I think the committee
will agree that I have not been taking up the time of the House to any great extent, and in view of that fact I will claim the indulgence of hon. gentlemen for a short time in order that I may place before the government the facts in regard to this item. This is too serious a

I intended explaining this question when the budget was under consideration but I was asked to let it stand until some other time, for the reason that it was desired to take the vote on the budget on the 23rd of May. Now the Peace river country embraces an area of 74,000,000 acres, the greater part of which is good agricultural land. Of this amount 43,000,000 acres are in Alberta and 31,000,000 acres in British Columbia. The Dominion government also owns 3,500,000 on the British Columbia side of the boundary. Some people have stated that the Peace river is a navigable stream. I say it is not; it is a difficult stream to get at. The

Supply-Railways and Canals
banks of the river are from 500 to 1,500 feet high, and even if the river were navigable you cannot get up and down the banks to take anything to the river. In that district there is a water power at Hudson's Hope, which is supposed to be second only to Niagara, and it would be capable of furnishing power for all the trains of the Canadian National railways west of Lucerne. At Findlay Fort, above Hudson's Hope, where some five rivers meet, it has been stated by men who have prospected in the district for many years that if a pulp mill were erected in the locality there is timber enough to supply the mill with pulpwood, enough to turn out 1,000 tons of paper per day for 100 years. This is on the British Columbia side of the boundary. At Hudson's Hope there are to be found some of the best anthracite coal fields in Canada, and the Imperial Oil Company has bored a number of wells and is installing machinery to drill more. I am referring, of course, to the British Columbia side. On the Alberta side there are railway facilities. There is the Edmonton and Dunvegan line which was built by Mr. McArthur and later on taken over by the Alberta government. That line runs about 130 miles north from Edmonton then West to McLellan, a branch of it runs north again from McLellan, crosses the Peace river at Peace river crossing, and extends about 25 miles north of the river. The other branch runs east to Spirit river and there is still another branch running south from Spirit river to Grande Prairie. These lines provide the Alberta side of the Peace river country with a fair railway proposition; it gives ample railway transportation.
It is suggested that a line be run from Brule lake to Grande Prairie, and this is the line to which I want to direct the attention of the government. At Brule lake it would strike the Canadian National line at an elevation of 3,265 feet above the sea level. The Peace river country is from 1,300 to 1,400 feet above sea level, therefore it is obvious that the line would have a heavy grade from the Peace river country up to Brule lake. At Brule lake there are coal mines from which is obtained almost all the coal used by the Canadian National railways west of Edmonton and north of Kamloops. It has been stated that this coal is of first-class quality. That is not correct; only about 20 per cent of it is of first class quality; the rest of it, I should say, is third class quality, although the Canadian National Railways are using it. I might say that before the Canadian National railways were taken over by the government a contract was entered into by the owners of these mines which were directly
connected with the railways to supply them with coal for a number of years. That contract, I understand, has not yet expired.

I am dealing with the question before the committee in regard to the extension of the railway from Brule lake tc Grande Prairie, and why it is suggested that this line should be built. There were three men around this building lobbying for over three months in connection with this line.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is no objection to the vote carrying.

But I object to the vote being carried so far as this particular line is concerned. This line is supposed to tap some coal fields about half way between Brule lake and Grande Prairie, and it is suggested that these are the finest coal fields in Canada. Well, I question that for I have it on the authority of men who know these fields that this statement is not correct. It has been stated, and evidence was given to the effect before the committee on Mines and Minerals that these coal fields would look to Vancouver for their market, and the statement was also made that they would give from 3,000 to 4,000 tons a day to the railways to carry. I want to say that they have no market in Vancouver; and will not be able to sell their coal there.
Why?

I will tell you why. I have said that Brule is 3,265 feet above the sea level. In his evidence before the committee Mr. Errington said:
The market is undoubtedly on the Pacific coast.
Then he was asked:
I suppose this coal is better than most coal in the West?
He does not answer that question. Then he was asked where he could get a market for it, and he said, the Pacific coast, Vancouver. He was asked how much he expected to get for the coal, and he said $4 or $5 at the mines. He said he would deliver it at Vancouver at $7 per ton. He says in another place in his evidence that the grade going

Supply-Railways and Canals
in there is something the same as the Crow3-nest pass. Now if Crowsnest pass has a good grade is the railway prepared to haul the coal at $2 from there to Vancouver? It costs $12 a ton to haul potatoes from Prince George to Vancouver, which is practically the same distance. I will cut that in two and take it at $6 a ton; add $5 to that and the cost in Vancouver would be $11. The Comox coal on Vancouver island is pronounced by the British navy to be the best coal not only in Canada but in the world. According to engineers' report there is enough coal there to last over a hundred years and it can be bought to-day for $8 per ton. Yet these men say they will take that coal from Brule lake to Vancouver and sell it at $7 a ton, whereas at the very least, according to their own figures, it would cost $10 to get it there. How can it compete under those conditions? Not only that, but you can buy oil in Vancouver at $1.25 a barrel, and four barrels of oil are equal to a ton of coal. Three men will do the work of twelve on a steamer when oil is burned instead of coal. Then where is the market for coal out in Vancouver? There is absolutely no market for it, yet these people come down here and want the government to invest $10,000,000 or $12,000,000 in the building of a line to take coal to Vancouver.
Does my hon. friend not think that the propaganda carried on in connection with that road was more on behalf of the wheat interests than of the coal business?

Well, I am coming to that. I will admit that if that line was built to Grand Prairie many million bushels of wheat would come out that way. The Grand Prairie district is one of the best mixed farming districts in Canada, but why should this government build a line in there to take the freight away from a railraod that has been built in good faith at the request of the people? What right has this government to tap a country that has been already tapped, when there is another section of this country equally as good without any railway facilities? Some years ago a line was supposed to be built from Vancouver into the Peace river country, known as the Pacific Great Eastern, but that line has practically been abandoned. I would just like the committee to note a few of the grades on that line in order to show that it would not be possible for it to carry grain or anything else out of the Peace river country at a fair rate to the farmer. It starts at North Vancouver and it 
runs out 12J miles to White Cliff. Then, because it gets into a difficult country, it skips 29 miles and starts in at Squamish. At Squamish it is on the sea leVel, but at Alta lake a little distance above Squamish, it rises to a height of 2,100 feet; then it drops down again to 700 feet. Then at Birkenhead it rises to 1,600 feet, and at Lillooet it drops again to 750 feet. Then at Kelly's lake it rises to 3,500 feet and it drops again at Clinton to 3,200. Then it rises again at Horse lake to 3,860 feet and at Quesnel it drops to 1,600 feet. How in the name of common sense could that road ever take grain out of the Peace river country to compete with a line which has a good grade? I am referring now to the Grand Trunk Pacific grade which is the best that can be found on the continent of America. About two years ago the provincial government got an expert engineer, Mr. Sullivan, to examine that railway and report upon it. That was done after they spent $42,000,000 on the Pacific Great Eastern Railway. I will read just a few lines of the engineer's report. Speaking of that portion of the road from Quesnel to Prince George which runs 82 miles south of Prince George, he says:
I have never before seen such a large area of country so adverse to railway construction and if built the maintenance of this section would be almost prohibitive.
He says further:
If such conditions had been encountered at the Panama canal I do not think the undertaking would ever have been completed. I therefore recommend that the road between Quesnel and Prince George be abandoned at once and that the tracks be taken up and sold.
I give this simply to show that that line will never be able to take grain out of the Peace river country; it is absolutely beyond reason. If the farmers would charge a sufficient freight rate to justify operation, the people would be prohibited from raising grain in the Peace river country. What I suggest is that there is a line started at Prince George: The highest altitude from Prince George into the Peace river country is less than 2,400 feet. When you leave Prince George if you take the Parsnip river you would be going through good agricultural land practically all the way. If you go through the Pine pass, which is a shorter route, there would be a portion of land that would not be very good for agricultural purposes, but that area extends only about half the way. Now, you may ask: Why start the line at Prince George? Prince George is a divisional point on the Grand Trunk Pacific. It has a population of over 2,000. It is built where

Supply-Trade and Commerce
the Fraser and the Nechako rivers meet. It is a good townsite; it has a never-failing supply of water, and, there are good routes from there into the Peace river country.
As I have already said, the highest point between Prince George and the Peace river country is 2,400 feet, which would make a very small resisting grade from the Peace river country to Prince George. There you could connect with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and it would only be a little over 500 miles from Prince George. In other words, you would bring the Peace river country within about 600 miles of the seaport at Prince Rupert. That would put the Peace river country in a position to raise wheat, and the freight rate would be less than any other section of the prairie. There is nothing to equal it. There are great possibilities in that country-and this government owns three and a half million acres of the land in the Peace river district. Within a few years of this line being built there are possibilities of anywhere from ten to fifteen to twenty million bushels of wheat being raised every year. It is a splendid country, and if the government wants to connect up with the Edmonton-Dunvegan line, that line is graded through to the boundary at Pouce Coupe. There are some fifty-two miles of the line from Pouce Coupe to Spirit river. The grade is in but the rails are not laid. If this line was built in there it would supply freight enough to the western section of the Grand Trunk Pacific to put the road on a paying basis. If it is not built in there, I do not see where the road is going to get freight to put it on a paying basis. I do not ask the government to build this line if it is not a good business proposition, but I ask them to investigate and see what the possibilities of that country are.
I may say that the Canadian Pacific railway has four parties in that country at the present time investigating and if the government cannot see their way to build that line after investigating I would ask them to leave the course free to the Canadian Pacific. Do not. hold the country back. If the government will not build a line let the Canadian Pacific build out of Prince George and have running rights over the government railway on a rental basis. From the information I have the Canadian Pacific, if the government are not prepared to build, are quite prepared to go ahead and build.

Item agreed to.
Grant to the Scottish Pioneer Association to assist in the "Hector" celebration, $15,000.

I would
like to have an explanation of this item.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
A hundred
and fifty years ago there came from the western islands to this country of ours certain Scottish settlers who laid the foundation of the future development of Canada through their successors. They landed in the province of Nova Scotia, and an association of Scottish Pioneers has been formed which has at its head as horn, president the Right Hon. Bonar Law, the former Premier of Great Britain, and as vice-presidents distinguished men in all parts of Canada, This association was formed to commemorate the landing of these Scottish pioneers. The celebration will take place, beginning the 15th July next. The monument has been obtained by subscription entirely apart from this grant. The monument is to be unveiled by His Excellency Lord Byng, and the events which usually follow an occasion of that kind will take place in the town and county during that week. Men of the Scottish race in all parts of Canada, including prominent men in British Columbia and in the western provinces, are interested in this event. I hope the committee, in appreciation of those men who came out in days of privation and difficulty and whose successors have gone to all parts of Canada, will gladly give this grant which will be expended by an organization made up of men whose character and reputation are undoubted in the celebration which everyone ought to attend.

The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) was interested in this matter. I think he wanted to find out why this grant was recommended, in view of the fact that refusals were made of requests for grants for exactly similar purposes. He told me that he did not expect to be here himself.
He said he had asked my hon. friend for a grant for a celebration of a very historic event at Kingston, and that my hon. friend had told him that he would have to reject it, having rejected a similar request for Nova Scotia, having reference to this same vote. Apparently the Nova Scotia request which was refused is now being granted, and the Kingston request remains refused. He also said that a large gathering was to be held at Belleville of the United Empire Loyalists, and a grant was refused on the same grounds. Perhaps my hon. friend can tell me what difference there was to change his mind other than the fact that we have now as a member of the cabinet the acting Minister of National Defence-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: The matter is not a local one at all.
-who represents the country and whose by-election is not yet fixed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not remember any applications made for a grant either at Kingston or Belleville, but I would have to know something more about these matters before I could speak definitely. I am quite sure it was nothing of a similar character because I know the applications would be dealt with on the same basis. There is a grant further down the list to aid in the construction of a monument at Orillia. While I do not say that no applications were made either by Kingston or Belleville, I should like tc look into these matters before speaking definitely.
The Orillia case is not a parallel one at all.

The grant at Orillia is to aid in the construction of the Champlain monument.

object to the celebration?
I certainly do not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: It is not fair to speak of this celebration at Pictou as being purely local. The British government are sending four warships of the North Atlantic squadron. The United States government are sending two of their war vessels. The Governor of Massachusetts is to be in attendance, and His Excellency, the Governor General, is to be there. There will be no celebration at Kingston, in regard to anything relating to Scotch people coming to this country, that would be at all comparable with this one. One of the things the people of Nova Scotia take pride in is that Sir John A. Macdonald came to Ontario via Nova Scotia.
A number of Scotchmen came into the Red River valley about a hundred years ago. Would the Minister of Finance consider an appropriation to cover a picnic in Winnipeg?

The acting Minister of National Defence a moment ago made a little appeal to us on behalf of those pioneers who had come to this country in times of stress and hardship. We in western Canada went into that country in times of stress, and we have been suffering a considerable amount of hardship. In western Canada we require railways; we are not getting them on the plea that the expense is too great; but we are still voting sums of money of this size for little picnics on the Nova Scotia coast.
I,	like all Irishmen, love Scotchmen, but I do not love Scotchmen dearly enough to vote [DOT] them money like this at a time like this. I move, seconded by the 'hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) that this item be reduced by $14,000.

I think this is establishing a very bad precedent. I have sufficient confidence in Scotchmen generally to believe that in those 150 years the descendants of the particular gentlemen who came over have long since accumulated much more than $15,000 and can readily put up the money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: A few years ago we celebrated at Quebec the tercentenary of the landing of Champlain. I think it was a source of pride to all citizens of Canada that in that manner there was celebrated the beginning of the French settlement in Canada. This particular celebration is to commemorate the landing of the Scotch for a first time in this country. It was the beginning of the settlement of the Scotch race throughout the Dominion of Canada. It is not a local celebration. As every hon. member knows, there are different strains that go to make up the composition of our people. There are the French, the English, the Scotch and the Irish. I hope in some appropriate way the country will take cognizance of the beginning in this country of settlement from Ireland and from England as well as the beginning of settlement from Scotland. I think it is advisable that these landmarks in our history should be celebrated. The children of the country grow up to know a little more about their country's history. This is a small amount that we are voting at the present time to commemorate the first migration from Scotland to this country, when one thinks of the part the Scotch have played in the settlement of Canada. This is something, I think, this parliament is entitled to pay some attention to.
What about the Japs?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend regards the Japanese as being a part of the Canadian population in the same way.

We have heard a great deal of this band of Scotsmen that came 150 years ago, but we have not heard much tonight about that other band that came a few weeks ago and went to western Canada. I think that some money might have been spent in connection with them.
Amendment negatived.

Item agreed to.
To provide for the expenses of a Royal Commission to inquire into proposed prohibition or restriction of the export of pulpwood, $20,000.
What does the government hope to accomplish by the appointment of this royal commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question whether or not it is expedient to prohibit the export of p.ulpwood is quite a controversial one. I know some people think it is a very one-sided question, but we have abundant evidence that there are two sides to it. Our purpose is to afford all parties interested an opportunity to state their views.

The government has already stated that there will be no prohibition of the pulpwood grown on farms, and if you except the pulpwood grown on farms and the pulpwood grown on Crown lands the rest of the pulpwood is hardly worth the commission. We have the bill now, and we have the commission, and we have to pay for the commission, and I may just venture the prediction that we will end up with the same policy with which we began.
It is the provinces that prohibit on Crown lands, is it not?
I know.

This would appear to me to be a matter that the government ought to be able to decide without the appointment of a commission. In any event there are enough officials in the employment of the government to obtain any information that any commission could obtain. This certainly should be a question of policy. This
seems to me a most absurd vote in view of the stand the government have already taken as pointed out by the leader of the Opposition with regard to the exportation of pulpwood from lands owned by private individuals.
I therefore move to reduce the item by $19,999.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is one aspect of this question that I think is important and should be taken into account by the committee. There is probably no single economic problem more important than the conservation of our forests, and the extent to which the forests are being depleted partly through insects, largely through fires and to a certain extent through the export of our pulpwood is a factor that should become more generally known than it is. If pulpwood is to be prohibited from export it will be because of the rapidity of our forest depletion. The commission will be most helpful in helping to educate the public as to the extent to which the forests are being depleted, and if such action became necessary as to prohibit the export of pulpwood, will make it perfectly apparent to our neighbouring nation that the government's action in the matter is not prompted by any thought of retaliation for any purpose, but that the reason is an important economic one. I think that is one factor that the House should take into account in considering how very necessary and advisable it is that a commission should be appointed at this time to help give the country the fullest information with respect to the extent to which our forests are being depleted.

It has occurred to me that if in connection with this commission appointed to look into the depletion of our forests as outlined by the Prime Minister some provision were made for cruising our timber limits to find out just what our timber resources are, a good purpose might be served. A vote of $20,000, of course, would not be sufficient to carry on that work in addition to what this commission is going to do. I think such a cruise would be worth while from an economic point of view, for then we would know just what our timber resources are.

Canada Grain Act, administration of-additional amount required, $80,000
What are the particulars of this?

This is to provide for a reel assification and salary increases for the grain men at Fort William and other points. The
Supply-Trade-Grain

records show that the Board of Grain Commissioners have recommended these salary increases after discovering that most of the grain houses in Canada are paying higher wages than the board, and the board was in consequence losing many of its good men. This is to provide for the increase recommended by the board.
Are the officers in this branch under the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission?
Yes.
Were these salary increases recommended by the Grain Commission?

Yes, to the Civil Service Commission. The procedure is this: The Grain Commissioners make a recommendation for classification and salary increases which is submitted to the Civil Service Commission, and if approved by them the minister puts through an order in council covering it.

The minister states that private companies can afford to pay larger salaries than the Board of Grain Commissioners. That is undoubtedly due to the exorbitant profits they have taken from the people in the West through their practices in the past. If their profits were cut down to a legal point it is possible they would not become such great competitors with the Board of Grain Commissioners for help as the minister indicates, and consequently there would not be the necessity for increasing the salaries of these employees.
I would not admit that.
Has the government any method or any habit of inquiring into a request for increased expenditure, or is it the invariable rule to grant whatever is asked?
Oh, no. Every request is goue into very carefully and sometimes it is [DOT]ejected.
I am glad to hear that. The minister might give me an instance of anything that has been rejected.

I will tell my hon. friend right now, and I think it will come before the House at its next session if there are any amendments to the Canada Grain Act. We find that it is not easy to get men on the Grain Commission staff. For instance, one man who came to us recently claims that the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator Company were offering more money than was paid him by the Board of Grain Commissioners.
fMr. Robb,)

I have in mind a return that was brought down by the Department of Trade and Commerce for one of our members here a short time ago, in which I noticed that the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur weighed out 19,000,000 bushels more in 1922 than they had taken in. I know part of this goes into the consolidated revenue fund but I wish to point out to the minister that the profits rightly belong to the people of the West who grew those nineteen million and odd bushels of wheat. In view of the profits made by these private companies it is no wonder they can afford to pay such salaries, and that the Grain Commissioners find it necessary to increase the stipends of their officers.

I am not disputing the statement because there is really no evidence to prove it but I will give my hon. friend the other side of the shield. The eastern millers and grain buyers contend they have to pay for a shortage, because there is a shortage in the shipments that come across the lakes.
Has the judgment of the Supreme Court as to the validity of the Grain Act been received yet?
No.

through Reuters, to send out news of business conditions generally throughout Canada and other matters that will interest readers overseas wherever Reuters have a connection. I cannot see, with all the services that we have at present, that we require to still subsidize another service. We have exhibitions of all kinds, and are simply spending untold money advertising the country. If conditions were as they ought to be in this country I think the regular news services would look after that.

That is the unfortunate part of it. The news going out from Canada is not such as would place Canada in a right light in another country. I hold in my hand-and my
[Mr. Cahill.1
hon. friend may have observed the item, because it has been published in the press-a despatch from London, England, dated 25th June, intimating that while the news going to England from Australia, New Zealand and South Africa placed those countries in a favourable light before the British people, the news going out from Canada sent out by news agents did not have that effect. The things that go on in this House are not the best kind of advertising. At the same time these conditions prevail, and I might say that nearly all the labour papers in the Old Country are carrying news, a great deal of it taken from Hansard, which is not the best advertisement for Canada.
It is the fault of those who make the speeches.
It is the truth nevertheless.
We deny it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. member tell the House from whose speeches they quote?

They make their own selection, but they are quoting Hansard in the Daily Herald as well as in the Glasgow Forward and the Labour Leader. You might: find extracts from speeches given during the last few sessions in which are stated the actual
conditions which prevail in western Canada?
I would like to ask the minister about a grant of $50,000 to the Canadian Press. I have never come across it.
That is not in this department. It is in the main estimates and we will come to it later.
It has not been reached.
Not yet.

In connection with this item, I do not know what control the minister

Supply-Trade-Gram
has. I fancy Reuters will get the news that sells, as well as the other people. It is the news that sells that is dealt with.
And it favours the Tory party.

The Rogers murder at North Bay, and those terrible things that have occurred lately, would indicate that we have not got the new Heaven and earth under this party although we were promised it. The kind of news sent out is frequently the product of the conditions that the times are cursed with. A little while ago I asked the minister if he could think of anything in the way of appeal for money or a voracious demand that this government had refused? Looking back over the years and seeing them one by one yielding to these requests, I thought I would inquire if anything had been refused at any time. The minister did not give me any answer at the time. Perhaps he can think of an item now.

The proposed scheme is not new. It was originally presented to the government three years ago. It was recommended to council for acceptance by Sir Robert Borden on June 11th 1920, but action was deferred until September of that year, when the proposals were reconsidered by Mr. Meighen at a conference with Sir Roderick Jones, chairman and managing director of Reuters. The proposals however have since been left in abeyance, owing, it is stated, wholly to various other exigencies, though the scheme went as far as having the Justice department prepare a draft agreement.
The item for British and foreign news service, $21,333,34, suggests to me that it is a third of the total item.
I should have told my hon. friend that the contract is for $32,000 a year, but as the service will begin on the 1st of August, this amount is for the balance of the fiscal year.

Item agreed to.
Towards the construction of a grain elevator at Halifax, N.S., $200,000.

The information I have is that there was an elevator there that had a little grain in it some years, and for some years none. I fancy it was burned down. Any way it is not there now. I had a return on this the other day. I think it was used substantially just once. I believe it was partly built by the railway and partly by the city. At any rate there were joint contributions. Can the hon. member tell us just what special event the government has in mind that caused it to deem it the part of wisdom to build a large elevator there?

I am rather at a loss to understand just what the right hon. leader of the Opposition means by the lemarks he has made and the remarks which he has previously made, but which I did not hear. He was criticizing the remarks of another hon. member this evening and suggesting that the hon. member was tired or sleepy, possibly dreaming. This may be the reason of the remarks of my hon. friend iu respect of certain expenditures in the county of Halifax.
The estimates are no dream.

I might say that the construction of a grain elevator at Halifax was projected in 1912, under the government then led by Sir Robert Borden, and which my hon. friend supported. In that year my right hon. friend will remember that it was decided that the railway terminals of Halifax were to be properly or improperly- improperly, I think-removed from one end of the city to the other, and the erection of this elevator was a portion of that project. The present elevator, which was constructed jointly, I think, by the city, the government of Nova Scotia, and the Dominion government many years ago, cannot now very well be used by reason of the fact that the railway terminal facilities have been moved to another end of the city. Further, the present grain elevator is obsolete and not suitable for the handling of grain.
I cannot say, and I am sure my hon. friend cannot very accurately tell us, what quantity of grain has gone through the Halifax elevator. It is true that port is not a big grain exporting port. The business men of Halifax hardly expect it to be a large grain exporting port, but still a certain quantity may very profitably find an outlet through Halifax. I have been personally advised by two or three of the largest shipping companies using that port during the past winter, that a modem elevator of a million bushels capacity would be of great service to the port and to shipping. At the present time a great deal of shipping might go to Halifax were it not for the reason that they are unable to secure grain as a partial cargo.

Could the hon. gentleman not think of something that might be useful to Halifax and at the same time would cost a little less money?
Supply-Trade-Grain

Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax) I am told by shipping men and business men of Halifax that this expenditure would be extremely useful to the port of Halifax. I believe that is a fact. The quantity of shipping which enters or leaves any Canadian port is largely determined by whether or not they can obtain a partial loading of grain. That is necessary as regards the * port of Halifax.

My hon. friend knows perfectly well that Halifax has not handled grain for years, except during the war. When there was the grain to handle, the elevator handled it all right. But the business there is absolutely negligible and must be so as long as we have a charge for hauling grain on the railway and railway costs are heavy.

My hon. friend is entirely wrong in saying that very small grain shipments have gone through the port of Halifax. It is true that grain shipments from Halifax have not been large in any one year, but a substantial quantity of grain has gone through that port. There is a difference in the freight rates as between St. John and Halifax of one cent per 100 pounds. I hope, however, this differential will be abolished as it should be. I am instructed that it costs more to move grain from St. John to St. John West where the grain is placed on board steamers than it would cost to move that grain to Halifax.
No.

I have that
from persons who have actual knowledge.

If my hon.
friend thinks any business for the elevator is going to come in that way, he is very much mistaken. I think my hon. friend really knows there is no business there. How much is to be the total cost of this elevator which may be very useful in another direction in a very short time?

We have put this amount
in the estimates primarily to prepare the plans and to be in a position, if such is deemed proper, to start work on that elevator early enough so that it will be ready for next season's crop. There is no probability of getting it ready for this season's crop. We shall be guided by the advice of experts as to the capacity of an elevator that would pay at that port. My hon. friend has hinted at a reclassification of rates. That will be taken into consideration.
{Sir Henry Drayton.]

Is the situation this that the government has no idea of the quantity of grain likely to go through that port or the capacity of the elevator required? They are sure of nothing except that there is to be an election.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did the large and expensive scheme of terminals constructed by the late government not include an elevator? They spent, I do not know how many millions there. I would almost think this elevator would be as useful as the terminals.

That may be;
but the elevator was not gone on with for a very good reason, and that was that the business was not offering for it. Business is not now offering for the elevator. If I am wrong, I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to correct me. According to his own statement, he does not know what size of an elevator he has to put up or the business likely to be obtained. He is to have somebody inquire into the matter.
Why did the late government spend $22,000,000 there on terminals?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
My hon.
friend overlooked one thing, namely that the quantity of grain moved depends upon whether ships will be available to carry it. Contracts to carry grain are not made by the railway people themselves, and the grain broker who wants to ship to Liverpool will ship via Halifax if there are facilities and ships there to carry the grain. During the past few years merchants have not been regularly shipping to Halifax because there has not been space. Indications are that this space will be obtained and work will come for the elevator. My hon. friend ought surely to encourage the idea that we should have facilities in our ports in winter for shipments of grain instead of sending the ships to American ports. If he wants to oppose the idea that we should have within our own boundaries and harbours facilities by which Canadian produce can be carried abroad and imports can be brought to our ports, that is a very curious policy. If he wishes to have the ships in winter going to Boston and other American ports instead of to Canadian ports, that will be the policy of my hon. friend.

My hon. friend always conveniently forgets everything he likes to forget. There is another winter port, that is neither Portland nor any other American port, and that is St. John. He also forgets that usually grain travels by the cheapest railway route.
