speechtext:
Halifax is
the nearest port to the British Isles.

I suppose he
says it is just as cheap to carry grain by rail as by water.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I have not
said that at all.

It is the same thing. You have an extra 276 miles' haul, if I remember rightly. That, however, is getting away from the point. What information has my hon. friend as to the income of the port and the quantity of grain to be handled?

My information is, according
to the estimates of the previous government, that the requirements of that port would be for an elevator with a capacity of from 750,000 to 1,000,000 bushels.
My recollection is that we used to use about 60,000 bushels in trimming during the busy period.
Each trip?
In a day when things were busy-60,000 bushels in and 60,000 out.

That is an admission that an
elevator is required.
That was during the war period.
No grain went through the port of Halifax during the war.
We had at one time a movement of as much as thirty cars a day.
I do not think so.

I would not like to get into
a dispute between my two hon. friends who
were members of the same government at that time.

It seems to me that the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) takes a very pessimistic and gloomy view of the development of an eastern national port, namely the port of Halifax. It is equally as pessimistic a view as my hon. friend took when, as chairman of the Railway Commission, he laid down that very explicit doctrine that geographical disadvantages should not be taken into consideration in the fixing of rates. We are a part of this great confederation; and the great leaders who have passed to the beyond held out to us in Nova Scotia and to the citizens of Halifax the promise that if the province remained in confederation Nova Scotia and Halifax would become the Atlantic

frontage of the Dominion. And if my hon. friend will only go and look at the motto above the entrance to this magnificent structure, raised and reared by his government, he will see there written these words:
The wnoiesome sea is at her e,utes,
Her gates both East and West.
We may have the wholesome sea but we have not the gates. But it was in the wisdom of the late Liberal Chieftain, Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier,to foresee the future and build the Transcontinental, taking the road to Moncton as a common centre for the shipment of grain and other products of the West in winter, from Halifax and St. John. When the short line is completed from a point above Port Arthur on the Canadian National up to the Transcontinental, with easier grades and shorter mileage, the people of Halifax feel that it will be the duty of the Canadian National system to see that grain and other products of the West not routed through any other ports shall be carried to the ports of Halifax and St. John in winter. If these things are not done then perhaps, some of the things spoken of by a gentleman in the legislature of Nova Scotia and referred to in the press of the Maritime provinces may come to be more than mere words and cold type. I regret that the state of my health to-night forbids my entering as largely into this subject as I should like. But it is vital to the interests of Nova Scotia, it is vital to the city of Halifax, that proper attention be given this matter. I say it is vital to the city of Halifax, which Sir Charles Tupper declared would be, as a result of this national policy, a forest of masts if that province remained true to confederation. We are spending to-day millions of money for the development of the port of Portland, and this is the result of an act of administration on the part of the right hon. the leader .of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen in the taking over of the Grand Trunk and the terminals at Portland. This was a legacy bequeathed to the present government, who have in turn handed it over to Sir Henry Thornton and his board of management. I believe that Sir Henry Thornton is willing to do the right thing by the Maritime provinces, and my hon. friend must know that Sir Henry has recommended that an elevator should be built at Halifax with a capacity of at least 750,000 bushels, if not a million. It is his intention to divert to Halifax, as he has a right to do, that proportion of the grain and other products from the West that can and ought to be carried through this port. The rate to Halifax will then be the same as to St. John or Portland or
Supply-T rade-Grain

New York. Montreal carries one cent less and when the differential referred to by my hon. colleague (Mr. Maclean) is removed as between St. John and Halifax, then New York, Portland, St. John and Halifax will be on a parity. There is no sound reason why Halifax should not share as a national port in the shipment of products of the West and of central Canada to the Old Country and the Mediterranean in future. These are my hopes; and I regret that my hon. friend should take the gloomy, pessimistic view he has displayed in reference to the future of Halifax as a port. I do not share that view and I am sure that if we both live a few years longer and Halifax is given an opportunity he will have reason to revise his opinion and will be quite willing to help to make it what it was always intended to be, the eastern gateway, one of the national ports of Canada.

I have listened with a great deal of interest, not to say amazement, to some of the remarks which have been made in this House by the representatives from the East and the West, who suggest that, if certain concessions are not granted them, certain veiled threats which they make are going to be carried into effect. I have almost come to the conclusion that the government are prepared to outdo that last awful night in the city of Toronto, a few sessions ago. We are nearing the dawn of another day and we hear now the story of the building of the Transcontinentl railway and what it is going to bring about in this country; and this is the justification for an expenditure of $200,000 to be voted in the Supplementary Estimates, which certainly, at any rate, should have appeared in the Main Estimates. There are two items here of a similar nature, notwithstanding that there are many parts of this country where the government would be much. more justified in expending money in the building of elevators than at these particular points. I refer to the province of Ontario where there are no internal elevators for the accommodation of the farmers. They are not receiving any consideration of this kind, but we are not coming before the government and making all sorts of veiled threats as to what may take place; we are not hinting at secession if certain concessions are not made. I never heard a more absurd argument advanced in support of any proposition than that which has been offered by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Finn). No doubt the nature of his argument is due to the fact, which he mentioned a moment ago, that he i* not in good health to-night.
I Mr. Finn.]

When I made the remark in regard to threats I said that the leader of the Opposition in Nova Scotia, the gentleman that was responsible for the statement, was the leader of the Tory party in the legislature of the province; and the Halifax Herald, the leading Tory paper in Nova Scotia, echoed the same thing.

Item agreed to.
Towards the construction of a grain elevator at Edmonton, Alta, $200,000.

In whatever I may say on this vote I do not want to be construed either by the administration or by the people of Edmonton as opposing any legitimate wish that might be expressed founded on the necessities of the grain trade there or of the railways for the construction of an internal elevator at that point. I object to the government overlooking a claim that has been admitted by Dr. Magill, Chairman of the Grain Commission, and that has been on record for the last ten or twelve years, a claim for the establishment of an internal storage elevator at Lethbridge. I was very much surprised when I saw this item of $200,000 in the Estimates. I want to point out the difference between the crop production and the
5 a.m. facilities afforded at Edmonton compared with Lethbridge. Three transcontinental railways run into Edmonton, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific, and two of these lines run to western ports. On the other hand, in the Lethbridge district we are tied up to one railway system, the Canadian Pacific, which, in spite of a most efficient administration, has always fallen short of its ability to cope with the demands connected with the handling of our grain in that district. One of the main reasons for the establishing of this elevator at Edmonton is to facilitate the movement of grain westward to the Pacific coast and to try to effect a saving for the farmer. I heartily agree with that, but I would point out that last year in the freight district of Lethbridge we produced 22,000,000 bushels of wheat, over one-third the entire production of Alberta, a condition which, however, resulted in a serious shortage of cars in that district. At one time last season there were in Cardston at least one hundred four-horse teams with loads of wheat, some of it drawn from a distance of twenty miles, and that wheat was there from one to three days because of lack of elevator space, due, in turn, to the lack of cars. The same was true at Woolford Station, east of Cardstoi* and at other points throughout that district. In

Supply-Trade-Grain
1915 we had a crop in the Lethbridge freight district of 41,000,000 bushels of wheat, nearly one-half the entire crop production of Alberta. The result was that the elevators were filled up and the delivery was continued until June and July of the following season. I believe the ex-Minister of Finance was given that record when he was out in our countrv investigating the railway situation. Thousands upon thousands of acres of wheat remained in the stook all winter, simply on account of that car shortage and lack of elevator space. Thousands upon thousands of bushels of grain were threshed into open bins in the fields; the grain bleached and deteriorated in quality and the farmers suffered losses running into hundreds of thousands of dollars. If there is a district in Canada that needs an internal storage elevator it is in Lethbridge district. This whole system of internal storage elevators originated in the Lethbridge district.
With what government?

That was in 1904 or 1905. The whole thing was founded upon the acute shortage of cars which was occurring year after year and of course, the large crops we were producing in that district. Lethbridge is one of the largest coal producing districts in Canada, and the season for the hauling of coal is concurrent with the period during which the heavy hauling of wheat should proceed. At least 200 cars a day are required to move the coal product at that period, and it is natural that when there are two demands of that kind the more urgent should be met, namely, the transport of coal to the people of the prairies. I have two telegrams here that I want to read. The first is dated at Lethbridge, June 27, and reads as follows:
Press despatch to-day states supplementary estimates provide internal e/levators Edmonton. No mention Lethbridge. Urge you press our claim. One-third Alberta wheat last year grown on Lethbridge Railway division. Manifestly unfair government overlook this district where grain grown and elevator badly needed.
That is from the president of the Lethbridge Board of Trade. Here is another telegram I got early this morning from the secretary of the Lethbridge Board of Trade:
Our board passed strong resolution to-day urging you to protest government's action locating proposed elevator at Edmonton. Northern Alberta heaviest crop is oats-
That means in the Edmonton district.
-which is not exportable commodity via Vancouver and the Panama canal. Provincial government estimates between forty and fifty million bushels wheat crop on Lethbridge Railway division this year. Dry lands crops augmented by future irrigation crops
warrant and will sustain elevator here. Farmers in this district have been led to belive that favorable consideration would be given to Lethbridge when any additional elevators were establishd.
They have been led to believe that for years. The movement for the construction of these internal storage elevators, as I have already stated, began in that district, and began on account of the yearly shortage which we experienced there of cars necessary to handle our grain crop. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I claim that I am the parent of the internal storage elevator idea It is the only thing in the country I can lay claim to being parent to. On account of the difficulty of securing sufficient storage and sufficient cars in southern Alberta a conference was called some twenty years ago by the Hon. Mr. Rutherford, at that time premier of the province of Alberta. Mr. Rutherford kindly sent me an invitation to attend that conference, which was composed of farmers, business men, railway men, grain men and bankers. At that conference the main subject of discussion was the western shipment of grain. Delegates were there from Vancouver, Victoria, New Westminster, from all over Alberta, and one or two I think from Saskatchewan, and the burden upon their thoughts at that time was shipping by the A.B.C. route as it was called, which meant the Alberta-British Columbia route. At that conference the question of car shortage came up. I was asked to open the discussion on what was known as our old Manitoba Grain Act, and in connection therewith I advocated the building of internal storage elevators to relieve the shortage of cars for one thing, in the second place to encourage the development of the milling industry in our principal cities in the West, and in the third place to minister to the wants of our mixed farming industry. These were the three points that were involved.
A short time after that convention this matter was taken up by the Board of Grain Commissioners. They came out to Lethbridge and held quite a long sitting there. I was before the board at that time and this question of the establishment of internal storage elevators was thoroughly canvassed. The board returned and presented their report to parliament recommending the building of these internal storage elevators for the purposes to which I have referred. Then the board went out again through the western country to determine where they should locate these internal storage elevators. They thoroughly canvassed every locality in which their meet-
Supply-Trade-Grain

mgs were held, and they decided that Lethbridge was one of the points where one of these elevators should be located, and they so reported to parliament. The recommendation was made by Dr. Magill, the chairman of the Grain Board. The Minister of Trade and Commerce will find that recommendation in his files. I do not know how it happened but the government built three of these storage elevators, one at Moose Jaw, one at Saskatoon, and one at Calgary. It is not for me to comment upon the location of these elevators, but the government overlooked the one place where the movement had orginated and where the car situation is at different times the most acute of any place in the country that I know of. They placed these elevators at these other points. Now continually from that time up till now, born of necessity of the situation there, petition after petition, letter after letter, presentation after presentation has been sent to Ottawa urging the construction of an internal storage elevator to meet our needs at that point, and I cannot see why that request has not been granted. I cannot see why these other elevators should be provided for at this time and Lethbridge again be left out. We have here in this telegram the statement, and I am sure this will be pleasing to the Minister of Finance because he was speaking of the prospects of the West a few nights ago, that the estimate of the provincial government is that we shall have a wheat crop of from forty to fifty million bushels in the Lethbridge district this year. If that is the case the same situation will be repeated that occurred in 1915, and all over that part of the country grain will be standing in the stook all winter, and there will be a loss of thousands and thousands of dollars to those farmers. Now I am going to make this appeal to the government. I am not finding fault with these elevators. If they need that elevator at Edmonton in order to facilitate the shipment eastward or westward-
Is there any reason why the farmers in the West cannot have granaries to take care of their grain?

It is impossible to build granaries in the condition we are in to house all that grain. The condition is largely one of car shortage, and that can only be met by giving your rolling stock a shorter journey, letting them run back and forth to the internal elevator, for in that way they give ten times the car service that you get when the rolling stock is moving 1,200 miles to Winnipeg or 780 miles to the west coast. That is the kernel

of the whole situation. Now I am going to appeal to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture, who knows what that situation means to these mixed farmers to bring down a further Supplementary Estimate and provide for the construction of an elevator at Lethbridge.
Let us get to bed and we will give you half a dozen elevators.

I think the government
is the cause of the lateness of the hour and not I. I sincerely beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman, for delaying you so long but this cause is one that has been dear to my heart for the last twenty years. It is time it was attended to, and attended to right off. I appeal to the Prime Minister to bring down a further Supplementary Estimate and build that elevator.

Into the division of opinion
as to Edmonton and Lethbridge, I am not going to enter. It is only fair to my hon. friend to say that he has urged upon the government the construction of an elevator at Lethbridge, and as I listened to his speech to-night it almost seemed as though we were back in other days because I can recall when the former member for that constituency, Mr. Buchanan, had tried with equal force to impress upon previous governments the importance and necessity of an elevator at Lethbridge. But another thought came to my mind when my hon. friend was speaking. Listening to the account of the crop they had in his district last year, the crop they expect to have this year, and the number of cattle and sheep they have, it occurred to me that the hard luck stories we have been hearing have not been quite well founded.

If I may interrupt, I may
say that some time ago the Lethbridge Board of Trade prepared a statement as to the situation last year. One copy was presented to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, a second to the Prime Minister, and the third to the Minister of the Interior. The facts which I have recited as to last year's crop are given there. They were carefully taken from the Canadian Pacific Railway records and I am very sure they are correct.

I do not dispute that. I am
quite of that opinion.

I do not think I painted
a very gloomy picture myself. I believe there is the very greatest hope for the future of

Supply-Trade-Grain
Alberta, although we did have two or three seasons there when we ran badly behind.

It is true there are three railways running into Edmonton to fill the elevator there, but the door has not been closed to Lethbridge. In order that my hon. friend may take something home, I may say that the Grain Commissioners have promised to review the whole situation and make a recommendation to us.
Carried.

Just a minute. I want to point out to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the situation was very carefully canvassed out there years ago by the grain commission. The facts are all known; there is no need of any further investigation. Lethbridge has been side tracked without reason, and I hope that the Prime Minister will do as I have suggested, bring down a supplementary estimate to help our cause.

I agree with what the
hon. gentleman has said about the necessity for an elevator for this district. Additional elevator accommodation is needed for the whole of Canada. We are behind the times in that respect. I also agree with what has been sajid regarding the dire need of a terminal elevator in central Ontario. In the debate the other night I read the remarks of Mr. Julius H. Barnes, one of the ablest transportation and grain men on the American continent about the elevator capacity of this country and the United States. This statement, which was published in the last month's issue of the National City Bank shows that the elevators across the border, from Dakota right down to Buffalo are congested and cannot contain any more grain. We are going to be in the same position in this country unless additional elevator accommodation is provided. What is needed for Canada is a big, forward elevator policy which will provide for elevators all along the great lakes and the St. Lawrence. On the 2nd of May, 1919 a deputation came down to Ottawa to interview the government. I prepared a memorandum for the deputation which was laid before the government of the day. Mr. Manning Doherty, Minister of Agriculture for Ontario, was present on that occasion, with representatives of the United Farmers of Ontario, the United Farmers' Cooperative Company, and representatives of the grain trade.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that the item relates to the elevator at Edmonton, and that
what he is saying is hot relevant to the question.
But you have allowed the hon. member for Lethbridge to urge the need of an elevator in that district.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That does not make
any difference.

We have as much right
to urge the establishment of an elevator for central Ontario as the hon. member in question has to argue in favour of an elevator for Lethbridge. The government must adopt a forward and progressive policy upon this elevator question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not a question of policy at all.

I have a memorandum
here but I do not wish to read the whole of it. It urges the need and utility of a terminal elevator, such as is being built in Edmonton and Halifax, in central Ontario. There was an election the other day in the province of Ontario and one of the main questions argued at that time was the need of these elevators.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must again draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that he is out of order.

Surely I am in order in making a few quotations from the memorandum. We were told that when the estimates for the construction of elevators were brought down opportunity would be afforded for a discussion of the whole elevator policy of the country and yet we are not to be permitted to discuss it. I brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when his estimates were before the House, and we would not have allowed those estimates to go through so quickly if the minister had not promised to afford me an opportunity of bringing the need of a terminal elevator in central Ontario before the committee. I shall only occupy four or five minutes. An elevator is not a luxury; it is a necessity.

I must rise to a point of
order. The hon. member has been out of order for some time. If he wishes to appeal against the decision of the Chair he may do so by calling for a vote of the committee, otherwise he is entirely out of order. If the hon. member does not call for a vote let us pass this item and proceed to the next one.

It is only fair that the hon. member for North Toronto should be afforded the same opportunity as the hon. member for Lethbridge who spoke on the
Supply-Trade-Grain

necessity of an elevator in his section of the country. The hon. member for North Toronto is giving reasons why there should be a terminal elevator for central Ontario.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The difficulty is that the hon. member cannot move a capital expenditure or a public charge. The distinction is that the hon. member for Lethbridge was suggesting to the committee that, instead of the Edmonton elevator there should be a provision for the construction of an elevator at Lethbridge, for that same province, but in a different part. In this debate the hon. member for North Toronto is speaking of the establishment of elevators and the general policy of elevator construction in Ontario which is altogether different.

I may say that Ontario produces approximately 200,000,000 bushels of grain annually. In 1919 that total aggregated nearly 225,000,000 bushels, but this was an exceptionally favourable year for grain crops. It will be seen that in the average year Ontario produces enormous quantities of grain. A very considerable quantity of this grain is used for live stock feeding as the live stock industry is a prominent one in the province of Ontario. At the same time there is no doubt out that millions of bushels change hands each year the grain being sold either in the local trade, in interprovincial trade, or for export. At the present time there is no government interior terminal elevator in the province at which grain may be officially weighed and graded, as is done in the other provinces. At the present time the Grain Commission is endeavouring to purchase over 500,000 bushels of oats in Ontario, but there is no central point at which this grain can be officially assembled, weighed and graded. The absence of these facilities in Ontario has proven a loss to the farmers, a great inconvenience to those engaged in the grain trade, and a handicap to the province in competing in these lines with other provinces which have the benefit of such facilities.

The member for Lethbridge argued that the short haul would enable so many cars to be used. This is an old question in this country. The western farmer has been contending for years that he should have cars available as soon as he threshes, in order to take care of his grain; consequently we are bound to have a car shortage at certain times in the year, and now we are asked to meet this condition, to enable those people to avoid this cost. The people in Ontario have always had to take care of their grain, and I believe that if the farmers in western Canada would pursue the policy carried out in other parts they would not have as many difficulties as they have to-day, and you would not find a glut of wheat on the market at one time, and then for several months nothing for the railways to do. Western farmers are not able to take advantage of the market to the same extent that they would if they were carrying their own grain, as the farmers do in other parts of the country. It may be said that, owing to the immense quantities of grain grown by the farmers in the West, it is absolutely impossible for them to do it.	.

We have sat till broad daylight, and the government is still endeavouring to crowd these estimates through. An item of $200,000 in the supplementaries is altogether too large to be passed in this manner. There was ample opportunity to have these items passed in the main estimates, if it was desired to put them through, or if there was any justification for putting them through. The fact that they appear in the estimates in the dying hours of the session indicates that they are not items such as should be passed by this House without reasonable discussion.

As I understand the ruling on the point of order when an item relating to a post office is before the committee you can discuss the needs of any post office in another part of the country. Now, I am not preventing the committee from rising. I would have been glad to see the House rise two months ago. We have tried to play the game with the government and we have done our best but we do not want anything unfair. The counties which are asking for this particular item are Liberal counties and have gone Liberal. Regarding these particular elevators at Edmonton and at Halifax, I would like to
ask the minister one or two questions. I think it is necessary when an elevator is to be built that it should be constructed in the proper place. Some mistakes have been made in erecting elevators in certain localities. Can the minister tell the committee whether these elevators will provide sufficient accommodation for weighing, drying, cleaning, storing and grading of all kinds of grain in Nova Scotia and Alberta? Second, will they be of advantage to individual farmers of those two provinces by enabling them to ship carload lots of grain which would be officially weighed and stored and for which there would be issued an official certificate which would be recognized by the bank at once, thus broadening the farmer's market, and will similar accommodation be available to the grain trade? Another point in connection with these elevators is this: Will the erection of these two $200,000 elevators provide facilities for the storing, cleaning and grading of different kinds of seed? This would be of great advantage to the farmers of Nova Scotia and Alberta, particularly with reference to grass and clover seed. Will they be of much advantage to the live stock industry of those provinces by facilitating the distribution of feeding stock from one section to another in the case of short crops in the local districts or in the provinces as a whole? Will these elevators be able to perform a distinct service in preventing the deterioration of certain crops in the provinces in years of too much moisture, as was illustrated in the bean crop in recent years? The crop of buckwheat in one year had to be dried because of wet weather which prevailed at the time of harvesting. Special emphasis, 1 might say, should be laid on the fact that such an elevator as these two elevators, should be a public elevator, and certificates should be issued that would be official government certificates, both of which are advantages affording great protection to the public and not available in the same sense from private enterprise.
From the commercial side, I believe these two elevators may be a success. I am not speaking in order to kill time. I appreciate the work of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, (Mr. Robb). I think he has been a very fair minister. He has no doubt been very busy in the past, and I should like to be fair to the ministers because they are overworked. I should like the Minister of Trade and Commerce to come up to Toronto, meet the United Farmers, the Harbour Commissioners, the Peterborough people, and the other people interested in this matter and see if something can be done to relieve the situation.

At flag stations, throughout central Ontario, the railways will not take the crops, there is a great hardship owing to lack of these facilities. For that reason I presented this memorial, which I hold in my hand, to the government in 1919, but not a thing has been done since. The central counties of Ontario, the Yorks, Peel, Brant, the Simcoes, and many other counties have no way of putting their crops into cars at a railway station; they have no place to leave their crops and in some cases they are rotting in the ground for lack of transportation.

Harbours and rivers-Nova Scotia-Little Anse-In full and final settlement of T. D. Morrison's claim in connection with contract for construction of a breakwater, J3.234.60.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Last evening this item stood on account of the fact that I did not have before me full data in connection with the matter. The committee is aware of the circumstances under which I was dealing with the estimates. The situation regarding this matter I will put very briefly before the committee. Mr. Morrison obtained a contract in 1911-12 for the construction of a breakwater at Little Anse. He had proceeded with the construction of the work, and it had been completed, when on December 28, 1912, one of those abnormal storms and, in fact, gales which sometimes sweep the eastern coasts of our country, came up and destroyed the outer end of the breakwater. In the contract which he had signed for its construction was a clause providing that the contractor was to take the risk of a storm. He proceeded to replace the part that was destroyed, and then he made a claim upon the department asking that he should be compensated for this extra work which he was compelled to do by reason of the storm. The engineer at that time, Mr Bemas-coni, took the ground that by reason of the strict terms of the contract no allowance should be made to him on account of this. The next year, 1913, a broader construction was placed upon contracts under conditions like these. The department, in the case of a contract at Devil's Island was authorized by order in council, to pay the contractor $4,813, to compensate him for the extra work which he was compelled to do as a result of the storm. In the next year, in a place called Sandy Cove, a contracting firm called John E. Bigelow & Son was paid amounts which together reached $1,995, under exactly similar circumstances. Again at Dipper Harbour and again at Three Fathom Harbour, amounts were paid by the department to contractors whose work had been destroyed by storms. The Department of Public Works proceeded to change the form
mfr Church. 1
of contract by which the liability occasioned by result of abnormal gales was taken from :the contractor and admitted by the department.
This contractor, Mr. Morrison, then came to the Department of Public Works and asked that his claim should be reviewed. It was considered by Mr. Locke, who was second in command amongst the engineering staff of the province pf Nova Scotia. Mr Locke, reviewing the whole circumstances, held that this storm of 1921 was an absolutely abnormal, one, one which could not have been contemplated at the time the contract was made, and his report winds up as follows:
I, therefore, beg to report that Mr. Morrison's claim for extras be allowed and as to what the amount of this claim should be I respectfully submit the following figures:
He goes into details and makes the figures to be $3,234.60. Going into the matter in detail, he further concludes:
I would, therefore, recommend that Mr. Morrison be paid in connection with this work the additional sum of $3,234.60. As to the question of whether interest should be allowed or not for the nine years which have expired since that time, I consider this a matter for the higher officials of the department to decide upon.
What is the date of that report?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
June 27, 1922. Then Mr. Dodwell who has been Chief Engineer of Public Works in Nova Scotia for the last twenty-five years, a man of long experience who has served under every government, appointed originally by the government of Sir John Thompson and who has been an official ever since, reviewed the claim of Mr. Morrison. Speaking of the conditions he said:
The evidence goes to show that this was a storm of extraordinary and almost unprecedented severity. It was a whole gale from the S.S.E., the direction of greatest exposure, and it was accompanied by a tide or tidal wave of a height unknown for many years.
He went on to say:
It is true that Morrison's contract explicitly provided that he would be responsible during the whole period of the construction for all damage done thereto by gales, storms and other causes, and no relief from responsibility is given or implied in the case of a storm of extraordinary or unprecedented magnitude. That this provision in the form of contracts in vogue in 1911 was deemed of an arbitrary or unfair severity is shown by the fact that in contracts of later date, as for instance the one at Sandy Cove, clause 21 of the specification provides that the contractor is responsible for all damage	" excepting in such
cases of an uncontrollable action of nature which it would be impossible to guard against." It is admittedly difficult to draw a line between an ordinary storm doing damage that the contractors must make good at their own expense, and an extraordinary one with its resultant damage for which a contractor is not liable.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
but if we suppose that the breakwater at Little Anse before its completion had been damaged or destroyed by an earthquake, the department would hardly be justified-not in equity at least-in penalizing the contractor for such a catastrophe.
After a careful and thorough review of the circumstances of this claim, I find myself unable to reach any other opinion than that Mr. T. D. Morrison is fairly and properly entitled to be paid the amount of damages estimated by Mr. Locke in his report attached hereto at $3,324.60. If, moreover, he is entitled to this amount as principal, he would also be entitled to interest and the amount payable to him would therefore be

Here is a case in which the two leading officers of the department have recognized the claim. I am aware that Mr. Bernasconi in 1920 reported against the claim. He was a young man and a junior engineer who had charge of the construction, and he reported, on account of the contract at that time making the explicit provision in regard to the liability of the contractor, that he was prevented from considering the claim. But inasmuch as my hon. friend's government changed the form of contract and allowed in proper cases in which the evidence was cleat that the work of the contractor had been destroyed by storms of unusual severity, that compensation should be made, the minister of this department felt that he had a right to ask that the money be paid. I submit with absolute confidence, after going through the records and speaking not from any legal standpoint but with full responsibility as acting minister, that the vote is justifiable.

This is a very good kind of case for discussion, because it shows what can be done if a minister wants to put through a supplementary estimate. One of the best things to do is to bring in witnesses afterwards who knew nothing about the facts at the time. For example, if you want to obtain a different decision from the one that was previously arrived at just send an engineer who was not originally on the work, and have his report considered by some one who was not the original engineer either.

Now I am going to try to get at the facts. This contract was entered into in 1911 or 1912 and the report on the storm was made on January 7, 1913. There was no claim put in for damages as a result of the storm; at that time no reform politician had come upon the scene to tell this gentleman that he might get his claim settled. The final estimate under this precious contract was given on August 27, 1913, and in that final estimate there was an allowance for $300 extra, the original contract being for $21,500. These extras were accepted, and the first- reference I find to any claim appears in the file on the 29th of July, 1920. The claim was referred by the then minister to the local engineer, Mr. Bernasconi and he reported upon it in the ordinary way. The district engineer reported against the claim on October 22, 1920, to the chief engineer, Mr. St. Laurent, who endorsed the report. The report of the chief engineer is dated November 8, 1920, and a letter was written to Mr. Morrison refusing his claim on November 10. The next thing I find is a letter from the initial engineer to the minister who at that time was the Hon. Mr. McCurdy. The matter was again considered and referred to the engineers, and again on March 14, 1921, a letter was written to Mr. Morrison stating that his claim could not be acceded to. Then a long petition is worked up winding up with a statement that is forwarded "through our worthy and popular representative Mr. George W. Kyte". When this petition comes in Mr. St. Laurent gets hold of it in the first instance. The memorandum filed by Mr. St. Laurent on the 21st of April, 1922, is against the claim, and so it is necessary, of course, that there should be a new set of engineers, if this claim, which never really existed at any time between 1913 and 1920, was to be made alive. There were therefore two other engineers whose names we have heard. Now there is only one thing I can say about this matter. The claim had been refused regularly by engineers that were familiar with the whole thing, and it was declined when appeal was had to the former Minister of Public Works.
Was the engineer who recommended it a senior engineer?

The engineer who did not recommend it was the chief engineer. There is just one moral to be drawn from the whole matter and that is as to what politics can do.

You are measuring every one by your own half measure.

We have

I have not heard the previous discussion in connection with this item, but it is rather peculiar that a claim so long out-lawed as this can now be resurrected. Mr. Dodwell is a man of long experience who was appointed under Sir John Thompson's government. My hon. friend's suggestion about politics is therefore perfectly ridiculous. My hon. friend's insinuation about the utilizing of engineers is wholly unwarranted. went down in 1916 and reported in favour ol it? If this be so proper and right and legal why does not the government waive any question of statutory limitation and give a fiat and let the man sue?

I am rather surprised at the unwonted heat displayed by my hon. friend from West York with regard to this matter. And they call that democracy.

The second item of $8,000 for an Imperial or overseas press service is no more justifiable than is the $50,000 grant. I think the government are ill advised in voting $50,000 of the people's money for a press service, especially at this hour in the morning. I think the government should at least hold this vote over until we have had time to reconsider the proposition, and sleep over it;
no harm will be done by deferring it until later in the day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think we are all anxious to conclude the consideration of the estimates. These are the last items and there would be no advantage in holding them over until later in the day. The item of $50,000 is one which has appeared in the estimates for a number of years. No exception has been taken to it until this year when there was some reason to believe that possibly the Press more or less controlled a number of papers that might be entitled to new3 which, perhaps, they were receiving notwithstanding the government's assistance. I confess there was considerable doubt in the mind of the government as to the wisdom of continuing this vote in view of that circumstance. However, the government has gone carefully into the matter and, as far as we are able to learn, the immediate cancellation of this vote would simply mean that some of the smaller papers of the country would lose considerable news which they are at present receiving. It would make no difference to the larger papers; but we are told, and I believe on reliable authority, that a few of the papers in the Maritime Provinces and some in western Canada would suffer a considerable cut in the news they receive if that course were pursued. Under the circumstances, and bearing in mind the fact that this item appeared in the estimates before this matter came up for consideration, and inasmuch as the Press may have counted on it, the government has thought that for this year the item should be allowed to stand. However, I should like to intimate to my hon. friend that the government has decided that in subsequent estimates these amounts will not be included.

I should like to make just one thing clear. Since I have been in this House, and I entered it in 1917, I have always opposed this item in the estimates. The present leader of the government, who came in in 1919 I think, agreed with me in opposition to this amendment when we sat on the other side. The estimate ever since it came into effect has always been opposed by the Liberal party. It originated in 1917, and I never could see any justification for it. I never could see why the press of Canada should tax the people of this country to the extent of $50,000 in order to put over on the Canadian public the propaganda that they wish to put from year to year. I opposed this item when we were in opposition, I was opposed to it last year when it was voted, and I am opposed to it to-day. I think the principle

472S
Supply-Canadian Press

involved is a wrong one. I can see no advantage to the Canadian people in this vote, and if I have any support in this House this morning I will have much pleasure in voting against it. The Canadian Press have no more claim on the Canadian people than any other enterprise. I am sure that the members of the official opposition in the House will oppose this vote. I repeat the Canadian Press have no more right to a vote of $50,000 of the people's money to carry on their enterprise than any other business organization has. Not only should they be debarred this vote, not only should they fail to receive the support ox the people, but they are a big combine in Canada. When the Liberal party applied for a newspaper franchise in Ottawa the Canadian Press told those who made the application they could not have it. This vote looks too much like blackmail for me to support it. I think the government are using bad judgment in voting $50,000 towards the support of this enterprise, and I shall oppose it.

I am going to take up just a few minutes time in stating facts which I think should be made known to the members of the committee at this time. I do this because I personally was brought into the controversy in regard to the Canadian Press during the discussion which occurred when Bill No. 54 was before the House. Fortunately we have the report of the annual meeting of the Canadian Press, we have the official report of the gentlemen who are working for and receiving this donation from the people of Canada, and I wish to draw the attention of members of the committee to the attitude taken by the directors at their annual meeting. I wish simply to quote one clause from the by-laws of this association. The gentlemen who control the Canadian Press took it upon themselves to define the business conditions and public service that should govern in the granting of a new franchise. They say that such application should not be granted " except under conditions which, in the opinion of the Board of Directors are essential to commercial success, and lacking which no real, adequate permanent and satisfactory service can be rendered to the country." Two cases occurred this year in which the question of granting a franchise arose. The first was in my home city of Windsor, and finally, after a writ had been issued, after these gentlemen were to be brought before a judge and jury, after the facts were to be disclosed to the public, the franchise in that city was granted. The next case occurred in Ottawa when these gentlemen took it upon themselves to say that because the franchise in this city was owned by three individuals they would not grant a franchise

to any other individual or company that desired to start a newspaper. These gentlemen have already received from the people of Canada the sum of $350,000. The government may feel that they are committed to the grant this year and perhaps it will be necessary in order to give these gentlemen a fair deal. This is a news gathering association. They gather the news at cost to themselves and they sell it at a tremendous profit to the public. For that reason I do not believe that the people of Canada should be asked to grant a subsidy year by year to this association. If the government feel it is necessary in order to be square with this association that the grant should be given this year, I am not going to say it should not be given, but I simply wish to point out that I do not believe the government, or parliament, or the people of this country, should be called upon to support what is really the creation of monopolies throughout this country. I will show how it works. I know of one company which owns a string of five franchises, and I know another which owns eight or ten franchises. In the province of Ontario when a man goes into a city and purchases two papers, he combines them into one; that gives him an absolute monopoly in that city, and the privilege of charging what he wishes for advertising and for subscriptions and it is a notice to the other newspaper men in this country that, for all time to come, no other paper can be established in that locality. It is absolutely an offence against British fair play and free speech. That 'has been carried to such an extent that an inside ring controls the Canadian press of this country. The great newspapers of Canada are not in accord with this monopoly, because when a writ was issued, and these people brought into court and were going to be placed in the position of being compelled to tell their sordid tale to a judge (and jury, the great newspaper owners were men enough to say " Grant this franchise." I do not know whether it was the fear of the law or the desire for fair play of the newspaper men that caused them to grant the franchise in my own city.

I am opposed to this subsidy, but in view of the fact that the government is going to grant it, I desire to say that I am informed that the association uses the Canadian Pacific Company as the means of its telegraph communication. Is there no way by which a large proportion of this sum might be used by our own telegraph system? The grant might be made subject to the use of the Canadian National lines.

Supply-Canadian Press

I do not believe we will
have a free press, if it is to be subsidized. There is a strong prejudice against this vote. There are many industries in Canada which have been driven to the wall and are not receiving help; but here is an industiy which is self sustaining and yet coming to parliament for a subsidy. The people of Canada are sick and tired of this organization receiving a subsidy. They have never made out a case for it and it is wrong in principle.

If the rules of this House
are carried out and the committee continues until 11 o'clock, and if no other member will take the floor between now and that hour I will attempt to occupy the time until then rather than submit to having this vote carried over my head. It is a wrong vote and never should have been authorized by the parliament of Canada. There never was any authority from the people of Canada to vote $50,000 to the subsidized press. There was never any authority for it from any government, let alone a Liberal government. I fought this matter when I was in opposition. I fought it in the country during my election, just as I have fought other things in my life, and I say it is not a Liberal principle. I want to tell the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister that Canada cannot afford to spend $50,000 of the people's money to subsidize the press, or to prostitute the news. This vote will defeat this government as it would defeat any government. We have voted many million dollars to-night, and every member of this government has attempted to justify the different expenditures; but not one has attempted to justify this expenditure. I ask the leader of the Government to try and justify this vote which is designed to prostitute the press of Canada. Can any minister defend it?

speechtext: Who made the demand on the government for this grant?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not seen any human being on the subject. I am speaking from my knowledge of the public service.

Would the minister be good enough to answer the request which I addressed to the Prime Minister, that is, whether or not the government will attach a string to this grant to see that the benefit of it accrues as far as possible to the Canadian National Railways?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not mean not to reply to my hon. friend. The government is not in a position to know at the present time what contracts the Canadian press
4V30
Supply-Canadian Press

has entered into for its communications. I cannot say at the moment whether my hon. friend's view is right or wrong that the Canadian press send their despatches over the Canadian Pacific line. I imagine that any arrangements they would have would be arrangements that would bind throughout the year. Under the circumstances I do not think the government would be justified in adopting the particular condition which my hon. friend suggests. Three months of the year have already gone by during which the Canadian press have had reason to believe that parliament would vote this amount. This js simply an obligation, perhaps not the most urgent in the world, but nevertheless one which the government should respect and having regard to the sum in the estimates, I think we should vote it at least for the present year.

If there is any obligation, certainly the government must meet its obligations. But as regards the Canadian National Railways receiving fair consideration, I would like the assurance of the minister that that would be taken into consideration now, and if the grant is continued next year that due consideration will be given.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have intimated that it is the intention of the government to discontinue this grant at the end of the year, not to renew it.

What is the information of this government with regard to this vote? When did it originate? I understand in 1917 there was a vote of $7,000 or $8,000 for the overseas service. In 1917, when many of us had to suffer in this country, my hon. friends who are now occupying the opposition benches voted $50,000 to the Canadian press. Eor what purpose? For the pure purpose of propaganda, against whom? Against the Liberal party and against the people of Quebec, against my province. There is no justification for this vote in past history. There never has been any justification for a vote of $50,000 of the money of the people of this Dominion to the Canadian press. It was promoted by the Union government in 1917 and they could, not justify the vote. I opposed it in 1917 and I have opposed it ever since. It has been proposed in this parliament from that time to this, and I think the government are making a great mistake to-day in again proposing it. They say that the vote has been going on for a few years. Is that any justification for the vote? Should the government not treat every estimate that comes before them on its merits? Should they not take the vote when it comes before them as a business proposition? No, they say that [Mr. Mackenzie King.l
this vote has been in the estimates for the last five, six or seven years, and they propose to pass it now because it has been in the estimates in the past. Who is asking for this vote? The government do not propose to tell me. They do not know who is asking for it. This vote of $50,000 for the Canadian press is being proposed without any justification on the part of the government. The Liberal party of Canada a few months ago asked the Canadian press for a franchise for a Liberal paper at Ottawa and they waved their hand at the Liberal party and said: "No, we do not propose to grant you a franchise; we are a law unto ourselves." They did not grant that franchise. It was intimated, I understand, to the Canadian press that this appropriation of $50,000 might not be voted, but they said: "Oh, I guess it will; it is all right: we will leave it at that." The $50,000 item was not proposed in the main estimates, but it came in the supplementaries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon. It is in the Main Estimates.
It is in the Main Estimates, but it was not proposed before now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It has been in the Main Estimates before the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This is two-thirds of $8,000 and two thirds of $50,000.
The Chairman of this committee should know better than to quibble about calling an item-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This item was called by me in the House one evening and was asked to stand.

This item was called for one-twelfth or one-sixth of the amount. It is well understood in this House that a proportion of a vote is not considered as a vote of the estimate. I told the leader of the Government that this was bad legislation and that I proposed to oppose it. I object to voting the money of the people of Canada and of the county of Pontiac to be given to the press that will not allow the establishment of free and independent newspapers throughout Canada. The press of this country should be as free as trade. You must have freedom or slavery. If you do not stand for the freedom of the press and freedom of speech, what do you stand for? You must have a free press and a free and a liberal government, or you have nothing.
Let us have a vote on it.

Hon. gentlemen spoke at great length last night on the freedom of

Supply-Canadian Press
Hindus, who are an infinitesimal proportion of the population of this country; but their freedom is of absolutely no account compared to the freedom of the press. If you are to be hobbled and bound by a press that is subsidized by the government to peddle news that is paid for you cannot be a free people. The leader of the Government knows that as well as I do. Let us get away from this bondage. Is the government afraid of the press of this country? If it is, I can tell the Prime Minister that the people are not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend and I talked this matter over and we know each other's mind fairly well, I think. It is not the intention of the government, I can assure my hon. friend, to renew the subsidy another year. The government has viewed the matter from all aspects in the endeavour to see that there is no injustice, or misunderstanding, or misrepresentation regarding its attitude, but we have thought it wrell to allow the vote to pass this year.
What justification is there for voting $50,000 of the people's money for this purpose?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is veo' much in the interests of the whole Dominion that the various parts of the country should be kept in touch with one another. This subsidy has been used to distribute news throughout Canada to a greater extent than would have been possible but for it, particularly in the West and in the Maritime provinces. We are informed, and I think reliably, that if the subsidy were cut off immediately the effect would be very injurious, not to the large newspapers but to the smaller ones which would not receive that amount of news, concerning various occurrences in different parts of the country, which in the interests of the people as a whole should be circulated. I think hon. members will agree to let the vote go through when they realize the loss that would be involved in its withdrawal.

I am informed by some of
the newspaper men of the country that the subsidy has not the effect which the Prime Minister suggests, of distributing news to the East and the West. In my opinion it is simply used as a threat to the smaller papers. The larger newspapers say, " If we do not get the subsidy we shall have to charge you a higher rate for the news service you get." I am also informed by people who I think are fairly conversant with the facts that the cost to the smaller newspapers would be a trifling matter, not more than $200 or $300 a year. This grant, or dole, or subsidy, has been opposed
by some of the newspapers of Canada for a great many years.

I wonder whether the government would consider the advisability of allowing this matter to stand until the next sitting of the House. It is getting so near the breakfast hour now that it might be well to postpone the matter until we meet again.
I am willing to allow it to go over until eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is a Supply Bill
to follow which it is absolutely necessary to get to the Senate. That Chamber is meeting at eleven o'clock, and, if I may be permitted the remark, I think the object in view is to dispose of Supply now.

There are no items in the Supply Bill except this one. All the other items of supply are in the Supplementary Estimates. I do not see any necessity for rushing this matter now; it could very welt stand over until eleven o'clock.
What would be gained?
That is for you to answer.

Then my answer is that
nothing would be gained.

My hon. friend is a poor
guesser.

It is not a guess, it is a
question of fact.

He has proved so in the
past and I should not be surprised if he were the same in the future.

Fortunately I know youi
judgment.
Just as I know your inclination.
What is it?
There is nothing to be lost to me in pressing this objection. I am speaking purely on principle.

Does the hon. member
want to keep the House sitting until eleven o'clock? If he does we are prepared to stay.

If the government is going to continue to vote money at this rate they will find themselves in a very difficult position. I have not heard any reason why this vote should be io the estimates. What is the benefit to the Canadian people? Is 't proposed to propagate the idea of the protected interests, of the financial interests of this country? I asked the late government
Supply-Canadian Press

how they justified a similar vote; they were not able to answer the question, and their failure to answer it was responsible to some extent for the result of the election of 1921. The people cannot afford to subsidize a press in order that they may be fed with the kind of news that the interests of this country wish them to be provided with. It is not legitimate; it is not Canadian; it is not free; it certainly is not Liberal. Every item of the estimates that has been voted, with the exception of this vote to the Canadian press, has had some justification and has been accompanied by some reasonable explanation. But. this item should not be in the estimates. It should not have been voted in 1917. It should not have been voted in 1918, and I opposed it. It should not have been voted in 1919, and I opposed it, as members of the Liberal party did. It should not have been voted in 1920, 1921, and in 1922, and there is no justification for its appearance this year. The people of Canada are suffering from excessive taxation, from business depression, and from bad conditions generally, and they are not prepared to sanction additional taxation for the benefit of the newspaper publishers of this country. They are willing to bear the burden of taxation provided that the purposes of that taxation are legitimate. They felt that the Liberal party would, when they came into power in 1921, give them a new deal, give them less taxation, bring about better conditions, and they are still hopeful that conditions will be better. But with the present newspaper propaganda they are beginning to doubt, and that doubt is increased when they are asked by this vote to contribute $50,000 to the Canadian Press. I think the government should leave this matter over till eleven o'clock and reconsider it, and give this House some reason why this vote should be continued. If the elimination of this vote would work a hardship on the smaller papers I think the Minister of Finance should tell the House just how they would be affected, and how it would affect the dissemination of news between the East and the West and as between the different provinces. If the government wishes to give us this information as to the news service that is to be distributed among the different provinces I am quite prepared to hear their representations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think all the members of the House are anxious that we should prorogue to-day, and as there are still some measures on the order paper that have not been disposed of and which it is important should get over to the Senate as soon as the 	j

And where the person accused is a person duly licensed by the Government of Canada to carry on the business or trade of a distiller, the burden shall also be on him of proving that all intoxicating liquor imported by him is imported solely for the purpose of being used for blending with or flavouring the products of the business or trade of a distiller carried on by him in the province and that all intoxicating liquor

Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 203 to amend the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act.
He said: In connection with the three bills passed by this House relating to returned soldiers, that to amend the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act is not so long and not so important as that relating to the Pension Act. The Senate has made several amendments to this bill, but they are of the same nature as applied to the three different bills. The intention of the original bill was that in cases where the insurance policies had been refused for certain reasons and on account of certain regulations, the policies should now be issued without any question. The bill was prepared with that end in view. The Senate provides in the amendment to the preamble that only those soldiers with actual dependents may have their policies revived; and only in the case of deceased men having, at the time of their death, actual dependents can the benefit of insurance be availed of. When the amendment to the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act was under consideration in the House last year, some restrictions were provided for in the schedule which was attached to the act. On that occasion the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) moved that all applicants for insurance before the 1st January, 1903; having dependents should not be subjected to the schedule attached to the act. Originally the insurance was available to every returned soldier; but the main object was to provide insurance for the dependents of returned soldiers, and the same clauses of the original act, if they are perused, will tend to reveal that that was the spirit that permeated the

House at the time of the passing of the original measure. I think, as only 71 cases are involved, and as the majority of them had dependents when they died w*e can concur in the Senate amendments. I will therefore move accordingly.

It seems very regrettable that we should be called upon to pass this legislation at this hour of the morning and at this stage of the session. Asking the House to pass upon these amendments to the Insurance Bill is really not giving the members of the House, the people of the country and the returned men as a whole, the fair chance they should have. After one solid year's consideration of this question by a commission appointed by this government, this bill with others has been passed. Now it is returned to us in its present shape; and it does not seem right that we should be asked to pass it before we really have a knowledge of it. I do not wish to obstruct any legislation, but I desire to place my own personal views upon record in connection with the manner in which this legislation has been returned to us and the reasons given for it. It is a well known fact that these amendments have been made on account of the increased cost of administration and other reasons. I have not hesitated to attend the sessions of the committee and devoted my time to the consideration of these matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: There is no desire to press for the passing of the amendment before the House. The most important bill by far is the Pension Act, but I have no objection to postpone the consideration of the amendment until the next sitting of the House at 11 o'clock.

I was prefacing my remarks in a general way, in order to cover the three bills at once, perhaps extending over a little wider area than the insurance question. I do not wish it to be inferred that this legislation is being hurried through in any way; but I think adequate time should be given to this legislation. Whatever action this House takes, I wish it to be made clear in every way that I feel that I cannot concur in the changes which have been made. I simply wish now to cover, in a brief manner, some of my objections to this bill, and perhaps at the same time cover the amendments to the Pension Act. The principal reason, as I have gathered, for the changes which have been proposed is the expense of the administration, particularly in regard to the Insurance Act. After the country has gone to the expense of appointing a royal commission which went into the matter thoroughly and brought reports to this House,.

it is only fair that members of the House should stand firm, and insist upon passing the bills as they left the House of Commons. Although we are in the dying days of the session, if it is necessary to stay another week or month I am quite prepared to remain in order to see that legislation which will be to the advantage of the returned soldier is enacted.
I have followed with great interest the discussion during the night, and have noticed how the government, with the sanction of the House, have approved money grants, which probably are justified, for celebrations and monuments. I wish to assure hon. members this morning that there are throughout the Dominion of Canada to-day many walking monuments without any provision. I wish again to assure hon. members that the only way the returned men throughout the country have of presenting the different cases and of asking what they consider is within their rights, is through their united efforts and their organized method of procedure. I feel sure that the changes that are now taking place in the Insurance bill, the Pension bill, and the Re-establishment bill will not meet with the approval of this country, and this is going to continue in every way the dissatisfaction that at present exists. I am well aware of the attitude assumed by the present government and of the attitude assumed by the minister. I am well aware of the opposition with which they have met. On the other hand, while I hesitate delaying this legislation, I feel so keenly on the subject that I wish to place on record my views on this legislation, the changes that have taken place regarding the Insurance Act, and in respect to other changes that have taken place contrary to the findings of the royal commission and contrary to the sanction of this House of Commons. I do not wish to be a party to those changes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is desirable that there should be ample opportunity to discuss the changes made by the Senate to this legislation, and for that reason I think it would be advisable if we postpone further discussion at the present time and take the matter up at the next sitting of the House.

I quite agree with my right hon. friend's suggestion, but it is also of importance that we get something; that the legislation ought not to be wasted in any way. I would assume the House would appoint managers to go into conference with the Senate, and we should make that provision at the earliest possible moment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I move that the debate be adjourned.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It will take
some little time to have concurrence to Supply moved and I think that if possible we should immediately complete the voting of the Supply. I therefore suggest that the House return to Supply.
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Canadian Press, Limited-Canadian telegraph service, $50,000.
Canadian Press, Limited-British cable service, $8,000. Items agreed to.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to ask the consent of the House to motions for concurrence. I beg to move the following resolution:
Resolved, that two-thirds of the amount of the resolutions reported from Committee of Supply from the 20th February last to the 20th March last, inclusive, forming a total of $33,540,785.30; and two-thirds of the amount of resolutions reported from Committee of Supply from the 27th March last to the 8th June last, inclusive, forming a total of $103,857,326.70; and two-thirds of the amount of the resolutions reported from Committee of Supply from the 11th J line instant to the 29th June instant, inclusive, and forming a total of $41,477,010.06; granting to His Majesty amounts voted of the Main Estimates, be now concurred in.
Motion agreed to, and resolution concurred in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to move the following resolution:
Resolved, that two-thirds of the amount of the resolution reported from Committee of Supply on the 13th April, 1923, providing provisional bonus allowance for the Inside and Outside Services of the Civil Service for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1924, and forming a total of $3,666,666.67 be now concurred in.
Motion agreed to, and resolutions concurred in.
On motion of Mr. Fielding the House went into Committee of Ways and Means, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Resolved, that towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty on account of certain expenses of the public service for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1924, the sum of $196,870,229.79 be granted out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Resolved, that towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty on account of certain expenses of the public service for the financial year ending 31st March, 1923, the sum of $18,202,105.66 be granted out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.

Motion agreed to.
Redistribution

Resolutions reported and concurred in. Mr. Fielding thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 252 for granting to His Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the fiscal years ending respectively March 31, 1923, and March 31, 1924.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first and second time, considered in committee, reported, read the third time and passed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their honours that this House doth agree to their address to His Excellency the Governor General respectfully requesting that His Excellency will be pleased to transmit our joint resolution that parliament do approve of the treaty between His Majesty and the United States of America providing effective measures for the preservation of the halibut fishery of the northern Pacific ocean, which was signed at Washington on the 2nd day of March, 1923, a copy of which has been laid before parliament and which was signed on behalf of His Majesty acting for Canada by the plenipotentiary therein named, by filling up the blank therein with the words " and Commons
Motion agreed to.

Hon. A. B. COPP (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 190 to amend the Companies Act.
Motion agreed to; amendments read the second time and concurred in.

Mr. MACKENZIE KING moved the adjournment of the House.
He said: The House reassembles at eleven o'clock. I think the Government is fairly safe in assuming that it will be possible to arrange prorogation for three o'clock in the afternoon. It is impossible to fix the time definitely, because there is no telling what debate we may have after we assemble at eleven o'clock. There are one or two matters to be taken up, but for the time being we might assume that prorogation will be at three.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 7.55 a.m. (Saturday).
Saturday, June 30, 1923.
